2025.text: Consider the set [latex]S[/latex] of points [latex](x, y) \in  \mathfrak{R}^2[/latex] which minimize the real-valued function [latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex] Which of the following statements is true about the set [latex]S[/latex]?
2025.html:
Consider the set [latex]S[/latex] of points [latex](x, y) \in \mathfrak{R}^2[/latex] which minimize the real-valued function

[latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex]

Which of the following statements is true about the set [latex]S[/latex]?
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2025.explanation_text: We are given: [latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex] Step 1: Substitute a single variable Let [latex]u = x + y[/latex] Then, the function becomes: [latex]f(x, y) = (u - 1)^2 + u^2 = u^2 - 2u + 1 + u^2 = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex] Step 2: Minimize [latex]f(u) = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex] This is a quadratic function in [latex]u[/latex] with a positive coefficient, so it has a unique minimum. The minimum occurs at: [latex]u = \frac{-(-2)}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] So, the function is minimized when [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] Step 3: Analyze the set [latex]S[/latex] All points [latex](x, y)[/latex] satisfying [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] will minimize [latex]f(x, y)[/latex]. There are infinitely many such points in [latex]\mathbb{R}^2[/latex]. Final Answer: [latex]\boxed{\text{The number of elements in the set } S \text{ is infinite}}[/latex] Correct Option: (B)
2025.explanation_html:
We are given:
[latex]f(x, y) = (x + y - 1)^2 + (x + y)^2[/latex]

Step 1: Substitute a single variable
Let [latex]u = x + y[/latex]
Then, the function becomes:
[latex]f(x, y) = (u - 1)^2 + u^2 = u^2 - 2u + 1 + u^2 = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex]

Step 2: Minimize [latex]f(u) = 2u^2 - 2u + 1[/latex]
This is a quadratic function in [latex]u[/latex] with a positive coefficient, so it has a unique minimum.
The minimum occurs at:
[latex]u = \frac{-(-2)}{2 \cdot 2} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]

So, the function is minimized when [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]

Step 3: Analyze the set [latex]S[/latex]
All points [latex](x, y)[/latex] satisfying [latex]x + y = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] will minimize [latex]f(x, y)[/latex].
There are infinitely many such points in [latex]\mathbb{R}^2[/latex].

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\text{The number of elements in the set } S \text{ is infinite}}[/latex]
Correct Option: (B)

From the given: [latex] P(X=1, Y=0) = \frac{1}{8}, \quad P(X=1, Y=1) = \frac{1}{8} [/latex] So, total probability [latex] P(X=1) = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{4} [/latex] Step 2: Compute the conditional probabilities: [latex] P(Y=0 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=0)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex] [latex] P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=1)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex] Step 3: Compute the expected value: [latex] \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=1] = 0 \cdot P(Y=0 \mid X=1) + 1 \cdot P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex] Final Answer: (B) [latex] \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

So, total probability [latex] P(X=1) = \frac{1}{8} + \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{4} [/latex]

Step 2: Compute the conditional probabilities:
[latex] P(Y=0 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=0)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]
[latex] P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = \frac{P(X=1, Y=1)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}}{\frac{1}{4}} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Step 3: Compute the expected value:
[latex] \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=1] = 0 \cdot P(Y=0 \mid X=1) + 1 \cdot P(Y=1 \mid X=1) = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Final Answer: (B) [latex] \frac{1}{2} [/latex]

Outside this interval, [latex]x(t) = 0[/latex]. Also given: We are to compute the value of the integral: [latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) \delta(\mathrm{t}+3) , \mathrm{dt}[/latex] Step 1: Use the sifting property of the delta function: [latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \delta(t - t_0) , dt = f(t_0)[/latex] Similarly, [latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \delta(t + 3) , dt = f(-3)[/latex] Step 2: Evaluate [latex]x(-3)[/latex] [latex]x(t) = -t^2 {u(t+4) - u(t-4)}[/latex] At [latex]t = -3[/latex], [latex]u(-3 + 4) = u(1) = 1[/latex] and [latex]u(-3 - 4) = u(-7) = 0[/latex] So, [latex]x(-3) = -(-3)^2 (1 - 0) = -9[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) \delta(\mathrm{t}+3) , \mathrm{dt} = x(-3) = -9[/latex]

[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) \delta(\mathrm{t}+3) , \mathrm{dt}[/latex]

[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \delta(t - t_0) , dt = f(t_0)[/latex]
Similarly,
[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \delta(t + 3) , dt = f(-3)[/latex]

At [latex]t = -3[/latex],
[latex]u(-3 + 4) = u(1) = 1[/latex] and [latex]u(-3 - 4) = u(-7) = 0[/latex]
So,
[latex]x(-3) = -(-3)^2 (1 - 0) = -9[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathrm{x}(\mathrm{t}) \delta(\mathrm{t}+3) , \mathrm{dt} = x(-3) = -9[/latex]

2025.text: Instrument(s) required to synchronize an alternator to the grid is/are
2025.html: Instrument(s) required to synchronize an alternator to the grid is/are
2025.subject: Electrical Machines - Synchronous Machines
2025.explanation_text:
To synchronize an alternator with the grid, the following conditions must be satisfied: The terminal voltage of the alternator should match the grid voltage. The frequency of the alternator must be equal to the grid frequency. The phase sequence should be identical. The phase angle difference should be nearly zero at the instant of synchronization. Instruments used to verify these conditions are: (A) Voltmeter:
Used to ensure the voltage of the alternator matches the grid voltage. (B) Wattmeter:
Measures power; not used for synchronization. (C) Synchroscope:
Used to indicate the phase angle and frequency difference between the alternator and the grid. It shows whether the alternator is running fast or slow and when to close the circuit breaker. (D) Stroboscope:
Used to measure rotational speed visually; not used in electrical synchronization.

Instruments used to verify these conditions are:

(C) Synchroscope: Used to indicate the phase angle and frequency difference between the alternator and the grid. It shows whether the alternator is running fast or slow and when to close the circuit breaker.

2025.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Series
2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Find the period [latex]T[/latex] The signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] consists of cosine terms with frequencies [latex]2\pi, 4\pi, 6\pi[/latex], which correspond to fundamental frequencies [latex]1 , \text{Hz}, 2 , \text{Hz}, 3 , \text{Hz}[/latex]. The period of the signal [latex]T[/latex] is the least common multiple (LCM) of the periods of these individual cosine terms. The period of [latex]2\pi t[/latex] (1 Hz) is [latex]T_1 = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex]. The period of [latex]4\pi t[/latex] (2 Hz) is [latex]T_2 = 0.5 , \text{sec}[/latex]. The period of [latex]6\pi t[/latex] (3 Hz) is [latex]T_3 = \frac{1}{3} , \text{sec}[/latex]. The LCM of [latex]T_1, T_2, T_3[/latex] is [latex]T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex]. Step 2: Calculate [latex] |x(t)|^2 [/latex] The signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] is real, so we can calculate [latex]|x(t)|^2[/latex] directly: [latex]|x(t)|^2 = (1 + 2 \cos(2\pi t) + 2 \cos(4\pi t) + 2 \cos(6\pi t))^2[/latex] Expanding the square: [latex]|x(t)|^2 = 1 + 4 \cos(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(4\pi t) + 4 \cos(6\pi t) + 4 \cos^2(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) + \ldots[/latex] Step 3: Integrate over one period We now need to compute the integral of [latex]|x(t)|^2[/latex] over one period [latex]T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex]. Many of the cross-term integrals, like [latex]\int_0^T \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) dt[/latex], will be zero due to the orthogonality property of the cosine functions. For the terms that do not vanish: [latex] \int_0^T 1 , dt = T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex] [latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(2\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2} T = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] (using the identity [latex]\cos^2(x) = \frac{1 + \cos(2x)}{2}[/latex]) Similarly, [latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(4\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] and [latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(6\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}[/latex]. Step 4: Sum up the integrals After evaluating the integrals and summing them up, the result of the integral is: [latex] \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = 1 + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7[/latex]. Step 5: Compute the final result Now, we divide by the period [latex]T = 1] sec: [latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = \frac{7}{1} = 7[/latex]. Final Answer: The value of [latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt[/latex] is closest to 7.
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Find the period [latex]T[/latex]
The signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] consists of cosine terms with frequencies [latex]2\pi, 4\pi, 6\pi[/latex], which correspond to fundamental frequencies [latex]1 , \text{Hz}, 2 , \text{Hz}, 3 , \text{Hz}[/latex]. The period of the signal [latex]T[/latex] is the least common multiple (LCM) of the periods of these individual cosine terms.

The period of [latex]2\pi t[/latex] (1 Hz) is [latex]T_1 = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex].
The period of [latex]4\pi t[/latex] (2 Hz) is [latex]T_2 = 0.5 , \text{sec}[/latex].
The period of [latex]6\pi t[/latex] (3 Hz) is [latex]T_3 = \frac{1}{3} , \text{sec}[/latex].
The LCM of [latex]T_1, T_2, T_3[/latex] is [latex]T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex].

Step 2: Calculate [latex] |x(t)|^2 [/latex]
The signal [latex]x(t)[/latex] is real, so we can calculate [latex]|x(t)|^2[/latex] directly:
[latex]|x(t)|^2 = (1 + 2 \cos(2\pi t) + 2 \cos(4\pi t) + 2 \cos(6\pi t))^2[/latex]
Expanding the square:
[latex]|x(t)|^2 = 1 + 4 \cos(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(4\pi t) + 4 \cos(6\pi t) + 4 \cos^2(2\pi t) + 4 \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) + \ldots[/latex]
Step 3: Integrate over one period
We now need to compute the integral of [latex]|x(t)|^2[/latex] over one period [latex]T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex]. Many of the cross-term integrals, like [latex]\int_0^T \cos(2\pi t) \cos(4\pi t) dt[/latex], will be zero due to the orthogonality property of the cosine functions.
For the terms that do not vanish:
[latex] \int_0^T 1 , dt = T = 1 , \text{sec}[/latex]

[latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(2\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2} T = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] (using the identity [latex]\cos^2(x) = \frac{1 + \cos(2x)}{2}[/latex])

Similarly, [latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(4\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}[/latex] and [latex] \int_0^T \cos^2(6\pi t) , dt = \frac{1}{2}[/latex].

Step 4: Sum up the integrals
After evaluating the integrals and summing them up, the result of the integral is:
[latex] \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = 1 + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} + 4 \times \frac{1}{2} = 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 7[/latex].

Step 5: Compute the final result
Now, we divide by the period [latex]T = 1] sec:
[latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt = \frac{7}{1} = 7[/latex].

Final Answer:
The value of [latex]\frac{1}{T} \int_0^T |x(t)|^2 , dt[/latex] is closest to 7.

2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Given: [latex] Y = X^2 [/latex], and [latex] X \in (0, 1] [/latex] with uniform distribution: [latex] P_X(x) = 1 [/latex] for [latex] x \in (0, 1] [/latex] Step 2: Use the change of variable technique for continuous random variables. If [latex] Y = g(X) = X^2 [/latex], then [latex] X = \sqrt{Y} [/latex] (since [latex] X > 0 [/latex]), and the PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is: [latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(x) \cdot \left| \frac{dx}{dy} \right| [/latex] We know [latex] x = \sqrt{y} [/latex], so: [latex] \frac{dx}{dy} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex] Therefore: [latex] P_Y(y) = P_X(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \left| \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \right| = 1 \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex] Step 3: So the correct PDF of [latex] Y [/latex] is: [latex] P_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, & y \in (0, 1] \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} [/latex] Final Answer: (A) [latex] \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} [/latex], for [latex] y \in (0, 1] [/latex]

2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Open-loop transfer function: [latex] G(s) = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex], So the forward path becomes: [latex] K(s-1)G(s) = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex] Step 2: Closed-loop transfer function (unity feedback): [latex] T(s) = \frac{K(s-1)G(s)}{1 + K(s-1)G(s)} = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2) + K(s-1)} [/latex] Step 3: Characteristic equation: [latex] (s+1)(s+2) + K(s-1) = 0 [/latex] Compute: [latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 + K(s - 1) = 0 [/latex] [latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 + Ks - K = 0 [/latex] [latex] s^2 + (3 + K)s + (2 - K) = 0 [/latex] Step 4: Apply Routh-Hurwitz criterion: For a second-order system [latex] s^2 + a_1 s + a_0 [/latex] to be stable, both coefficients must be positive: [latex] a_1 = 3 + K > 0 \Rightarrow \text{always true for } K > -3 [/latex] [latex] a_0 = 2 - K > 0 \Rightarrow K < 2 [/latex] So the system is stable for [latex] K < 2 [/latex], and unstable for [latex] K \geq 2 [/latex]. Final Answer: (B) unstable for all [latex] K \geq 2 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Open-loop transfer function:
[latex] G(s) = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex],
So the forward path becomes:
[latex] K(s-1)G(s) = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2)} [/latex]

Step 2: Closed-loop transfer function (unity feedback):
[latex] T(s) = \frac{K(s-1)G(s)}{1 + K(s-1)G(s)} = \frac{K(s-1)}{(s+1)(s+2) + K(s-1)} [/latex]

Step 3: Characteristic equation:
[latex] (s+1)(s+2) + K(s-1) = 0 [/latex]
Compute:
[latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 + K(s - 1) = 0 [/latex]
[latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 + Ks - K = 0 [/latex]
[latex] s^2 + (3 + K)s + (2 - K) = 0 [/latex]

Step 4: Apply Routh-Hurwitz criterion:
For a second-order system [latex] s^2 + a_1 s + a_0 [/latex] to be stable, both coefficients must be positive:
[latex] a_1 = 3 + K > 0 \Rightarrow \text{always true for } K > -3 [/latex]
[latex] a_0 = 2 - K > 0 \Rightarrow K < 2 [/latex]

So the system is stable for [latex] K < 2 [/latex], and unstable for [latex] K \geq 2 [/latex].

Final Answer: (B) unstable for all [latex] K \geq 2 [/latex]

2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Capacitance of a cylindrical capacitor
The capacitance of a coaxial cylindrical capacitor filled with dielectric of permittivity [latex] \varepsilon [/latex] is given by:
[latex] C = \frac{2\pi \varepsilon L}{\ln(b/a)} [/latex]
So, for Fig. (i) with air throughout (i.e., permittivity [latex] \varepsilon_0 [/latex]):
[latex] C_0 = \frac{2\pi \varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(b/a)} [/latex]

Step 2: For Fig. (ii)
The cross-section is split into two equal parts (in parallel):
One half is filled with air [latex] \varepsilon_0 [/latex]
The other half is filled with dielectric [latex] \varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0 [/latex]

Since they are in parallel, total capacitance is:
[latex] C = \frac{1}{2} C_0 + \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_r C_0 = \frac{C_0}{2}(1 + \varepsilon_r) [/latex]

We are given that [latex] C = 5C_0 [/latex]. So:
[latex] \frac{C_0}{2}(1 + \varepsilon_r) = 5C_0 [/latex]
Divide both sides by [latex] C_0 [/latex]:
[latex] \frac{1 + \varepsilon_r}{2} = 5 [/latex]
[latex] 1 + \varepsilon_r = 10 \Rightarrow \varepsilon_r = 9 [/latex]

Final Answer: (C) 9

2025.text: Let [latex]{a}_{{R}}[/latex] be the unit radial vector in the spherical co-ordinate system. For which of the following value(s) of [latex]n[/latex], the divergence of the radial vector field [latex]f(R)=a_{R} \frac{1}{R^{n}}[/latex] is independent of [latex]R[/latex] ?
2025.html: Let [latex]{a}_{{R}}[/latex] be the unit radial vector in the spherical co-ordinate system. For which of the following value(s) of [latex]n[/latex], the divergence of the radial vector field [latex]f(R)=a_{R} \frac{1}{R^{n}}[/latex] is independent of [latex]R[/latex] ?
2025.subject: Electromagnetic Theory - Coordinate Systems and Vector Calculus
2025.explanation_text:
We use the divergence formula for a purely radial vector field in spherical coordinates: [latex]
\nabla \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R^n} \mathbf{a}_R \right)
= \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^2 \cdot \frac{1}{R^n} \right)
= \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^{2-n} \right)
= \frac{1}{R^2} \cdot (2 - n) R^{1 - n}
= (2 - n) R^{-1 - n}
[/latex] We want this expression to be independent of [latex] R [/latex], so the power of [latex] R [/latex] must be zero: [latex]
-1 - n = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = -1
[/latex] So clearly [latex] n = -1 [/latex] is one valid value. Now check another special case: Case: [latex] n = 2 [/latex] Try plugging [latex] n = 2 [/latex] directly into the divergence expression: [latex]
\nabla \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R^2} \mathbf{a}_R \right)
= \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^2 \cdot \frac{1}{R^2} \right)
= \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} (1) = 0
[/latex] So the divergence is zero, which is also independent of [latex] R [/latex].
2025.explanation_html:
We use the divergence formula for a purely radial vector field in spherical coordinates:

[latex] \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R^n} \mathbf{a}_R \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^2 \cdot \frac{1}{R^n} \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^{2-n} \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \cdot (2 - n) R^{1 - n} = (2 - n) R^{-1 - n} [/latex]

We want this expression to be independent of [latex] R [/latex], so the power of [latex] R [/latex] must be zero:
[latex] -1 - n = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n = -1 [/latex]

So clearly [latex] n = -1 [/latex] is one valid value. Now check another special case:

Case: [latex] n = 2 [/latex]
Try plugging [latex] n = 2 [/latex] directly into the divergence expression:
[latex] \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{1}{R^2} \mathbf{a}_R \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} \left( R^2 \cdot \frac{1}{R^2} \right) = \frac{1}{R^2} \frac{d}{dR} (1) = 0 [/latex]

So the divergence is zero, which is also independent of [latex] R [/latex].

[Based on given options it has to be mutally adding only]

Now put both condition's together only [latex]\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{s}}[/latex] is minimum,

2025.html:
Let [latex](\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y}) \in \mathfrak{R}^{2}[/latex]. The rate of change of the real valued function,

[latex]\mathrm{V}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})=\mathrm{x}^{2}+\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}^{2}+1[/latex]

at the origin in the direction of the point [latex](1,2)[/latex] is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2025.explanation_text:
Step 1: Direction vector and its unit vector The direction vector from origin to point (1, 2) is: [latex] \vec{u} = \langle 1, 2 angle [/latex] Magnitude of this vector is: [latex] |\vec{u}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5} [/latex] Unit vector in the given direction is: [latex] \hat{u} = \left\langle  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}},  rac{2}{\sqrt{5}} ightangle [/latex] Step 2: Compute the gradient of V(x, y) [latex] 
abla V = \left\langle  rac{\partial V}{\partial x},  rac{\partial V}{\partial y} ightangle = \left\langle 2x + 1, 2y ightangle [/latex] At the origin (0, 0), the gradient becomes: [latex] 
abla V(0, 0) = \langle 1, 0 angle [/latex] Step 3: Compute the directional derivative Directional derivative of V in the direction of unit vector [latex] \hat{u} [/latex] is: [latex] D_{\hat{u}} V = 
abla V \cdot \hat{u} = \langle 1, 0 angle \cdot \left\langle  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}},  rac{2}{\sqrt{5}} ightangle =  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}} [/latex] Numerical value: [latex]  rac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \approx  rac{1}{2.236} \approx 0.447 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Direction vector and its unit vector
The direction vector from origin to point (1, 2) is:
[latex] \vec{u} = \langle 1, 2 \rangle [/latex]
Magnitude of this vector is:
[latex] |\vec{u}| = \sqrt{1^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5} [/latex]
Unit vector in the given direction is:
[latex] \hat{u} = \left\langle \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \right\rangle [/latex]

Step 2: Compute the gradient of V(x, y)
[latex] \nabla V = \left\langle \frac{\partial V}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} \right\rangle = \left\langle 2x + 1, 2y \right\rangle [/latex]
At the origin (0, 0), the gradient becomes:
[latex] \nabla V(0, 0) = \langle 1, 0 \rangle [/latex]

Step 3: Compute the directional derivative
Directional derivative of V in the direction of unit vector [latex] \hat{u} [/latex] is:
[latex] D_{\hat{u}} V = \nabla V \cdot \hat{u} = \langle 1, 0 \rangle \cdot \left\langle \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} [/latex]
Numerical value:
[latex] \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \approx \frac{1}{2.236} \approx 0.447 [/latex]

[/latex] Given [latex]{x}_{1}(0)=1:(4) \Rightarrow 1=0+{K}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow {K}=1[/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] From (4) [latex]{x}_{1}={t}^{2}+1[/latex] Now [latex]{X}_{1}(1)=1+1=2[/latex]

[latex]\Rightarrow \frac{{dx}_{2}}{{dt}}=1[/latex] for [latex]{t} \geq 0 \quad ...(2)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow {x}_{2}={t}+{c} \quad ...(3)[/latex]

[latex]\therefore[/latex] From (4) [latex]{x}_{1}={t}^{2}+1[/latex]

2025.text: Let [latex]C[/latex] be a clockwise oriented closed curve in the complex plane defined by [latex]|z|=1[/latex]. Further, let [latex]f(z)=j z[/latex] be a complex function, where [latex]j=\sqrt{-1}[/latex]. Then, [latex]\oint_{{C}} {f}({z}) {dz}=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.html:
Let [latex]C[/latex] be a clockwise oriented closed curve in the complex plane defined by [latex]|z|=1[/latex]. Further, let [latex]f(z)=j z[/latex] be a complex function, where [latex]j=\sqrt{-1}[/latex].
Then, [latex]\oint_{{C}} {f}({z}) {dz}=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Express the function We are given [latex] f(z) = jz [/latex], and we want to compute: [latex] \oint_C jz , dz [/latex] Step 2: Use properties of contour integrals [latex] j = \sqrt{-1} [/latex] is a constant, so it can be pulled out of the integral: [latex] \oint_C jz , dz = j \oint_C z , dz [/latex] Step 3: Recall the standard result For a closed contour [latex] C [/latex] enclosing the origin (like [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex]), [latex] \oint_C z , dz = 0 [/latex] because [latex] z [/latex] is an analytic function inside and on [latex] C [/latex]. Step 4: Apply the result [latex] \oint_C f(z) , dz = j \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Express the function
We are given [latex] f(z) = jz [/latex], and we want to compute:
[latex] \oint_C jz , dz [/latex]

Step 2: Use properties of contour integrals
[latex] j = \sqrt{-1} [/latex] is a constant, so it can be pulled out of the integral:
[latex] \oint_C jz , dz = j \oint_C z , dz [/latex]

Step 3: Recall the standard result
For a closed contour [latex] C [/latex] enclosing the origin (like [latex] |z| = 1 [/latex]),
[latex] \oint_C z , dz = 0 [/latex] because [latex] z [/latex] is an analytic function inside and on [latex] C [/latex].

Step 4: Apply the result
[latex] \oint_C f(z) , dz = j \cdot 0 = 0 [/latex]

2025.text: The op-amps in the following circuit are ideal. The voltage gain of the circuit is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.html: The op-amps in the following circuit are ideal. The voltage gain of the circuit is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.subject: Analog Electronics - Operational Amplifiers
2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Recognize the configuration The circuit consists of two inverting amplifier stages connected in cascade. Step 2: Analyze the first op-amp For an inverting amplifier, the gain is: [latex] A_{v1} = -\frac{R_f}{R_{in}} [/latex] From the diagram: Input resistor: [latex] R_{in1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex] Feedback resistor: [latex] R_{f1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex] So, [latex] A_{v1} = -\frac{10}{10} = -1 [/latex] Step 3: Analyze the second op-amp This stage is also an inverting amplifier: Input resistor: [latex] R_{in2} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex] Feedback resistor: [latex] R_{f2} = 20\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex] (notice the input is tapped from the junction between two 10 kΩ resistors in series, so it's effectively 10 kΩ from input and 10 kΩ in feedback, making total feedback resistance = 10k + 10k = 20k) So, [latex] A_{v2} = -\frac{20}{10} = -2 [/latex] Step 4: Total Gain Overall voltage gain is: [latex] A_v = A_{v1} \cdot A_{v2} = (-1) \cdot (-2) = 2 [/latex] Final Answer: 2
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Recognize the configuration
The circuit consists of two inverting amplifier stages connected in cascade.
Step 2: Analyze the first op-amp
For an inverting amplifier, the gain is:
[latex] A_{v1} = -\frac{R_f}{R_{in}} [/latex]
From the diagram:
Input resistor: [latex] R_{in1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex]
Feedback resistor: [latex] R_{f1} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex]
So,
[latex] A_{v1} = -\frac{10}{10} = -1 [/latex]
Step 3: Analyze the second op-amp
This stage is also an inverting amplifier:
Input resistor: [latex] R_{in2} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex]
Feedback resistor: [latex] R_{f2} = 20\ \text{k}\Omega [/latex] (notice the input is tapped from the junction between two 10 kΩ resistors in series, so it's effectively 10 kΩ from input and 10 kΩ in feedback, making total feedback resistance = 10k + 10k = 20k)
So,
[latex] A_{v2} = -\frac{20}{10} = -2 [/latex]
Step 4: Total Gain
Overall voltage gain is:
[latex] A_v = A_{v1} \cdot A_{v2} = (-1) \cdot (-2) = 2 [/latex]
Final Answer: 2

2025.text:
An ideal low pass filter has frequency response given by [latex]
H(j \omega)= \begin{cases}1, & |\omega| \leq 200 \pi \\ 0, & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
[/latex] Let [latex]h(t)[/latex] be its time domain representation. Then 
[latex]h(0)=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.html:
An ideal low pass filter has frequency response given by

[latex] H(j \omega)= \begin{cases}1, & |\omega| \leq 200 \pi \\ 0, & \text { otherwise }\end{cases} [/latex]

Let [latex]h(t)[/latex] be its time domain representation. Then [latex]h(0)=[/latex] ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Transform
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Frequency response
[latex] H(j\omega) = \begin{cases} 1, & |\omega| \leq 200\pi \ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} [/latex]
Step 2: Find impulse response [latex] h(t) [/latex] by inverse Fourier transform
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} H(j\omega) e^{j\omega t} d\omega [/latex]
But since [latex] H(j\omega) = 1 [/latex] for [latex] |\omega| \leq 200\pi [/latex], and 0 otherwise:
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-200\pi}^{200\pi} e^{j\omega t} d\omega [/latex]
Step 3: Evaluate the integral
This is a standard Fourier inverse transform result:
[latex] h(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \cdot \frac{2 \sin(200\pi t)}{t} = \frac{200 \sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t} [/latex]
This is the sinc function scaled:
[latex] h(t) = 200 \cdot \text{sinc}(200 t) [/latex] where [latex] \text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin(\pi x)}{\pi x} [/latex]
Step 4: Find [latex] h(0) [/latex]
Use the standard limit:
[latex] \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{\sin(200\pi t)}{\pi t} = 200 [/latex]
So:
[latex] h(0) = \frac{200 \sin(0)}{\pi \cdot 0} = 200 [/latex]
Final Answer: 200

2025.html:
Consider the state-space model

[latex] \begin{aligned} \dot{x}({t}) & ={Ax}({t})+{Br}({t}) \\ {y}({t}) & ={Cx}({t}) \end{aligned} [/latex]

Where [latex]{x}({t}), {r}({t}), {y}({t})[/latex] are the state, input and output, respectively. The matrices [latex]{A}, {B}, {C}[/latex] are given below

[latex] A=\left[\begin{array}{cc} 0 & 1 \\ -2 & -3 \end{array}\right], {B}=\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right], {C}=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \end{array}\right] [/latex]

The sum of the magnitudes of the poles is ________ (round off to nearest integer).
2025.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Write the state matrix [latex] A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] Step 2: Find the characteristic equation We compute the determinant of [latex] sI - A [/latex]: [latex] \det(sI - A) = \left| \begin{array}{cc} s & -1 \ 2 & s + 3 \end{array} \right| = s(s + 3) - (-2)(1) = s^2 + 3s + 2 [/latex] Step 3: Find the roots of the characteristic equation [latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 = 0 [/latex] Factorizing: [latex] (s + 1)(s + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow s = -1, -2 [/latex] Step 4: Compute the sum of the magnitudes of the poles [latex] |{-1}| + |{-2}| = 1 + 2 = 3 [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Write the state matrix
[latex] A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]

Step 2: Find the characteristic equation
We compute the determinant of [latex] sI - A [/latex]:
[latex] \det(sI - A) = \left| \begin{array}{cc} s & -1 \ 2 & s + 3 \end{array} \right| = s(s + 3) - (-2)(1) = s^2 + 3s + 2 [/latex]

Step 3: Find the roots of the characteristic equation
[latex] s^2 + 3s + 2 = 0 [/latex]
Factorizing:
[latex] (s + 1)(s + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow s = -1, -2 [/latex]

Step 4: Compute the sum of the magnitudes of the poles
[latex] |{-1}| + |{-2}| = 1 + 2 = 3 [/latex]

2025.html: Using shunt capacitors, the power factor of a 3-phase, 4 kV induction motor (drawing 390 kVA at 0.77 pf lag ) is to be corrected to 0.85 pf lag. The line current of the capacitor bank, in A, is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).

2025.explanation_text: Given: Line voltage of motor: [latex] V_L = 4000\ \text{V} [/latex] Apparent power: [latex] S = 390\ \text{kVA} [/latex] Initial power factor: [latex] \cos\phi_1 = 0.77\ (\text{lagging}) [/latex] Target power factor: [latex] \cos\phi_2 = 0.85\ (\text{lagging}) [/latex] Step 1: Compute the active power (real power) [latex] P = S \cdot \cos\phi_1 = 390 \cdot 0.77 = 300.3\ \text{kW} [/latex] Step 2: Compute reactive power before correction [latex] Q_1 = \sqrt{S^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{390^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{152100 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{61919.91} \approx 248.8\ \text{kVAR} [/latex] Step 3: Compute reactive power after correction New apparent power [latex] S_2 = \frac{P}{\cos\phi_2} = \frac{300.3}{0.85} \approx 353.3\ \text{kVA} [/latex] [latex] Q_2 = \sqrt{S_2^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{353.3^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{124821.89 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{34641.8} \approx 186.0\ \text{kVAR} [/latex] Step 4: Required reactive power by capacitor bank [latex] Q_c = Q_1 - Q_2 = 248.8 - 186.0 = 62.8\ \text{kVAR} [/latex] Step 5: Convert to line current In a 3-phase system, reactive power is: [latex] Q = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \Rightarrow I_L = \frac{Q}{\sqrt{3} V_L} [/latex] [latex] I_L = \frac{62.8 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3} \cdot 4000} = \frac{62800}{6928.2} \approx 9.1\ \text{A} [/latex] Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{9.1\ \text{A}} [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Given:
Line voltage of motor: [latex] V_L = 4000\ \text{V} [/latex]
Apparent power: [latex] S = 390\ \text{kVA} [/latex]
Initial power factor: [latex] \cos\phi_1 = 0.77\ (\text{lagging}) [/latex]
Target power factor: [latex] \cos\phi_2 = 0.85\ (\text{lagging}) [/latex]

Step 1: Compute the active power (real power)
[latex] P = S \cdot \cos\phi_1 = 390 \cdot 0.77 = 300.3\ \text{kW} [/latex]

Step 2: Compute reactive power before correction
[latex] Q_1 = \sqrt{S^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{390^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{152100 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{61919.91} \approx 248.8\ \text{kVAR} [/latex]

Step 3: Compute reactive power after correction
New apparent power [latex] S_2 = \frac{P}{\cos\phi_2} = \frac{300.3}{0.85} \approx 353.3\ \text{kVA} [/latex]
[latex] Q_2 = \sqrt{S_2^2 - P^2} = \sqrt{353.3^2 - 300.3^2} = \sqrt{124821.89 - 90180.09} = \sqrt{34641.8} \approx 186.0\ \text{kVAR} [/latex]

Step 4: Required reactive power by capacitor bank
[latex] Q_c = Q_1 - Q_2 = 248.8 - 186.0 = 62.8\ \text{kVAR} [/latex]

Step 5: Convert to line current
In a 3-phase system, reactive power is:
[latex] Q = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \Rightarrow I_L = \frac{Q}{\sqrt{3} V_L} [/latex]
[latex] I_L = \frac{62.8 \times 10^3}{\sqrt{3} \cdot 4000} = \frac{62800}{6928.2} \approx 9.1\ \text{A} [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{9.1\ \text{A}} [/latex]

2025.text: Two units, rated at 100 MW and 150 MW , are enabled for economic load dispatch. When the overall incremental cost is 10,000 Rs./MWh, the units are dispatched to 50 MW and 80 MW respectively. At an overall incremental cost of [latex]10,600 \mathrm{Rs} . / \mathrm{MWh}[/latex], the power output of the units are 80 MW and 92 MW , respectively. The total plant MW-output (without overloading any unit) at an overall incremental cost of 11,800 Rs./MWh is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.html: Two units, rated at 100 MW and 150 MW , are enabled for economic load dispatch. When the overall incremental cost is 10,000 Rs./MWh, the units are dispatched to 50 MW and 80 MW respectively. At an overall incremental cost of [latex]10,600 \mathrm{Rs} . / \mathrm{MWh}[/latex], the power output of the units are 80 MW and 92 MW , respectively. The total plant MW-output (without overloading any unit) at an overall incremental cost of 11,800 Rs./MWh is ___________ (round off to the nearest integer).
2025.subject: Power Systems - Generating Power Stations
2025.explanation_text:
Let’s define: Unit 1 outputs:
At 10,000 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_1 = 50\ \text{MW} [/latex]
At 10,600 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_1 = 80\ \text{MW} [/latex] Unit 2 outputs:
At 10,000 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_2 = 80\ \text{MW} [/latex]
At 10,600 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_2 = 92\ \text{MW} [/latex] We are to find outputs at 11,800 Rs./MWh using extrapolation for both units (assuming linearity of power vs incremental cost curve). Step 1: Find slope of output with respect to cost for each unit Unit 1 slope:
[latex] \frac{80 - 50}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{30}{600} = 0.05\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh} [/latex] Unit 2 slope:
[latex] \frac{92 - 80}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{12}{600} = 0.02\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh} [/latex] Step 2: Extrapolate to 11,800 Rs./MWh Cost increase: [latex] 11,800 - 10,600 = 1,200\ \text{Rs./MWh} [/latex] Unit 1 output:
[latex] P_1 = 80 + (0.05)(1200) = 80 + 60 = 140\ \text{MW} [/latex]
(but Unit 1 is rated for 100 MW max ⇒ limit to 100 MW) Unit 2 output:
[latex] P_2 = 92 + (0.02)(1200) = 92 + 24 = 116\ \text{MW} [/latex]
(but Unit 2 is rated for 150 MW ⇒ no limit hit) Step 3: Total Output [latex] P_{\text{total}} = 100 + 116 = \boxed{216\ \text{MW}} [/latex] Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{216} [/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Let’s define:
Unit 1 outputs: At 10,000 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_1 = 50\ \text{MW} [/latex] At 10,600 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_1 = 80\ \text{MW} [/latex]

Unit 2 outputs: At 10,000 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_2 = 80\ \text{MW} [/latex] At 10,600 Rs./MWh → [latex] P_2 = 92\ \text{MW} [/latex]

We are to find outputs at 11,800 Rs./MWh using extrapolation for both units (assuming linearity of power vs incremental cost curve).

Step 1: Find slope of output with respect to cost for each unit
Unit 1 slope: [latex] \frac{80 - 50}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{30}{600} = 0.05\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh} [/latex]
Unit 2 slope: [latex] \frac{92 - 80}{10,600 - 10,000} = \frac{12}{600} = 0.02\ \text{MW per Rs./MWh} [/latex]

Step 2: Extrapolate to 11,800 Rs./MWh
Cost increase: [latex] 11,800 - 10,600 = 1,200\ \text{Rs./MWh} [/latex]

Unit 1 output: [latex] P_1 = 80 + (0.05)(1200) = 80 + 60 = 140\ \text{MW} [/latex] (but Unit 1 is rated for 100 MW max ⇒ limit to 100 MW)
Unit 2 output: [latex] P_2 = 92 + (0.02)(1200) = 92 + 24 = 116\ \text{MW} [/latex] (but Unit 2 is rated for 150 MW ⇒ no limit hit)

Step 3: Total Output
[latex] P_{\text{total}} = 100 + 116 = \boxed{216\ \text{MW}} [/latex]

Final Answer: [latex] \boxed{216} [/latex]

2025.text: A controller [latex]D(s)[/latex] of the form [latex]\left(1+K_{D} s\right)[/latex] is to be designed for the plant [latex]G(s)=\frac{1000 \sqrt{2}}{s(s+10)^{2}}[/latex] as shown in the figure. The value of [latex]\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}}[/latex] that yields a phase margin of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex] at the gain cross-over frequency of [latex]10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex] is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
2025.html: A controller [latex]D(s)[/latex] of the form [latex]\left(1+K_{D} s\right)[/latex] is to be designed for the plant [latex]G(s)=\frac{1000 \sqrt{2}}{s(s+10)^{2}}[/latex] as shown in the figure. The value of [latex]\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}}[/latex] that yields a phase margin of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex] at the gain cross-over frequency of [latex]10 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec}[/latex] is ___________ (round off to one decimal place).
2025.subject: Control Systems - Frequency Response Analysis
2025.explanation_text:
Given phase margin [P.M] [latex]=45^{\circ}[/latex] at gain cross over frequency [latex]\left[\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}\right]=10[/latex] O.L.T.F with controller [latex]=\mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{s})=\mathrm{D}(\mathrm{s}) . \mathrm{G}(\mathrm{s})[/latex] [latex]
\begin{gathered}
\mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{~s})=\frac{\left[1+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}} \mathrm{~S}\right] \times 1000 \sqrt{2}}{\mathrm{~s}[\mathrm{~s}+10]^{2}} \\
\text { P.M }=180^{\circ}+\left.\angle \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{~s})\right|_{\omega=\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}} \\
\text { Given P.M }=45^{\circ} \text { at } \omega_{\mathrm{gc}}=10 \\
45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}+\angle \frac{1000 \sqrt{2}\left[1+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}} \mathrm{~s}\right.}{} \mathrm{s}[\mathrm{~s}+10]^{2} \\
45^{\circ}=\left[180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{gc}} \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}}{1}\right]-2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}=10}{10}\right)\right]_{\mathrm{\omega gc}}=10 \\
45^{\circ}=90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]-2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{10}{10}\right) \\
45^{\circ}=90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]-2 \times 45^{\circ} \\
\tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]=45^{\circ} \\
10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}={\tan 45^{\circ}=1}\\{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{1}{10}=0.1}
\end{gathered}
[/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Given phase margin [P.M] [latex]=45^{\circ}[/latex] at gain cross over frequency [latex]\left[\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}\right]=10[/latex]
O.L.T.F with controller [latex]=\mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{s})=\mathrm{D}(\mathrm{s}) . \mathrm{G}(\mathrm{s})[/latex]
[latex] \begin{gathered} \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{~s})=\frac{\left[1+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}} \mathrm{~S}\right] \times 1000 \sqrt{2}}{\mathrm{~s}[\mathrm{~s}+10]^{2}} \\ \text { P.M }=180^{\circ}+\left.\angle \mathrm{G}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathrm{~s})\right|_{\omega=\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}} \\ \text { Given P.M }=45^{\circ} \text { at } \omega_{\mathrm{gc}}=10 \\ 45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}+\angle \frac{1000 \sqrt{2}\left[1+\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}} \mathrm{~s}\right.}{} \mathrm{s}[\mathrm{~s}+10]^{2} \\ 45^{\circ}=\left[180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{gc}} \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}}{1}\right]-2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}=10}{10}\right)\right]_{\mathrm{\omega gc}}=10 \\ 45^{\circ}=90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]-2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{10}{10}\right) \\ 45^{\circ}=90^{\circ}+\tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]-2 \times 45^{\circ} \\ \tan ^{-1}\left[10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}\right]=45^{\circ} \\ 10 \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{D}}={\tan 45^{\circ}=1}\\{\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{1}{10}=0.1} \end{gathered} [/latex]

2025.text: The relationship between two variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is given by [latex]x + py + q = 0[/latex] and is shown in the figure. Find the values of [latex]p[/latex] and [latex]q[/latex]. Note: The figure shown is representative.  ]
2025.html:
The relationship between two variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex] is given by [latex]x + py + q = 0[/latex] and is shown in the figure. Find the values of [latex]p[/latex] and [latex]q[/latex].
Note: The figure shown is representative. ]
2025.subject: General Aptitude - Numerical Ability
2025.explanation_text: The equation is of the form: [latex]x + py + q = 0[/latex] Rewriting it in slope-intercept form: [latex]py = -x - q[/latex] [latex]y = -\frac{1}{p}x - \frac{q}{p}[/latex] This is of the form [latex]y = mx + c[/latex] where slope [latex]m = -\frac{1}{p}[/latex] and intercept [latex]c = -\frac{q}{p}[/latex] From the figure: The y-intercept is [latex]c = 4[/latex] (line passes through point (0, 4)) The line passes through another point (2, 8), so slope is: [latex]m = \frac{8 - 4}{2 - 0} = \frac{4}{2} = 2[/latex] Equating this with [latex]-\frac{1}{p}[/latex], [latex]-\frac{1}{p} = 2 \Rightarrow p = -\frac{1}{2}[/latex] Now use y-intercept formula: [latex]-\frac{q}{p} = 4[/latex] Substitute [latex]p = -\frac{1}{2}[/latex]: [latex]-\frac{q}{-\frac{1}{2}} = 4 \Rightarrow \frac{q}{\frac{1}{2}} = 4 \Rightarrow q = 2[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]p = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad q = 2[/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
The equation is of the form: [latex]x + py + q = 0[/latex]
Rewriting it in slope-intercept form:
[latex]py = -x - q[/latex]
[latex]y = -\frac{1}{p}x - \frac{q}{p}[/latex]
This is of the form [latex]y = mx + c[/latex] where slope [latex]m = -\frac{1}{p}[/latex] and intercept [latex]c = -\frac{q}{p}[/latex]

From the figure:
The y-intercept is [latex]c = 4[/latex] (line passes through point (0, 4))
The line passes through another point (2, 8), so slope is:
[latex]m = \frac{8 - 4}{2 - 0} = \frac{4}{2} = 2[/latex]

Equating this with [latex]-\frac{1}{p}[/latex],
[latex]-\frac{1}{p} = 2 \Rightarrow p = -\frac{1}{2}[/latex]

Now use y-intercept formula: [latex]-\frac{q}{p} = 4[/latex]
Substitute [latex]p = -\frac{1}{2}[/latex]:
[latex]-\frac{q}{-\frac{1}{2}} = 4 \Rightarrow \frac{q}{\frac{1}{2}} = 4 \Rightarrow q = 2[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]p = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad q = 2[/latex]

P: Explains why tigers often fail-deer run much faster. This conclusion makes sense after R. Thus, the correct sequence is:

2025.html:
Scores obtained by two students P and Q in seven courses are given in the table below. Based on the information given in the table, which one of the following statements is INCORRECT?

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|l|} \hline P & 22 & 89 & 50 & 45 & 78 & 60 & 39\\ \hline Q & 35 & 65 & 60 & 56 & 81 & 45 & 50 \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
2025.subject: General Aptitude - Numerical Ability
2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Calculate average score of P and Q P total = [latex]22 + 89 + 50 + 45 + 78 + 60 + 39 = 383[/latex] Average of P = [latex]\frac{383}{7} \approx 54.71[/latex] Q total = [latex]35 + 65 + 60 + 56 + 81 + 45 + 50 = 392[/latex] Average of Q = [latex]\frac{392}{7} = 56[/latex] So, average of P is less than average of Q ->(A) is correct. Step 2: Calculate median score Sorted scores: P: 22, 39, 45, 50, 60, 78, 89 → Median = 50 Q: 35, 45, 50, 56, 60, 65, 81 → Median = 56 So, (B) is incorrect (they are not the same). Step 3: Difference between max and min P: Max = 89, Min = 22 → Difference = [latex]89 - 22 = 67[/latex] Q: Max = 81, Min = 35 → Difference = [latex]81 - 35 = 46[/latex] 67 > 46 → (C) is correct. Step 4: Check if average and median of Q are same Average of Q = 56, Median of Q = 56 → (D) is correct. Final Answer: The INCORRECT statement is: (B)
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Calculate average score of P and Q
P total = [latex]22 + 89 + 50 + 45 + 78 + 60 + 39 = 383[/latex]
Average of P = [latex]\frac{383}{7} \approx 54.71[/latex]

Q total = [latex]35 + 65 + 60 + 56 + 81 + 45 + 50 = 392[/latex]
Average of Q = [latex]\frac{392}{7} = 56[/latex]
So, average of P is less than average of Q ->(A) is correct.

Step 2: Calculate median score
Sorted scores:
P: 22, 39, 45, 50, 60, 78, 89 → Median = 50
Q: 35, 45, 50, 56, 60, 65, 81 → Median = 56
So, (B) is incorrect (they are not the same).

Step 3: Difference between max and min
P: Max = 89, Min = 22 → Difference = [latex]89 - 22 = 67[/latex]
Q: Max = 81, Min = 35 → Difference = [latex]81 - 35 = 46[/latex]
67 > 46 → (C) is correct.

Step 4: Check if average and median of Q are same
Average of Q = 56, Median of Q = 56 → (D) is correct.

Final Answer:
The INCORRECT statement is: (B)

2025.html:
Spheres of unit diameter are centered at ( [latex]l, {m}, {n}[/latex] ) where [latex]l, {m}[/latex], and [latex]n [/latex] take every possible integer values.
The distance between two spheres is computed from the center of one sphere to the center of the other sphere. For a given sphere, [latex]x [/latex] is the distance to its nearest sphere and [latex]y [/latex] is the distance to its next nearest sphere. The value of [latex]\frac{y}{x}[/latex] is:
2025.subject: General Aptitude - Numerical Ability
2025.explanation_text: Spheres are centered at all points [latex](l, m, n)[/latex] where [latex]l, m, n \in \mathbb{Z}[/latex] (i.e., all integer coordinates). That means the spheres are placed in a cubic lattice with unit spacing between centers. Step 1: Nearest sphere distance [latex]x[/latex] Each sphere has 6 immediate neighbors at a distance of 1 unit along the directions [latex]\pm x[/latex], [latex]\pm y[/latex], and [latex]\pm z[/latex]. So, [latex]x = 1[/latex] Step 2: Next nearest sphere distance [latex]y[/latex] The next nearest neighbors are along the diagonals of the faces (e.g., from (0,0,0) to (1,1,0)). Their distance is: [latex]y = \sqrt{(1)^2 + (1)^2} = \sqrt{2}[/latex] Step 3: Compute [latex]\frac{y}{x}[/latex] [latex]\frac{y}{x} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{1} = \sqrt{2}[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]\boxed{\sqrt{2}}[/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Spheres are centered at all points [latex](l, m, n)[/latex] where [latex]l, m, n \in \mathbb{Z}[/latex] (i.e., all integer coordinates).
That means the spheres are placed in a cubic lattice with unit spacing between centers.

Step 1: Nearest sphere distance [latex]x[/latex]
Each sphere has 6 immediate neighbors at a distance of 1 unit along the directions [latex]\pm x[/latex], [latex]\pm y[/latex], and [latex]\pm z[/latex].
So, [latex]x = 1[/latex]

Step 2: Next nearest sphere distance [latex]y[/latex]
The next nearest neighbors are along the diagonals of the faces (e.g., from (0,0,0) to (1,1,0)).
Their distance is:

2025.html:
In the triangle PQR, the lengths of PT and TR are in the ratio of [latex]3: 2[/latex].
ST is parallel to QR. Two semicircles are drawn with PS and PQ as diameters, as shown in the figure.
Which one of the following statements is true about the shaded area PQS?
Note: The figure shown is representative.
2025.subject: General Aptitude - Numerical Ability
2025.explanation_text: Step 1: Let us assume PQ = 5 units Given the ratio [latex]PT : TR = 3 : 2[/latex], then [latex]PT = 3[/latex] units and [latex]TR = 2[/latex] units, so total [latex]PR = PT + TR = 5[/latex] units. Since [latex]ST \parallel QR[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex] lies on [latex]PR[/latex], by Basic Proportionality Theorem: [latex]\frac{PS}{PQ} = \frac{PT}{PR} = \frac{3}{5}[/latex] So, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} \cdot PQ[/latex] Step 2: Area of semicircle is proportional to square of diameter Let the diameter [latex]PQ = d[/latex]. Then the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PQ[/latex] is: [latex]A_{PQ} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8}[/latex] Now, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} d[/latex], so area of semicircle on PS: [latex]A_{PS} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi (3d/5)^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8} \cdot \frac{9}{25} = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}[/latex] Step 3: Shaded Area = Area of semicircle on PQ − Area of semicircle on PS [latex]A_{\text{shaded}} = A_{PQ} - A_{PS} = A_{PQ} \left(1 - \frac{9}{25}\right) = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}[/latex] Now convert the shaded area as a multiple of the semicircle on PS: [latex]\frac{A_{\text{shaded}}}{A_{PS}} = \frac{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}}{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}} = \frac{16}{9}[/latex] Final Answer: [latex]\boxed{\frac{16}{9}}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PS[/latex]
2025.explanation_html:
Step 1: Let us assume PQ = 5 units
Given the ratio [latex]PT : TR = 3 : 2[/latex], then [latex]PT = 3[/latex] units and [latex]TR = 2[/latex] units, so total [latex]PR = PT + TR = 5[/latex] units.
Since [latex]ST \parallel QR[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex] lies on [latex]PR[/latex], by Basic Proportionality Theorem:
[latex]\frac{PS}{PQ} = \frac{PT}{PR} = \frac{3}{5}[/latex]
So, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} \cdot PQ[/latex]

Step 2: Area of semicircle is proportional to square of diameter
Let the diameter [latex]PQ = d[/latex].
Then the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PQ[/latex] is:
[latex]A_{PQ} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi d^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8}[/latex]

Now, [latex]PS = \frac{3}{5} d[/latex], so area of semicircle on PS:
[latex]A_{PS} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\pi (3d/5)^2}{4} = \frac{\pi d^2}{8} \cdot \frac{9}{25} = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}[/latex]

Step 3: Shaded Area = Area of semicircle on PQ − Area of semicircle on PS
[latex]A_{\text{shaded}} = A_{PQ} - A_{PS} = A_{PQ} \left(1 - \frac{9}{25}\right) = A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}[/latex]

Now convert the shaded area as a multiple of the semicircle on PS:
[latex]\frac{A_{\text{shaded}}}{A_{PS}} = \frac{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{16}{25}}{A_{PQ} \cdot \frac{9}{25}} = \frac{16}{9}[/latex]

Final Answer:
[latex]\boxed{\frac{16}{9}}[/latex] times the area of the semicircle with diameter [latex]PS[/latex]

2023.html:
In the following differential equation, the numerically obtained value of [latex]y(t)[/latex], at [latex]t=1[/latex], is ___ (Round off to 2 decimal places).

[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{t}}, \alpha=0.01 \text { and } y(0)=0 [/latex]
2023.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2023.explanation_html:
Given :
[latex] \frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha t} [/latex]
[latex]\alpha=0.01[/latex] and [latex]y(0)=0[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} \left.\frac{d^{2} y}{d t^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} & =y^{\prime \prime}(0) \\ & =-\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{2+\alpha \mathrm{T}}-\left.\frac{\alpha e^{-\alpha t}}{(2+\alpha \mathrm{t})^{2}}\right|_{\mathrm{t}=0} \\ & =-\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\alpha}{4}=-\frac{3 \alpha}{4} \end{aligned} [/latex]

We know,
Taylor's series
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(t) & =y(0)+y^{\prime}(0)+\frac{t^{2} y^{\prime \prime}(0)}{2 !}+\ldots \\ & =0+t\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+\frac{t^{2}}{2}\left(-\frac{3 \alpha}{4}\right) \\ & =\frac{t}{2}-\frac{3}{8} \alpha t^{2} \end{aligned} [/latex]

At [latex]\mathrm{t}=1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} y(1) & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8}(0.01) \times 1^{2} \\ & =0.5-\frac{3}{8} \times 0.01 \\ & =0.496 \approx 0.5 \end{aligned} [/latex]

2023.text: The expected number of trials for first occurrence of a "head" in a biased coin is known to be 4. The probability of first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is  ___ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
2023.html: The expected number of trials for first occurrence of a "head" in a biased coin is known to be 4. The probability of first occurrence of a "head" in the second trial is ___ (Round off to 3 decimal places).
2023.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2023.explanation_html:
Let probability of head [latex]=\mathrm{P}[/latex]
Let probability of Tail [latex]=q=P-1[/latex]
[latex] \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline Trial & 1 & 2 & 3 & ... \\ \hline Probability & [\mathrm{P} & \mathrm{qP} & [latex]\mathrm{q}^{2} \mathrm{P} & .... \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Expected No. of trail
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} p+2 P q+3 q^{2} P+\ldots \\ & =P\left(1+2 q+3 q^{2}+\ldots\right) \\ & =P(1-q)^{-2} \\ & =\frac{P}{P^{2}}=\frac{1}{P} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Given : Trial [latex]=4[/latex]
[latex] \frac{1}{P}=4 \Rightarrow P=\frac{1}{4} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \quad \mathrm{q}=\frac{3}{4}[/latex]

Now, probability of head for second trail. [latex] \begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{qP} \\ & =\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{16}=0.1875 \end{aligned} [/latex]

2023.text: Consider the state-space description of an LTI system with matrices [latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{array}\right], B=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], C=[3-2], D=1[/latex] For the input, [latex]\sin (\omega t), \omega \gt 0[/latex], the value of [latex]\omega[/latex] for which the steady-state output of the system will be zero, is ___ (Round off to the nearest integer).
2023.html:
Consider the state-space description of an LTI system with matrices

[latex]A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{array}\right], B=\left[\begin{array}{l}0 \\ 1\end{array}\right], C=[3-2], D=1[/latex]

For the input, [latex]\sin (\omega t), \omega \gt 0[/latex], the value of [latex]\omega[/latex] for which the steady-state output of the system will be zero, is ___ (Round off to the nearest integer).
2023.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2023.explanation_html:
We have, transfer function
[latex] \mathrm{T}(\mathrm{s})=\mathrm{C}[\mathrm{SI}-\mathrm{A}]^{-1} \mathrm{~B}+\mathrm{D} \quad (1) [/latex]
where, [latex][S I-A]=\left[\begin{array}{ll}S & 0 \\ 0 & S\end{array}\right]-\left[\begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ -1 & -2\end{array}\right][/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} & =\left[\begin{array}{cc} \mathrm{s} & -1 \\ 1 & \mathrm{~s}+2 \end{array}\right] \\ \therefore \quad[\mathrm{sl}-\mathrm{A}]^{-1} & =\frac{1}{\mathrm{~s}^{2}+2 \mathrm{~s}+1}\left[\begin{array}{cc} \mathrm{s}+2 & 1 \\ -1 & \mathrm{~s} \end{array}\right] \end{aligned} [/latex]

From eqn. (1), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{T}(\mathrm{s})&=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 3 & -2 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{cc} \frac{\mathrm{s}+2}{(\mathrm{~s}+1)^{2}} & \frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} & \frac{s}{(s+1)^{2}} \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]+1 \\ &=\left[\begin{array}{ll} 3 & -2 \end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c} \frac{1}{(s+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{s}{(s+1)^{2}} \end{array}\right]+1 \\ &=\frac{3}{(s+1)^{2}}-\frac{2 s}{(s+1)}+1 \\ &=\frac{3-2 s+s^{2}+2 s+1}{s^{2}+2 s+1} \\ &=\frac{s^{2}+4}{s^{2}+2 s+1} \end{aligned} [/latex]

Put, [latex]s=j \omega[/latex],
[latex] T(j \omega)=\frac{-\omega^{2}+4}{-\omega^{2}+\mathrm{j} 2 \omega+1} [/latex]

Now, condition for output is zero,
[latex] \begin{aligned} -\omega^{2}+4 & =0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad \omega & =2 \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{sec} . \end{aligned} [/latex]

2023.text: A three-phase synchronous motor with synchronous impedance of [latex]0.1+j0.3 [/latex]  per unit per phase has a static stability limit of 2.5 per unit. The corresponding excitation voltage in per unit is ____ (Round off to 2 decimal places).
2023.html: A three-phase synchronous motor with synchronous impedance of [latex]0.1+j0.3 [/latex] per unit per phase has a static stability limit of 2.5 per unit. The corresponding excitation voltage in per unit is ____ (Round off to 2 decimal places).
2023.subject: Electrical Machines - Synchronous Machines
2023.explanation_html:
Developed power for motor,
[latex] P_{d e v}=\frac{V_{f}}{Z_{s}} \cos \left(\theta_{s}-\delta\right)-\frac{E_{F}^{2}}{2} \cos \theta_{s} [/latex]

At max. power developed,
[latex] \delta=\theta_{\mathrm{S}} [/latex]

and this is decide steady state stability of motor.
[latex]\therefore \mathrm{SSSL}, \mathrm{P}_{\text {dev }(max)}=\frac{V E_{F}}{\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{S}}}-\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}}{\mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{S}}} \cos \theta_{\mathrm{s}}[/latex]
where, [latex]V=1.0 \mathrm{pu}[/latex]

[latex] \mathrm{Z}_{\mathrm{S}}=0.1+\mathrm{j} 0.3=0.316 \angle 71.6^{\circ} \mathrm{pu} [/latex]
and [latex]\mathrm{SSSL}=2.5[/latex]

[latex]\therefore \quad 2.5=\frac{1 \times E_{F}}{0.316}-\frac{E_{F}^{2}}{0.316} \cos 71.56^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex]1.001 \mathrm{E}_{F}^{2}-3.16 \mathrm{E}_{F}+2.5=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{F}}=1.595 \mathrm{pu}[/latex]

2023.explanation_html:
Given : Torque is constant.

Synchronous speed, [latex]N_{S}=\frac{120 f}{P}[/latex]
[latex] =\frac{120 \times 50}{6}=1000 \mathrm{rpm} [/latex]

[latex] \text { Slip, } S=\frac{1000-960}{1000}=0.04 [/latex]

Now, from eqn. (1), we get
[latex] \begin{aligned} \frac{0.04 \times \mathrm{V}^{2}}{\mathrm{~F}} & =\frac{\mathrm{S}_{\text {new }} \times(0.8)^{2} \mathrm{~V}}{0.8 \mathrm{~F}} \\ \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{S}_{\text {new }} & =0.05 \end{aligned} [/latex]

Synchronous speed at reduced frequency i.e. [latex]50 \times 0.8=40 \mathrm{~Hz}[/latex].
[latex] \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{new})}=\frac{120 \times 40}{6}=800 \mathrm{rpm} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Motor speed,

[latex] \begin{aligned} \mathrm{N}&=\left(1-\mathrm{S}_{\text {new }}\right) \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{s} \text { (new) }} & =(1-0.05) \times 800 \\ & =760 \mathrm{rpm} \end{aligned} [/latex]

 &=0.894 \\ 
 FDF&= \cos \frac{\pi}{3}=0.5 \\ 
 PF&=0.894 \times 0.5=0.447 
\end{aligned}[/latex]

Let the probability density function of a random variable [latex]x [/latex] be given as

The value of [latex] 'a'[/latex] is _________
2022.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2022.explanation_text:
[latex]f(x)=\left\{\begin{matrix}
ae^{2x} &x \lt 0 \\ 
 ae^{-2x} &x \gt 0 
\end{matrix}\right. [/latex] Therefore, [latex] \begin{aligned}
\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x)dx&=1\\
\int_{-\infty }^{0}ae^{2x}dx+\int_{0 }^{\infty }ae^{-2x}dx&=1\\
a\left [ \left [ \frac{e^{2x}}{2} \right ]_{-\infty }^0 +[ \left [ \frac{e^{-2x}}{-2} \right ]^{\infty }_0\right ]&=1\\
a\left [ \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \right ]&=1\\
a&=1
\end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} P_{i / p} &=40 \mathrm{~kW}, \quad \text { stator loss }=1 \mathrm{~kW}, \quad \mathrm{~F} \text { and } W=2.025 \mathrm{~kW} \\ \text { Stator } \mathrm{o} / \mathrm{p} &=40-1=39 \mathrm{~kW} \\ \qquad \text { Slip } &=\frac{1000-975}{1000}=0.025 \\ \text { Rotor } \mathrm{o} / \mathrm{p} &=\text { Rotor } \mathrm{i} / \mathrm{p} \times(1-\mathrm{s}) \\ &=39(1-0.025)=38.025 \mathrm{~kW} \\ \text { Motor } \mathrm{o} / \mathrm{p} &=38.025-2.025=36 \mathrm{~kW}\\ \eta&=\frac{\text { Motor output }}{\text { Motor input }}=\frac{36}{40} \times 100=90 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} W_{i 1} &=2500 \mathrm{~W} \text { at } 440 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz} \\ W_{i 2} &=850 \mathrm{~W} \text { at } 220 \mathrm{~V}, 25 \mathrm{~Hz} \\ W_{i 3} &=R_{e_{3}}+P_{H_{3}} \text { at } 440 \mathrm{~V}, 50 \mathrm{~Hz} \\ R_{\theta_{3}} &=?, \quad P_{h_{3}}=?, \quad \frac{v}{f}=\mathrm{constant} \\ \Rightarrow \qquad \qquad\quad 2500 &=A f+B f^{2} &\left\{\frac{400}{50}=\frac{220}{25}=\text { Constant }\right\} \\ \text { or, }\qquad \qquad \quad \frac{2500}{f} &=A+B f \\ \text{or},\qquad \qquad \frac{2500}{50}&=A+B(50) &\ldots(i)\\ \text{and}\qquad \qquad \frac{850}{25}&=\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}(25)&\ldots(ii) \end{aligned}[/latex] Solving (i) and (ii), we get [latex] \begin{aligned} 25 B &=\frac{2500}{50}-\frac{850}{25}=\frac{2500-1700}{50} \\ &=\frac{800}{50}=16 \\ B &=\frac{16}{25} \\ \text{and from (i)},\qquad A &=50-\frac{16}{25} \times 50=50-32=18\\ \text{So, at} 50 \mathrm{~Hz}\\ P_{h}&=A f=18 \times 50=900 \mathrm{~W} \\ P_{e}&=B f=\left(\frac{16}{25}\right) \times(50)^{2}=1600 \mathrm{~W} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.explanation_text: If voltage source is removed then in both cases charge O is constant. 2021.subject: Electrical Machines - DC Machines
2021.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} I_{L} &=\frac{100 \times 10^{3}}{200}=500 \mathrm{~A} \\ I_{S h} &=\frac{200}{50}=4 \mathrm{~A} \\ I_{a} &=504 \mathrm{~A} \\ E_{q} &=V+I_{a} R_{a}+\text { Brush drop } \\ &=200+504(0.025)+2 \mathrm{~V} \\ &=214.6 \mathrm{~V}\\ \text{In motoring case:} V I&=10 \mathrm{~kW}, V=200 \mathrm{~V}\\ \therefore \qquad \qquad I &=\frac{10000}{200}=50 A \\ I_{f} &=4 \mathrm{~A}, I_{a}=I_{L}-I_{f} \\ &=46 \mathrm{~A} \\ E_{b} &=V-I_{a} R_{a}-\text { Brush Drop } \\ &=200-46(0.025)-2=196.85 \mathrm{~V} \\ \frac{N_{m}}{N_{g}} &=\frac{E_{b}}{E_{g}} \\ N_{m} &=\frac{E_{b}}{E_{g}} \times N_{g} \\ \therefore \qquad \qquad N_{m} &=\frac{196.85}{214.6} \times 300=275.18 \mathrm{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.explanation_text: We know, RMS value of full wave rectified sine [latex]=\frac{V_{m}}{\sqrt{2}}=0.707 V_{m}[/latex] For clipped wave form As [latex]0 \rightarrow \frac{\pi}{4}[/latex] and [latex]\frac{3 \pi}{4} \rightarrow \pi[/latex] wave form are identical [latex] \begin{aligned} &\text { rms value of clipped wave } \\ &\left.=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\left[2 \int_{0}^{\pi / 4} V_{m}^{2} \sin ^{2} \omega t+\int_{\pi / 4}^{3 \pi / 4}\left(0.707 V_{m}\right)^{2} d \omega t\right.}\right] \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\left(\int_{0}^{\pi / 4} \frac{2 V_{m}^{2}}{2}[1-\cos 2 \omega t] d \omega t+\frac{1}{2} V_{m}^{2} \times \frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{1 / 2}}\\ &=\left[\frac{1}{\pi}\left[V_{m}^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2} \sin \frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{4} \pi\right]\right]^{1 / 2} \\ &=\left[\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{\pi}\left[\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\right]+\frac{V_{m}^{2}}{4}\right]^{1 / 2}=0.5838 V_{m} \\ \text { Ratio } &=\frac{0.707}{0.5838}=1.21 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2021.text: Which one of the following numbers is exactly divisible by [latex]\left(11^{13}+1\right)[/latex]?

2021.explanation_text:
Consider expression [latex]\frac{x^{n}-a^{n}}{x+a}.[/latex] Now assuming similar expression [latex]11^{52}-1=\left(11^{13}\right)^{4}-(1)^{4}[/latex] [latex]
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\left(11^{13}\right)^{4}-(1)^{4}}{11^{3}+1} &=\frac{\left.\left((11)^{13}\right)^{2}-(1)^{2}\right)\left(\left(11^{13}\right)^{2}+(1)^{2}\right)}{11^{3}+1} \\
&=\left[\left(11^{13}-1\right)\right]\left[\left(11^{13}\right)^{2}+(1)^{2}\right]
\end{aligned}[/latex] Hence, [latex]11^{52}-1[/latex] is divisible by [latex]11^{13}+1.[/latex]

2020.text:
[latex]ax^3+bx^2+cx+d[/latex] is a polynomial on real [latex]x[/latex] over real coefficients [latex]a, b, c, d[/latex] wherein
[latex]a \neq 0[/latex]. Which of the following statements is true?
2020.html: [latex]ax^3+bx^2+cx+d[/latex] is a polynomial on real [latex]x[/latex] over real coefficients [latex]a, b, c, d[/latex] wherein [latex]a \neq 0[/latex]. Which of the following statements is true?
2020.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Complex Variables
2020.explanation_text: Given Polynomial [latex]ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0;\; \; \; a\neq 0[/latex] Option (A): If d=0, then the polynomial equation becomes [latex]\begin{aligned} ax^3+bx^2+cx&=0\\ x(ax^2+bx+c)&=0 \\ x=0 \text{ or } ax^2+bx+c&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] d can be choosen to ensure x=0 is a root of given polynomial. Hence, Option (A) is correct. Option B: A third degree polynomial equation with all root equal is given by [latex](x+\alpha )^3=0[/latex] Thus, by selecting suitable values of a, b, c and d we can have all roots identical. Hence, option (B) is incorrect. Option (C): Complex roots always occurs in pairs, So, the given polynomial will have maximum of 2 complex roots and 1 real root. Hence, option (C) is incorrect. Option (D): Nature or roots depends on other coefficients also apart from coefficient 'c'. Hence, option (D) is correct. Hence, the correct options are (A) and (D).
2020.explanation_html:
Given Polynomial [latex]ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0;\; \; \; a\neq 0[/latex]

Option (A):
If d=0, then the polynomial equation becomes
[latex]\begin{aligned} ax^3+bx^2+cx&=0\\ x(ax^2+bx+c)&=0 \\ x=0 \text{ or } ax^2+bx+c&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
d can be choosen to ensure x=0 is a root of given polynomial.
Hence, Option (A) is correct.

Option B:
A third degree polynomial equation with all root equal is given by
[latex](x+\alpha )^3=0[/latex]
Thus, by selecting suitable values of a, b, c and d we can have all roots identical.
Hence, option (B) is incorrect.

Option (C): Complex roots always occurs in pairs,
So, the given polynomial will have maximum of 2 complex roots and 1 real root.
Hence, option (C) is incorrect.

Option (D): Nature or roots depends on other coefficients also apart from coefficient 'c'.
Hence, option (D) is correct.
Hence, the correct options are (A) and (D).

2020.text:
Consider the initial value problem below. The value of y at [latex]x = ln \;2[/latex]. (rounded off to 3
decimal places) is ________ . [latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=2x-y,\; y(0)=1[/latex]
2020.html:
Consider the initial value problem below. The value of y at [latex]x = ln \;2[/latex]. (rounded off to 3 decimal places) is ________ .

[latex]\frac{dy}{dx}=2x-y,\; y(0)=1[/latex]
2020.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2020.explanation_text:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=2x-y \\  y(0)&=1, \; y \text{ at } x=\ln  2\\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+y&=2x \\ P&=1, \;\;     Q=2x \\ I.F.&=e^{\int Pdx}=e^{\int 1dx}=e^{x}\\ \text{Solution, }   Y(I.F)&=\int Q(I.F.)dx\\ye^{x}&=\int 2x\cdot e^{x}dx \\&=2(xe^{x}-e^{x})+C \\ y&=2x-2+ce^{-x} \\ y(0)&=1 \\ 1&=0-2+C \\ C&=3 \\ \therefore \; \; y&=2x-2+3e^{-x} \\ \text{At }x&= \ln 2 \\ y&=2(\ln 2)-2+3e^{-\ln 2} \\ &=1.386-2+\frac{3}{2}\\
&=0.886\end{aligned} [/latex]
2020.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}&=2x-y \\ y(0)&=1, \; y \text{ at } x=\ln 2\\ \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} x}+y&=2x \\ P&=1, \;\; Q=2x \\ I.F.&=e^{\int Pdx}=e^{\int 1dx}=e^{x}\\ \text{Solution, } Y(I.F)&=\int Q(I.F.)dx\\ye^{x}&=\int 2x\cdot e^{x}dx \\&=2(xe^{x}-e^{x})+C \\ y&=2x-2+ce^{-x} \\ y(0)&=1 \\ 1&=0-2+C \\ C&=3 \\ \therefore \; \; y&=2x-2+3e^{-x} \\ \text{At }x&= \ln 2 \\ y&=2(\ln 2)-2+3e^{-\ln 2} \\ &=1.386-2+\frac{3}{2}\\ &=0.886\end{aligned} [/latex]

has rated no-load loss of 450 W. When the high-voltage winding is excited with 160 V,
40 Hz sinusoidal ac supply, the no-load losses are found to be 320 W. When the highvoltage winding of the same transformer is supplied from a 100 V, 25 Hz sinusoidal ac
source, the no-load losses will be _________W (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
2020.html: A single-phase, 4 kVA, 200 V/100 V, 50 Hz transformer with laminated CRGO steel core has rated no-load loss of 450 W. When the high-voltage winding is excited with 160 V, 40 Hz sinusoidal ac supply, the no-load losses are found to be 320 W. 2020.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned}200 V,50 Hz, P_{c}&=450 Watt\\ 160 V,40 Hz, P_{c}&=320 Watt \\ 100 V,25 Hz,]P_{c}&=? Watt \\ \frac{v}{f}=\text{constant}&=\frac{200}{50}=\frac{160}{40}=\frac{100}{25}\\ \text{So, } P_{c}&=Af+Bf^{2} \\ 450&=A\times (50)+B\times (50)^{2} \;\; ...(i)\\ 320&=A\times (40)+B\times (40)^{2} \;\; ...(ii)\\ \text{From (i) and (ii),}\\ \frac{450}{50}&=A+B(50) \;\;...(iii) \\ \frac{320}{40}&=A+B(40) \;\;...(iv) \\ \text{Equation (iii)-(iv),} \\ (9-8)&=B(10)\\ B&=\frac{1}{10} \\ A&=9-\frac{1}{10}\times 50=4 \\ \text{Now at 100V,25 Hz,} \\P_{c}&=4\times 25+\frac{1}{10}\times (25)^{2}\\ &=100+62.5=162.50 Watt \end{aligned} [/latex]

2020.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} y(n)-ay(n-1)&=b_{0}x(n)-b_{1}x(n-2) \\ &\text{By applying ZT,} \\ Y(z)-az^{-1}Y(z)&=b_{0}X(z)-b_{1}z^{-1}X(z)\\ \Rightarrow \, \, H(z)&=\frac{Y(z)}{X(z)}=\frac{b_{0}-b_{1}z^{-1}}{1-az^{-1}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
By taking right-sided inverse ZT,
[latex]h(n)=b_{0}a^{n}u(n)-b_{1}a^{n-1}u(n-1)[/latex]
By taking left-sided inverse ZT,
[latex]h(n)=-b_{0}a^{n}u(-n-1)+b_{1}a^{n-1}u(-n)[/latex]
Thus system is not necessarily causal.

Let [latex]a_r, a_\phi \; and \; a_z[/latex] be unit vectors along [latex]r, \phi \; and \; z[/latex] directions, respectively in the cylindrical
coordinate system. For the electric flux density given by [latex]D = (a_r15 + a_\phi 2r - a_z3rz)[/latex] Coulomb/[latex]m^2[/latex], the total electric flux, in Coulomb, emanating from the volume enclosed
by a solid cylinder of radius 3 m and height 5 m oriented along the z-axis with its base
at the origin is:
2020.html: Let [latex]a_r, a_\phi \; and \; a_z[/latex] be unit vectors along [latex]r, \phi \; and \; z[/latex] directions, respectively in the cylindrical coordinate system. For the electric flux density given by [latex]D = (a_r15 + a_\phi 2r - a_z3rz)[/latex] Coulomb/[latex]m^2[/latex], the total electric flux, in Coulomb, emanating from the volume enclosed by a solid cylinder of radius 3 m and height 5 m oriented along the z-axis with its base at the origin is:
2020.subject: Electromagnetic Fields - Electrostatic Fields
2020.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} & \psi / \text{Crossing closed surface} \\ \oint \oint \vec{D}.\vec{ds}&=\int \int \int (\vec{\triangledown }\cdot \vec{D}) dv \\ (\vec{V}.\vec{D}) &=\frac{1}{\rho }\frac{\partial }{\partial p}(\rho D_{\rho })+\frac{1}{\rho }\frac{\partial D_{\phi }}{\partial \phi }+\frac{\partial D_{z}}{\partial z} \\ &=\frac{1}{\rho }\frac{\partial }{\partial p}(\rho 15)+\frac{1}{\rho }\frac{\partial }{\partial \phi }(2\rho )+\frac{\partial }{\partial z}(-3\rho z) \\ &=\frac{1}{\rho }15-3\rho \\ \int \int \int (\vec{\triangledown }\cdot \vec{D})dv&=\int \int \int \left ( \frac{15}{\rho}-3\rho \right )\rho d\rho d\phi dz \\ &=\int \int \int 15d\rho d\phi dz-3\int \int \int \rho ^{2}d\rho d\phi dz \\ &=15\int_{\rho =0}^{3}d\rho \int_{\phi =0}^{2\pi }d\phi \int_{z=0}^{5}-3\int_{\rho =0}^{3}\rho^{2}d\rho \int_{\phi =0}^{2\pi }d\phi \int_{z=0}^{5}dz \\ &= 15(3-0)(2\pi )(5)-3\left ( \frac{3^{3}}{3} \right )\times (2\pi )(5) \\ &=45(10\pi )-27(10\pi )=180\pi C \end{aligned}[/latex]

A stable real linear time-invariant system with single pole at p, has a transfer function [latex]H(s)=\frac{s^2+100}{s-p}[/latex]

gain is closed to:
2020.html: A stable real linear time-invariant system with single pole at p, has a transfer function [latex]H(s)=\frac{s^2+100}{s-p}[/latex] with a dc gain of 5. The smallest positive frequency, in rad/s at unity gain is closed to:
2020.subject: Control Systems - Frequency Response Analysis
2020.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} H(s)&=T.F.=[latex]\frac{s^{2}+100}{s-p} \\ \text{D.C. gain }&= 5 \\ \Rightarrow \; \; \frac{100}{-P}&=5=P=-20 \\ H(j\omega )&=\frac{-\omega ^{2}+100}{j\omega +20} \\ \left |H(j\omega ) \right |&=\frac{-\omega ^{2}+100}{\sqrt{\omega ^{2}+400}} \\ \frac{-\omega ^{2}+100}{\sqrt{\omega ^{2}+400}}&=1 \\ \Rightarrow \; \; \omega &=8.84 \text{rad/sec.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2020.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
2020.explanation_html:
As per GATE official answer key MTA (Marks to ALL)
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 &3 &3 \\ 3 &2 &1 \\ 3 &1 &7 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} I_{11} & 0 &0 \\ I_{21}&l_{22} & 0\\ l_{31} &l_{32} &l_{33} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_{11} &u_{12} &u_{13} \\ 0 &u_{22} &u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 &u_{33} \end{bmatrix} \\ \text{consider, }u_{11}&=u_{22}=u_{33}=1 \\ \begin{bmatrix} 2 &3 &3 \\ 3 &2 &1 \\ 3 &1 &7 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0 &0 \\ l_{21}&l_{22} & 0\\ l_{31} &l_{32} &l_{33} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 &u_{12} &u_{13} \\ 0 &1 &u_{23} \\ 0 & 0 &1 \end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix} 2 &3 &3 \\ 3 &2 &1 \\ 3 &1 &7 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & l_{11}u_{12} &l_{11}u_{13} \\ l_{21}& l_{21}u_{12}+l_{22} & l_{21}u_{13}+ l_{22}u_{23}\\ l_{31} &l_{31}u_{12}+l_{32} & l_{31}u_{13}+ l_{32}u_{23}+l_{33}\end{bmatrix} \\ l_{11}&=2 \; \; l_{11}u_{12}=3 \; \; l_{11}u_{13}=3 \; \; \\ l_{21}&=3 \; \; 2u_{12}=3 \; \; 2u_{13}=3 \\ l_{31}&=3\; \; u_{12}=\frac{3}{2} \; \; u_{13}=\frac{3}{2} \\ l_{21}u_{12}+l_{22}&=2\; \; l_{21}u_{13}+l_{22}u_{23}=1 \\ (3)\left ( \frac{3}{2} \right )+l_{22}&=2 \; \; (3)\left ( \frac{3}{2} \right )+\left ( -\frac{5}{2} \right )u_{23}=1 \\ l_{22}&=-\frac{5}{2} \; \; u_{23}=-\frac{7}{5} \\ l_{31}u_{12}+l_{32}&=1 \; \; l_{31}u_{13}+l_{32}u_{23}+l_{33}=7\\ (3)(\frac{3}{2})+l_{32}&=1 \; \; (3)\left ( \frac{3}{2} \right )+\left ( -\frac{7}{2} \right )\left ( \frac{7}{5} \right )+l_{33}=7 \\ l_{32}&=-\frac{7}{2} \; \; l_{33}=-\frac{74}{10}\\ L&=\begin{bmatrix} 2 &0 &0 \\ 3 &-5/2 &0 \\ 3 &-7/2 & 74/10 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]
The number of purely real elements of lower triangular matrix are 9.

A vector function is given by [latex]F = a_xy - a_yx[/latex] The line integral of the above function [latex]\int _c F\cdot dl[/latex] along the curve C, which follows the parabola [latex]y = x^2[/latex] as shown below is _______ (rounded
off to 2 decimal places).
2020.html:
Let [latex]a_x \; and \; a_y[/latex] be unit vectors along x and y directions, respectively. A vector function is given by

[latex]F = a_xy - a_yx[/latex]

The line integral of the above function

[latex]\int _c F\cdot dl[/latex]

along the curve C, which follows the parabola [latex]y = x^2[/latex] as shown below is _______ (rounded off to 2 decimal places).
2020.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2020.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \vec{F}&=y\hat{a}_{x}-x\hat{a}_{y} \\ \vec{r}&=x\hat{i}+y\hat{j} \\ \vec{F}&=y\hat{i}-x\hat{j} \\ d\vec{r}&=dx\hat{i}+dy\hat{j} \\ &=\int _{c}F.d\vec{r}\\ &=\int_{c}F_{1}dx+F_{2}dy \\ &=\int _{c}ydx-xdy \\ &\text{Where C is,}\\ y&=x^{2} \\ dy&=2x dx \\ x &\text{ varies from -1 to 2,}\\ \int _{c}\vec{F}dl&=\int_{-1}^{2}x^{2}dx-x\cdot 2xdx \\ &=\int_{-1}^{2}(x^{2}-2x)dx \\ &=\int_{-1}^{2}-x^{2}dx=\left.\begin{matrix} -\frac{x^{3}}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_{-1}^{2} \\ &=-\frac{8}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=-\frac{9}{3}\\ &=-3 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2020.explanation_text:
If initial charge polarities on the capacitor is opposite to the supply voltage then only 
the capacitor voltage crosses the zero line. [latex]\begin{aligned}
V_{c}(t) \; \Rightarrow  \;& \text{Final value} \\ &+ (\text{Initial value - Final value}) e^{-t/\tau }\\ 0&=10+(-V_{0}-10)e^{-0.4}  \\ 10&=(V_{0}+10)e^{-0.4}  \\ V_{0}&=4.918 V \\ \text{Now, } t&=0.2\tau \\  0&=10+(-{V_{0}}'-10)e^{-0.2}  \\ {V_{0}}'&=2.214 \\ \%\text{change in voltage}  &= \frac{4.918-2.214}{4.918}\times 100 \%\\ &=54.99\%
\end{aligned}[/latex]

With real power zero, load angle [latex]\delta =0[/latex]
with initial values, [latex]V_{1}=1.1, \; \; \; V_{2}=1[/latex]

[latex]\, \, =\frac{(1.1)^{2}}{X}-\frac{1.1\times 1}{X}\sin 0=\frac{0.11}{x}[/latex]

contain 8-bit numbers 98H and B1H respectively. The following program is executed: LXI H, 2001 H MVIA, 21H INX H ADD M INX H MOV M, A HLT At the end of this program, the memory location 2003H contains the number in decimal

2020.html:
An 8085 microprocessor accesses two memory locations (2001 H) and (2002H), that contain 8-bit numbers 98H and B1H respectively. The following program is executed:

LXI H, 2001 H
MVIA, 21H
INX H
ADD M
INX H
MOV M, A
HLT

At the end of this program, the memory location 2003H contains the number in decimal (base 10) form ________
2020.subject: Digital Electronics - Microprocessors
2020.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} LXI H, 2001 H & \rightarrow  [HL]  \rightarrow 2001 H \\MVI A, 21 H & \rightarrow [A]  \leftarrow 21 H \\INX H & \rightarrow [HL]  \rightarrow 2002 H \\ ADD M & \rightarrow [A] + [2002]  \rightarrow [A] \\ &= (21H + B1 H)  \rightarrow [A] \\ &= D2 H  \rightarrow [A] \\ INX H & \rightarrow [HL]  \rightarrow 2003 H \\  MOV M, A & \rightarrow [2003] \leftarrow [A] \\ [2003] &= D2 H = (1101\; 0010)_2 \\ &= 1 \times 2^7+1\times 2^6+1\times 2^4 +1\times 2^1 \\&= 128 + 64 + 16 + 2 \\&= 210 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2020.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} LXI H, 2001 H & \rightarrow [HL] \rightarrow 2001 H \\MVI A, 21 H & \rightarrow [A] \leftarrow 21 H \\INX H & \rightarrow [HL] \rightarrow 2002 H \\ ADD M & \rightarrow [A] + [2002] \rightarrow [A] \\ &= (21H + B1 H) \rightarrow [A] \\ &= D2 H \rightarrow [A] \\ INX H & \rightarrow [HL] \rightarrow 2003 H \\ MOV M, A & \rightarrow [2003] \leftarrow [A] \\ [2003] &= D2 H = (1101\; 0010)_2 \\ &= 1 \times 2^7+1\times 2^6+1\times 2^4 +1\times 2^1 \\&= 128 + 64 + 16 + 2 \\&= 210 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2020.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \phi &\propto I \\ \phi &=MI \\ \vec{B}&=\frac{\mu _{o}I}{2\pi \rho }\hat{a_{\phi }} \;\; (\vec{B} \text{ due to infinite long line}) \\ \text{Magnetic flux}& \text{ crossing square loop is}\\ \phi &=\int \int \vec{B}\cdot \vec{ds} \\ &=\int \int \frac{\mu _{o}I}{2\pi \rho }\hat{a_{\phi }}\cdot (d\rho dz)\hat{a_{\phi }}\\ &=\frac{\mu _{0}I}{2\pi }\int_{\rho =1}^{2}\frac{d\rho }{\rho }\int_{z=0}^{1}dz \\ \phi &=\frac{\mu _{o} I}{2\pi }(\ln \rho )_{\rho =1}^{2}(z)_{z=0}^{1} \\ \phi &=\frac{\mu _{o} I}{2\pi }(\ln 2)\\ M&=\frac{\phi }{I} \\ M&=\frac{\phi_{o}(\ln2)}{2\pi }=\frac{4\pi \times 10^{-7}(\ln _{2})}{2\pi } \\ M&=1.386\times 10^{-7}\, Henry \simeq 138.63\, nH \end{aligned}[/latex]

2019.text: If [latex]f=2x^3+3y^2+4z[/latex], the value of line integral [latex]\int _c grad \; f\cdot dr[/latex] evaluated over  contour C formed by the segments (-3,-3,2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (2,-3,2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (2,6,2) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] (2,6,-1) is_______

2019.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} f&=2x^3+3y^2+4z\\ \Delta f&=6x^2\hat{i}+6y\hat{j}+4\hat{k}\\ \text{curl} (\Delta f)&=\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\\ \frac{\partial }{\partial x}&\frac{\partial }{\partial y} &\frac{\partial }{\partial z} \\ 6x^2& 6y & 4\end{vmatrix}\\ \therefore \;\;\int _c\Delta f\cdot dr&=\int _c d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)=0\\ &=\int_{(-3,-3,2)}^{2,-3,2}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &+\int_{(2,-3,2)}^{(2,6,2)}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &+\int_{(2,6,2)}^{(2,6,-1)}d(2x^3+3y^2+4z)\\ &=70+81+(-12)=139 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2019.text: A periodic function [latex]f(t)[/latex], with a period of [latex]2\pi[/latex], is represented as its Fourier series, [latex]f(t)=a_0+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }a_n\cos nt+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }a_n\sin nt[/latex]. If [latex]f(t)=\left\{\begin{matrix} A \sin t, & 0\leq t\leq \pi\\ 0,& \pi\lt t\lt 2\pi \end{matrix}\right.[/latex] the Fourier series coefficients [latex]a_1 \; and \; b_1[/latex] of [latex]f(t)[/latex] are
2019.html:
A periodic function [latex]f(t)[/latex], with a period of [latex]2\pi[/latex], is represented as its Fourier series,
[latex]f(t)=a_0+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }a_n\cos nt+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty }a_n\sin nt[/latex].
If
[latex]f(t)=\left\{\begin{matrix} A \sin t, & 0\leq t\leq \pi\\ 0,& \pi\lt t\lt 2\pi \end{matrix}\right.[/latex]
the Fourier series coefficients [latex]a_1 \; and \; b_1[/latex] of [latex]f(t)[/latex] are
2019.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Series
2019.explanation_text:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
T_0 &=2\pi \Rightarrow \;\omega _0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=1 \\ 
\text{Now, }b_1 &=\frac{2}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0}f(t) \sin \omega _0 t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{2}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(t) \sin t \; dt\;\;[\because \omega _0=1]\\ 
 &= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} A \sin t \cdot \sin t\; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}2 \sin ^2 t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}[1-\cos 2t] \; dt \\ 
 &=\frac{A}{2 \pi} \left [ t-\frac{\sin 2t}{2} \right ]_0^{\pi} \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi} [(\pi-0)-(0-0)]=\frac{A}{2}\\ 
 a_1&=\frac{2}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0}f(t) \cos \omega _0 t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{2}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(t) \cos t \; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} A \sin t \cdot \cos t\; dt \\ 
 &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin 2t \; dt=0
\end{aligned}[/latex]
2019.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} T_0 &=2\pi \Rightarrow \;\omega _0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}=1 \\ \text{Now, }b_1 &=\frac{2}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0}f(t) \sin \omega _0 t \; dt \\ &= \frac{2}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(t) \sin t \; dt\;\;[\because \omega _0=1]\\ &= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} A \sin t \cdot \sin t\; dt \\ &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}2 \sin ^2 t \; dt \\ &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}[1-\cos 2t] \; dt \\ &=\frac{A}{2 \pi} \left [ t-\frac{\sin 2t}{2} \right ]_0^{\pi} \\ &= \frac{A}{2 \pi} [(\pi-0)-(0-0)]=\frac{A}{2}\\ a_1&=\frac{2}{T_0}\int_{0}^{T_0}f(t) \cos \omega _0 t \; dt \\ &= \frac{2}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(t) \cos t \; dt \\ &= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} A \sin t \cdot \cos t\; dt \\ &= \frac{A}{2 \pi}\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin 2t \; dt=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
