2014-set-1.html: [latex]C_0[/latex] is the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with air as dielectric (as in figure (a)). If, half of the entire gap as shown in figure (b) is filled with a dielectric of permittivity [latex]\epsilon _r[/latex] , the expression for the modified capacitance is

2014-set-1.explanation_text: Let A be the area of the parallel plate capacitor and d be the distance between the plates. Let [latex]C_1[/latex] be the capacitance of half portion with air as dielectic medium and [latex]C_2[/latex] be capacitance with a dielectic of permitivity, [latex]\varepsilon _r[/latex]. Then, [latex]C_1=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area become half) and [latex]C_2=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \varepsilon _r \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area becomes half) Now, these two capacitance will be in parallel if a voltage is applied between the plates as same potential difference will be there between both the capacitance. Let A be the area of the parallel plate capacitor and d be the distance between the plates.

Let [latex]C_1[/latex] be the capacitance of half portion with air as dielectic medium and [latex]C_2[/latex] be capacitance with a dielectic of permitivity, [latex]\varepsilon _r[/latex].
Then, [latex]C_1=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area become half)
and [latex]C_2=\frac{\varepsilon _0 \varepsilon _r \left ( \frac{A}{2} \right )}{d}[/latex] (As area becomes half)
Now, these two capacitance will be in parallel if a voltage is applied between the plates as same potential difference will be there between both the capacitance.

Equivalent capacitance is
[latex]\begin{aligned} C_{eqv} &= C_1+C_2\\ &=\frac{\varepsilon _0 A}{2d}+ \frac{\varepsilon _0 \varepsilon _r A}{2d}\\ &= \frac{\varepsilon _0 A}{2d}(1+ \varepsilon _r)=\frac{C_0}{2}(1+\varepsilon _r) \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]C_{eqv}=\frac{C_0}{2}(1+\varepsilon _r)[/latex]

A star connected 400 V, 50 Hz, 4 pole synchronous machine gave the following
open circuit and short circuit test results : Open circuit test : [latex]V_{oc}[/latex] = 400 V (rms, line-to-line) at field current, [latex]I_{f}[/latex] = 2.3 A Short circuit test : [latex]I_{sc}[/latex]= 10 A (rms, phase) at field current,
[latex]I_{f}[/latex] = 1.5 A The value of per phase synchronous impedance in [latex]\Omega[/latex] at rated voltage is_____.
2014-set-1.html:
A star connected 400 V, 50 Hz, 4 pole synchronous machine gave the following open circuit and short circuit test results :
Open circuit test : [latex]V_{oc}[/latex] = 400 V (rms, line-to-line) at field current, [latex]I_{f}[/latex] = 2.3 A
Short circuit test : [latex]I_{sc}[/latex]= 10 A (rms, phase) at field current, [latex]I_{f}[/latex] = 1.5 A

The value of per phase synchronous impedance in [latex]\Omega[/latex] at rated voltage is_____.
2014-set-1.subject: Electrical Machines - Synchronous Machines
2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given, for}\;\;V_{OC} &= 400V(rms)\\ &= \frac{400}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &= 230.94 \;\text{(Phase value),}\\ I_f&= 2.3A\\ \text{for}\;\; I_{sc}&=10A \;\text{(rms, phase)} \\ I_f&= 1.5A\\ & \therefore \;\;\text{Base impedance}\\ Z_{base}&=\frac{V_{OC}}{I_{sc}}\\ &=\frac{230.94}{10}=23.094\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex] For finding the synchronous impedance at rated voltage, saturation effect of the machine has to be considered (i.e. the adjusted value of [latex]Z_s[/latex]) short circuit ratio, [latex]\begin{aligned} SCR &=\frac{I_f \;for \; V_{OC}}{I_f \;for \; I_{sc}} \\ &=\frac{1}{Z_{s_{(sat)pu}}} =\frac{2.3}{1.5}\\ Z_{s_{(sat)pu}} &= 0.65 pu \end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, actual value of [latex]Z_s[/latex] at rated voltage [latex]\begin{aligned} &=Z_{s_{(sat)pu}} \times Z_{base} \\ &=0.65 \times 23.094=15.06\Omega \\ \therefore \;\;Z_s&= 15.06\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given, for}\;\;V_{OC} &= 400V(rms)\\ &= \frac{400}{\sqrt{3}}\\ &= 230.94 \;\text{(Phase value),}\\ I_f&= 2.3A\\ \text{for}\;\; I_{sc}&=10A \;\text{(rms, phase)} \\ I_f&= 1.5A\\ & \therefore \;\;\text{Base impedance}\\ Z_{base}&=\frac{V_{OC}}{I_{sc}}\\ &=\frac{230.94}{10}=23.094\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
For finding the synchronous impedance at rated voltage, saturation effect of the machine has to be considered (i.e. the adjusted value of [latex]Z_s[/latex])
short circuit ratio,
[latex]\begin{aligned} SCR &=\frac{I_f \;for \; V_{OC}}{I_f \;for \; I_{sc}} \\ &=\frac{1}{Z_{s_{(sat)pu}}} =\frac{2.3}{1.5}\\ Z_{s_{(sat)pu}} &= 0.65 pu \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, actual value of [latex]Z_s[/latex] at rated voltage
[latex]\begin{aligned} &=Z_{s_{(sat)pu}} \times Z_{base} \\ &=0.65 \times 23.094=15.06\Omega \\ \therefore \;\;Z_s&= 15.06\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-1.text: An incandescent lamp is marked 40 W, 240 V. If resistance at room temperature (26[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C) is 120 [latex]\Omega[/latex], and temperature coefficient of resistance is [latex]4.5\times 10^{-3}/^{\circ}[/latex]C, then its 'ON' state filament temperature in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C is approximately_____.
2014-set-1.html: An incandescent lamp is marked 40 W, 240 V. If resistance at room temperature (26[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C) is 120 [latex]\Omega[/latex], and temperature coefficient of resistance is [latex]4.5\times 10^{-3}/^{\circ}[/latex]C, then its 'ON' state filament temperature in [latex]^{\circ}[/latex]C is approximately_____.
2014-set-1.subject: Electric Circuits - Basics of Electric Circuit
2014-set-1.explanation_text: Let the resistance of incandescent lamp [latex]=R_T=\frac{V^2}{P}=\frac{(240)^2}{40}=1440\Omega[/latex] Given,  [latex]  R_0=120\Omega ,[/latex] [latex]\alpha =4.5 \times 10^{-3}/^{\circ}C [/latex] Let, [latex]R_T[/latex] be the resistance of the filament in ON state at temperature T. Then, [latex] R_T=R_0[1+\alpha \Delta T] [/latex] [latex][1+\alpha \Delta T]=\frac{R_T}{R_0}=\frac{1440}{120}=12[/latex] [latex] \alpha \Delta T=11 [/latex] [latex]\Delta T=2444.44^{\circ}C[/latex] [latex] T=2444.44^{\circ}C+26^{\circ} [/latex] [latex]T=2470.44^{\circ}C [/latex] Therefore, ON state temperature of filament [latex]= 2470.44^{\circ}C[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Let the resistance of incandescent lamp
[latex]=R_T=\frac{V^2}{P}=\frac{(240)^2}{40}=1440\Omega[/latex]
Given, [latex] R_0=120\Omega ,[/latex]
[latex]\alpha =4.5 \times 10^{-3}/^{\circ}C [/latex]
Let, [latex]R_T[/latex] be the resistance of the filament in ON state at temperature T.
Then, [latex] R_T=R_0[1+\alpha \Delta T] [/latex]
[latex][1+\alpha \Delta T]=\frac{R_T}{R_0}=\frac{1440}{120}=12[/latex]
[latex] \alpha \Delta T=11 [/latex]
[latex]\Delta T=2444.44^{\circ}C[/latex]
[latex] T=2444.44^{\circ}C+26^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]T=2470.44^{\circ}C [/latex]
Therefore, ON state temperature of filament [latex]= 2470.44^{\circ}C[/latex]

2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given, [latex]R=\left ( 25+\frac{I}{2} \right )\Omega [/latex] [latex]I=(2R-50) [/latex] Applying KVL in given loop, we have [latex] 300=IR[/latex] [latex] 300=(2R-50)\times R [/latex] we get, [latex]R=30\Omega \; or \; -5\Omega[/latex] Since, resistance can't be negative. therefore, [latex]R=30\Omega [/latex] Hence,  [latex] I=(2R-50) [/latex] [latex]\;\;=(2 \times 30-50)=10A [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; Current, I=10A[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]R=\left ( 25+\frac{I}{2} \right )\Omega [/latex]
[latex]I=(2R-50) [/latex]

Applying KVL in given loop, we have
[latex] 300=IR[/latex]
[latex] 300=(2R-50)\times R [/latex]
we get, [latex]R=30\Omega \; or \; -5\Omega[/latex]
Since, resistance can't be negative. therefore,
[latex]R=30\Omega [/latex]
Hence, [latex] I=(2R-50) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=(2 \times 30-50)=10A [/latex]

2014-set-1.explanation_text:
Given, [latex]\begin{aligned} I_a&= 1\angle (-90^{\circ})pu\\ I_b&= 4\angle (-150^{\circ})pu\\ I_c&= 3\angle (90^{\circ})pu \end{aligned}[/latex] As zero sequence current in all the three phases of unbalanced [latex]3-\phi[/latex] system are equal, therefore, [latex]I_{a_0}=I_{b_0}=I_{c_0}=3\angle 90^{\circ}pu[/latex] Also,  [latex]I_{b_2}=4\angle -150^{\circ}[/latex] =Negative phase sequence current of phase b. Therefore, referring to the negative phase sequence phasor, [latex]I_{b_2}=4\angle (-150^{\circ}-120^{\circ})=4\angle-270^{\circ}pu[/latex] We know that, phase current vectors in matrix form are given by [latex] \begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}
I_a\\ 
I_b\\ 
I_c
\end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix}
1 &1  &1 \\ 
 1& a^2 &a \\ 
1 & a &a^2 
\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}
I_{a_0}\\ 
I_{a_1}\\ 
I_{a_2}
\end{bmatrix} \\ 
\text{Here, } I_a&=I_{a_0}+I_{a_1}+I_{a_2} \\ 
\text{Given, } I_a&=1\angle -90^{\circ} \\ 
 I_{a_0}&=3\angle 90^{\circ} \\ 
 I_{a_2}&=4\angle -270^{\circ} \\ 
 \text{Therefore,}& \\ 
 I_{a_1}&=I_a-(I_{a_0}+I_{a_2}) \\ 
 &=(1\angle -90^{\circ})-(3\angle 90^{\circ}+4\angle 270^{\circ}) \\ 
 I_{a_1}&=8\angle -90^{\circ}pu \\ 
 \text{Therefore,}& \\
 I_b&=I_{a_0}+a^2I_{a_1}+aI_{a_2}\\
&=(3\angle 90^{\circ})+(1\angle 120^{\circ})^2 (8\angle -90^{\circ}) \\
&+(1\angle 120^{\circ})(4\angle -270^{\circ})\\
&=3\angle 90^{\circ}+8\angle 150^{\circ}+4\angle -150^{\circ}\\
I_b&=11.53\angle 154.3^{\circ}pu\\
&\text{Magnitude of phase current,}\\
I_b&=11.53\;pu
\end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]F(\omega)=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(t)e^{-j \omega t}dt[/latex]

[latex]g(t)=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{-jut}du[/latex]

2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given that, [latex]\begin{aligned} f(t)&\rightleftharpoons F(\omega )\\ g(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{-jut}du\\ \text{Now, }f(t)&=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(\omega)e^{j \omega t}d\omega \\ \Rightarrow \; 2 \pi f(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(\omega)e^{j \omega t}d\omega \\ \omega &\rightarrow u,\\ 2 \pi f(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{j u t}du \\ t &\rightarrow -t,\\ 2 \pi f(-t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }F(u)e^{-j u t}du \\ &=g(t)\\ \Rightarrow \; g(t)&=2 \pi f(-t)\\ &= 2\pi f(t) \end{aligned}[/latex] [If [latex]f(t)[/latex] is even then [latex]f(t)=f(-t)[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; g(t) \propto f(t) \text{ if }f(t) \text{ is even.}[/latex]

2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given, at 230V, 50 Hz, core loss =1050 W and at 138 V, 30 Hz, core loss =500 W Let, [latex]V_1=230 V, \;f_1=50Hz[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e1} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h1} \\ V_2=138V &, f_230Hz \\ \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e2} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h2} \\ \text{we know that, } & \\ \text{Eddy current loss,}\;& P_e \propto B_m^2f^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto B_m^xf\propto B_m^1.6 f \\ &(\text{Typical value of x=1.6}) \end{aligned}[/latex] The transformer induced emf equation is: [latex]\begin{aligned} V_1 &=\sqrt{2} \pi \phi _m N \\ V_1&= \sqrt{2} \pi f B_m A N\\ \text{where,}\;\; \frac{V}{t} &=\text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex] i.e. flux = constant ( to avoid over fluxing) [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss,} &P_e \propto V^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto\frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{e2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^2=0.36 \\ \text{or,} \;\; P_{e2} &= 0.36P_{e1}\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also,} \;\;\frac{P_{h2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{50}{30} \right )^{0.6} \\ &= (0.6)^{1.6} \times \frac{1}{(0.6)^{0.6}}=0.6\\ \therefore \;\; P_{h2} &=0.6P_{h1} \;\;...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex] Given at 230V, 50Hz [latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e1}+P_{h1}=1050W\;\;...(iii) [/latex] At 138V, 30Hz, [latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e2}+P_{h2}=500W [/latex] or,   [latex]0.36P_{e1}+0.6P_{h1}=500W\;\;...(iv)[/latex] solving equation (iii) and (iv), we get [latex]P_{h1}=508W [/latex] and [latex] P_{e1}=542W[/latex] Therefore, hysteresis and eddy current losses at 230V, 50Hz are 508W and 542W respectively.
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Given, at 230V, 50 Hz, core loss =1050 W
and at 138 V, 30 Hz, core loss =500 W
Let, [latex]V_1=230 V, \;f_1=50Hz[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e1} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h1} \\ V_2=138V &, f_230Hz \\ \text{Eddy current loss} &=P_{e2} \\ \text{Hysteresis loss}&=P_{h2} \\ \text{we know that, } & \\ \text{Eddy current loss,}\;& P_e \propto B_m^2f^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto B_m^xf\propto B_m^1.6 f \\ &(\text{Typical value of x=1.6}) \end{aligned}[/latex]
The transformer induced emf equation is:
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_1 &=\sqrt{2} \pi \phi _m N \\ V_1&= \sqrt{2} \pi f B_m A N\\ \text{where,}\;\; \frac{V}{t} &=\text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex]
i.e. flux = constant ( to avoid over fluxing)
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Eddy current loss,} &P_e \propto V^2 \\ \text{and hysteresis loss,}&P_h \propto\frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{P_{e2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^2=0.36 \\ \text{or,} \;\; P_{e2} &= 0.36P_{e1}\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also,} \;\;\frac{P_{h2}}{P_{e1}} &=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=\left ( \frac{138}{230} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{50}{30} \right )^{0.6} \\ &= (0.6)^{1.6} \times \frac{1}{(0.6)^{0.6}}=0.6\\ \therefore \;\; P_{h2} &=0.6P_{h1} \;\;...(ii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Given at 230V, 50Hz
[latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e1}+P_{h1}=1050W\;\;...(iii) [/latex]
At 138V, 30Hz,
[latex]\text{Core loss}=P_{e2}+P_{h2}=500W [/latex]
or, [latex]0.36P_{e1}+0.6P_{h1}=500W\;\;...(iv)[/latex]
solving equation (iii) and (iv), we get
[latex]P_{h1}=508W [/latex] and [latex] P_{e1}=542W[/latex]
Therefore, hysteresis and eddy current losses at 230V, 50Hz are 508W and 542W respectively.

2014-set-1.text: A 15 kW, 230 V dc shunt motor has armature circuit resistance of 0.4 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and field circuit resistance of 230 [latex]\Omega[/latex] . At no load and rated voltage, the motor runs at 1400 rpm and the line current drawn by the motor is 5 A. At full load, the motor draws a line current of 70 A. Neglect armature reaction. The full load speed of the motor in rpm is_____.

2014-set-1.subject: Electrical Machines - DC Machines
2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given, [latex]R_a=0.4\Omega , [/latex] [latex]R_f=230\Omega , [/latex]  [latex]V=230 \;\text{volt} [/latex] At no load, speed, [latex]N_0=1400 \;\text{rpm}, [/latex]  [latex]I_{L_0}=5A [/latex] Field current,  [latex]I_f=\frac{V}{R_f}=\frac{230}{230}=1A[/latex] No load armature current, [latex]I_{a_0}=5-1=4A[/latex] Induced emf at no-load, [latex]E_{a_0}=V-I_{a_0}R_a[/latex] [latex]\;\; \;\;=230-4 \times 0.4=228.4 V [/latex] Also, at full load, [latex]I_{L_{fl}}=70A [/latex] [latex]I_{a_{fl}}=I_{L_{fl}}-I_f=70-1=69A [/latex] Induced emf at full load, [latex]E_{a_{fl}}=V-I_{a{fl}}R_a [/latex] [latex]E_{a_{fl}}=230 -69 \times 0.4=202.4V [/latex] we know that, [latex]\begin{aligned} E_a&\propto \phi \omega _m \alpha \propto N \\ E_a &\propto N \\ (\text{as flux} \; \phi \; &\text{is constant in shunt motor}) \\ \therefore \; \frac{E_{a_{fl}}}{E_{a_{0}}} &=\frac{N_{fl}}{N_0} \\ N_{fl}&= \frac{E_{a_{fl}}}{E_{a_{0}}} \times N_0 \\ &=\left ( \frac{202.4}{228.4} \right ) \times 1400 \end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, full-load speed of motor = 1240.63 rpm

At no load, speed, [latex]N_0=1400 \;\text{rpm}, [/latex] [latex]I_{L_0}=5A [/latex]
Field current, [latex]I_f=\frac{V}{R_f}=\frac{230}{230}=1A[/latex]

No load armature current, [latex]I_{a_0}=5-1=4A[/latex]
Induced emf at no-load,
[latex]E_{a_0}=V-I_{a_0}R_a[/latex]
[latex]\;\; \;\;=230-4 \times 0.4=228.4 V [/latex]
Also, at full load,
[latex]I_{L_{fl}}=70A [/latex]
[latex]I_{a_{fl}}=I_{L_{fl}}-I_f=70-1=69A [/latex]
Induced emf at full load,
[latex]E_{a_{fl}}=V-I_{a{fl}}R_a [/latex]
[latex]E_{a_{fl}}=230 -69 \times 0.4=202.4V [/latex]
we know that,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_a&\propto \phi \omega _m \alpha \propto N \\ E_a &\propto N \\ (\text{as flux} \; \phi \; &\text{is constant in shunt motor}) \\ \therefore \; \frac{E_{a_{fl}}}{E_{a_{0}}} &=\frac{N_{fl}}{N_0} \\ N_{fl}&= \frac{E_{a_{fl}}}{E_{a_{0}}} \times N_0 \\ &=\left ( \frac{202.4}{228.4} \right ) \times 1400 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, full-load speed of motor = 1240.63 rpm

2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given, [latex]\begin{aligned} R'_2 &=0.1\Omega \\ X'_2&= 0.92\Omega \\ S_{fl}&=3\%=0.03 \end{aligned}[/latex] Slip at maximum torque, [latex] S_m=\frac{R'_2}{X'_2}=\frac{0.1}{0.92}=0.1087 [/latex] We know that, [latex]\begin{aligned}\frac{T_{fl}}{T_{em}}&=\frac{2}{\left ( \frac{S_m}{S_{fl}}+\frac{S_{fl}}{S_m} \right )}\\ \therefore \;\; \frac{T_{fl}}{T_{em}}&=\frac{2}{\left ( \frac{0.1087}{0.03}+\frac{0.03}{0.1087} \right )}\\ &=\frac{2}{3.623+0.275}=\frac{2}{3.898}\\ \frac{T_{em}}{T_{fl}}&= 1.949 \end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, ratio of maximum torque to full-load torque [latex]=\frac{T_{em}}{T_{fl}}= 1.949[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Given,
[latex]\begin{aligned} R'_2 &=0.1\Omega \\ X'_2&= 0.92\Omega \\ S_{fl}&=3\%=0.03 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Slip at maximum torque,
[latex] S_m=\frac{R'_2}{X'_2}=\frac{0.1}{0.92}=0.1087 [/latex]
We know that,
[latex]\begin{aligned}\frac{T_{fl}}{T_{em}}&=\frac{2}{\left ( \frac{S_m}{S_{fl}}+\frac{S_{fl}}{S_m} \right )}\\ \therefore \;\; \frac{T_{fl}}{T_{em}}&=\frac{2}{\left ( \frac{0.1087}{0.03}+\frac{0.03}{0.1087} \right )}\\ &=\frac{2}{3.623+0.275}=\frac{2}{3.898}\\ \frac{T_{em}}{T_{fl}}&= 1.949 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, ratio of maximum torque to full-load torque [latex]=\frac{T_{em}}{T_{fl}}= 1.949[/latex]

2014-set-1.html:
A distribution feeder of 1 km length having resistance, but negligible reactance, is fed from both the ends by 400 V, 50 Hz balanced sources. Both voltage sources [latex]S_1 \; and \; S_2[/latex] are in phase. The feeder supplies concentrated loads of unity power factor as shown in the figure.
The contributions of [latex]S_1 \; and \; S_2[/latex] in 100 A current supplied at location P respectively, are
2014-set-1.subject: Power Systems - Distribution Systems, Cables and Insulators
2014-set-1.explanation_text:
Let the resistance of whole length of feeder be [latex]R\;\Omega[/latex], length of feeder =1000m. [latex]\therefore \;[/latex] Resistance per unit length [latex]=\frac{R}{1000}\Omega /meter[/latex] [latex]\therefore \;[/latex] Resistance of 400 m length [latex]=\frac{R}{1000} \times 400 =\frac{2R}{5} \Omega [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;[/latex] Resistance of 200 m length [latex] =\frac{R}{5} \Omega [/latex] Let the current supplied by the sources be [latex]I_1 \text{ and } I_2[/latex]. Applying KVL from source [latex]S_1 \text{ and } S_2[/latex], we have: [latex]\begin{aligned}
400 &= \frac{2R}{5}I_1+\frac{R}{5}(I_1-200)\\ & -\frac{R}{5}(I_2-200)-\frac{R}{5}I_2+400\\ 
 0&= \frac{2}{5}I_1 +\frac{I_1-200}{5}+\frac{200-I_2}{5}-\frac{I_2}{5}\\ 
 0&=2I_1+I_1-200+200-I_2-I_2 \\ 
 0&=3I_1-2I_2\\
I_1&=\frac{2}{3}I_2\;\;\;...(i)\\
\text{also, }& I_1 +I_2-400=100\\
\text{or, }&I_1+I_2=500 \;\;\;...(ii)\\
&\text{Solvinf eq. (i) and (ii), we have}\\
I_1&=200A \text{ and }I_2=300A\\
&\text{Contribution of }S_1 \text{in 100 A at location}\\
P&=I_1-200=0A \\
&\text{Contribution of }S_2 \text{in 100 A at location}\\
P&=I_2-200=300-200=100A
\end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, [latex]S_2[/latex] alone supplies the total load at location P.

2014-set-1.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} P_2+jQ_2&=(1.0+j0.5)p.u.\\ P_2&=1=\frac{|V_1||V_2|}{|X|} \sin (\delta _1-\delta _2)\\ 1&=\frac{V_1}{0.1}\sin (-\delta _2)\\ -\frac{0.1}{\sin (-\delta _2)}&=V_1\;\;...(i)\\ Q_2&=0.5=\frac{|V_2|}{|X|}(|V_1| \cos \delta _2 -|V_2|)\\ 0.5&=\frac{1}{0.1}(V_1 \cos \delta _2-1)\\ \frac{1.05}{\cos \delta _2}&=V_1\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{From equation (i) and (ii),}\\ \tan \delta _2&=\frac{-0.1}{1.05}\\ \delta _2&=-5.44^{\circ}\\ \text{substituting } & \delta _2 \text{ value in equation (ii) gives,}\\ V_1&=1.05\;p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]

For the given system, it is desired that the system be stable. The minimum value
of [latex]\alpha[/latex] for this condition is ______.
2014-set-1.html: For the given system, it is desired that the system be stable. The minimum value of [latex]\alpha[/latex] for this condition is ______.
2014-set-1.subject: Control Systems - Concepts of Stability
2014-set-1.explanation_text: Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{(s+\alpha )}{s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )} [/latex] and  [latex] H(s)=1[/latex] Characteristic equation of given control system is given by [latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0 [/latex] or, [latex] 1+\left [ \frac{s+\alpha }{s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )} \right ]=0[/latex] or, [latex] s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )+s+\alpha =0 [/latex] or,  [latex] s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+\alpha s+1=0[/latex] Routh's array is For the given system to be stable, there should not be any sign change in the first column of Routh's array. Therefore, [latex]1+\alpha \gt 0 \;or, \; \alpha \gt -1\;\; ...(i)[/latex] Also,  [latex] \frac{\alpha ^2 +\alpha -1}{1+\alpha } \gt 0 [/latex] or,  [latex]   \alpha ^2 +\alpha -1 \gt 0 [/latex] or,  [latex] (\alpha +1.618)(\alpha -0.618) \gt 0 [/latex] or,   [latex] \alpha \lt -1.618[/latex] or,  [latex] \alpha \gt 0.618[/latex] As  [latex] \alpha \gt -1[/latex] (using equation (i)) therefore, [latex]\alpha \gt 0.618 \;\;...(ii) [/latex] Combining condition (i) and (ii), [latex] -1 \lt \alpha \lt 0.618 [/latex] Thus, for the system to be stable minimum value of  [latex]\alpha =0.618.[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{(s+\alpha )}{s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )} [/latex]
and [latex] H(s)=1[/latex]
Characteristic equation of given control system is given by
[latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0 [/latex]
or, [latex] 1+\left [ \frac{s+\alpha }{s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )} \right ]=0[/latex]
or, [latex] s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+(\alpha -1)s+(1-\alpha )+s+\alpha =0 [/latex]
or, [latex] s^3+(1+\alpha )s^2+\alpha s+1=0[/latex]
Routh's array is

For the given system to be stable, there should not be any sign change in the first column of Routh's array.
Therefore, [latex]1+\alpha \gt 0 \;or, \; \alpha \gt -1\;\; ...(i)[/latex]
Also, [latex] \frac{\alpha ^2 +\alpha -1}{1+\alpha } \gt 0 [/latex]
or, [latex] \alpha ^2 +\alpha -1 \gt 0 [/latex]
or, [latex] (\alpha +1.618)(\alpha -0.618) \gt 0 [/latex]
or, [latex] \alpha \lt -1.618[/latex]
or, [latex] \alpha \gt 0.618[/latex]
As [latex] \alpha \gt -1[/latex] (using equation (i))
therefore, [latex]\alpha \gt 0.618 \;\;...(ii) [/latex]
Combining condition (i) and (ii),
[latex] -1 \lt \alpha \lt 0.618 [/latex]
Thus, for the system to be stable minimum value of [latex]\alpha =0.618.[/latex]

2014-set-1.subject: Control Systems - Frequency Response Analysis
2014-set-1.explanation_text:
Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{K(1+0.5s)(1+as)}{s(1+\frac{s}{8})(1+bs)(1+\frac{s}{36})}[/latex] (1+as) is addition of zero to the transfer function whose contribution in slope=+20 dB/decade or -6 dB/octave. (1+bs) is addition of pole to the transfer function whose contribution in slope=-20 dB/decade or -6 dB/octave. Observing the change in the slope at different corner frequencies, we conclude that, [latex]
a=\frac{1}{4}[/latex] rad/s and [latex]b=\frac{1}{24}[/latex] rad/s From[latex] \omega =0.01[/latex] rad/s to [latex]\omega =8[/latex] rad/s, slope=-20dB/decade Let the vertical length in dB by y [latex]\therefore \;\; -20=\left ( \frac{0-y}{log8-log0.01} \right )[/latex] [latex] \;\;\;\; -20=\frac{y}{log 8+2}[/latex] [latex]
\;\;\;\; y=58 dB[/latex] Applying, [latex]y-mx+C[/latex] at [latex]\omega =0.01[/latex] rad/s, We have, [latex]58=-20log 0.01 +C[/latex] [latex]C=58-40=18[/latex] Now, [latex]C=20logK[/latex] [latex]
LogK=\frac{18}{20}=0.9[/latex] [latex]
\therefore \;\; K= log^{-1}(0.9)=(10)^{0.9}=7.94[/latex] [latex]
\therefore \;\; \frac{a}{bK}=\frac{\left ( \frac{1}{4} \right )}{\left ( \frac{1}{24} \right )\times 7.94}=\frac{24}{4 \times 7.94}=0.755[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{K(1+0.5s)(1+as)}{s(1+\frac{s}{8})(1+bs)(1+\frac{s}{36})}[/latex]
(1+as) is addition of zero to the transfer function whose contribution in slope=+20 dB/decade or -6 dB/octave.
(1+bs) is addition of pole to the transfer function whose contribution in slope=-20 dB/decade or -6 dB/octave.
Observing the change in the slope at different corner frequencies, we conclude that,
[latex] a=\frac{1}{4}[/latex] rad/s and [latex]b=\frac{1}{24}[/latex] rad/s
From[latex] \omega =0.01[/latex] rad/s to [latex]\omega =8[/latex] rad/s,
slope=-20dB/decade
Let the vertical length in dB by y
[latex]\therefore \;\; -20=\left ( \frac{0-y}{log8-log0.01} \right )[/latex]
[latex] \;\;\;\; -20=\frac{y}{log 8+2}[/latex]
[latex] \;\;\;\; y=58 dB[/latex]
Applying, [latex]y-mx+C[/latex] at [latex]\omega =0.01[/latex] rad/s,
We have, [latex]58=-20log 0.01 +C[/latex]
[latex]C=58-40=18[/latex]
Now, [latex]C=20logK[/latex]
[latex] LogK=\frac{18}{20}=0.9[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \;\; K= log^{-1}(0.9)=(10)^{0.9}=7.94[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \;\; \frac{a}{bK}=\frac{\left ( \frac{1}{4} \right )}{\left ( \frac{1}{24} \right )\times 7.94}=\frac{24}{4 \times 7.94}=0.755[/latex]

2014-set-1.text:
A system matrix is given as follows [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & -1\\ -6& -11&6 \\ -6 & -11 & 5 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] The absolute value of the ratio of the maximum eigenvalue to the minimum
eigenvalue is _______.
2014-set-1.html:
A system matrix is given as follows
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & -1\\ -6& -11&6 \\ -6 & -11 & 5 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The absolute value of the ratio of the maximum eigenvalue to the minimum eigenvalue is _______.
2014-set-1.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
2014-set-1.explanation_text: Characteristic equation [latex]|A-\lambda I|=0[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 1 & -1\\ -6 & -11-\lambda & 6\\ -6&-11 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda [-55+11\lambda -5\lambda +\lambda ^2+66] \\ -1[-30+6\lambda +36]-1[66-66-6\lambda ]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda (\lambda ^2+6\lambda +11)-1(6\lambda +6)+6\lambda =0 \\ \Rightarrow \;-\lambda ^3-6\lambda ^2-11\lambda -6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda ^3+6\lambda ^2+11\lambda +6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +3)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda =-1,-2,-3 \end{aligned}[/latex] The absolute values of [latex]\lambda[/latex] are [latex]|\lambda |=1,2,3[/latex] Ratio of maximum and minimum eigen value is [latex]=3:1=\frac{3}{1}=3[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
Characteristic equation [latex]|A-\lambda I|=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{vmatrix} -\lambda & 1 & -1\\ -6 & -11-\lambda & 6\\ -6&-11 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda [-55+11\lambda -5\lambda +\lambda ^2+66] \\ -1[-30+6\lambda +36]-1[66-66-6\lambda ]=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; -\lambda (\lambda ^2+6\lambda +11)-1(6\lambda +6)+6\lambda =0 \\ \Rightarrow \;-\lambda ^3-6\lambda ^2-11\lambda -6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda ^3+6\lambda ^2+11\lambda +6=0 \\ \Rightarrow \; (\lambda +1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda +3)=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\lambda =-1,-2,-3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The absolute values of [latex]\lambda[/latex] are [latex]|\lambda |=1,2,3[/latex]
Ratio of maximum and minimum eigen value is [latex]=3:1=\frac{3}{1}=3[/latex]

2014-set-1.text:
The dc current flowing in a circuit is measured by two ammeters, one PMMC
and another electrodynamometer type, connected in series. The PMMC meter
contains 100 turns in the coil, the flux density in the air gap is 0.2Wb/[latex]m^2[/latex], and
the area of the coil is 80 [latex]mm^2[/latex]. The electrodynamometer ammeter has a change in
mutual inductance with respect to deflection of 0.5 mH/deg. The spring constants
of both the meters are equal. The value of current, at which the deflections of the
two meters are same, is ______
2014-set-1.html: The dc current flowing in a circuit is measured by two ammeters, one PMMC and another electrodynamometer type, connected in series. The PMMC meter contains 100 turns in the coil, the flux density in the air gap is 0.2Wb/[latex]m^2[/latex], and the area of the coil is 80 [latex]mm^2[/latex]. The electrodynamometer ammeter has a change in mutual inductance with respect to deflection of 0.5 mH/deg. The spring constants of both the meters are equal. The value of current, at which the deflections of the two meters are same, is ______
2014-set-1.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Galvanometers, Voltmeters and Ammeters
2014-set-1.explanation_text: For a PMMC ammeter, at equilibrim, we have : controlling torque ([latex]T_c[/latex])=Deflecting torque([latex]T_d[/latex]) [latex]\begin{aligned} K\theta _1 &=GI \; \text{or}\; \theta _1=\frac{GI}{K}\\ where, \;\; G &= nBA\\ \therefore \; \theta _1 &= \frac{nBAI}{K} \end{aligned}[/latex] For an electrodynometer ammeter, at equilibrium, Controlling torque=Deflecting torque [latex]\begin{aligned} i.e. \;\; T_c &=T_d \; \text{or}\; K \theta _2=I^2 \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; \theta _2 &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\;\;...(ii)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] For the deflection in the two meter to be same, [latex]\begin{aligned} \theta _1 &=\theta _2\\ or, \;\; \frac{nBAI}{K} &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; nBA&=I\frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; I &=\frac{nBA}{\left ( \frac{dM}{d\theta } \right )} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} Given, \;\; n&= \text{number of turns}=100\\ B&= 0.2 Wb/m^2\\ A&=80mm^2=80 \times 10^{-6}m^2\\ \text{and}\;\; \frac{dM}{d\theta }&=0.5 mH/rad\\ &=0.5 \times 10^{-3}H/rad \\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Putting the values in I, we get [latex]\begin{aligned} I &=\left ( \frac{100 \times 0.2 \times 80 \times 10^{-6}}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} \right ) A\\ &= \frac{1.6}{0.5}=3.2A \end{aligned} [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex]  Required value of current, [latex]I=3.2Amp.[/latex]
2014-set-1.explanation_html:
For a PMMC ammeter, at equilibrim, we have :
controlling torque ([latex]T_c[/latex])=Deflecting torque([latex]T_d[/latex])
[latex]\begin{aligned} K\theta _1 &=GI \; \text{or}\; \theta _1=\frac{GI}{K}\\ where, \;\; G &= nBA\\ \therefore \; \theta _1 &= \frac{nBAI}{K} \end{aligned}[/latex]
For an electrodynometer ammeter, at equilibrium,
Controlling torque=Deflecting torque
[latex]\begin{aligned} i.e. \;\; T_c &=T_d \; \text{or}\; K \theta _2=I^2 \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; \theta _2 &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\;\;...(ii)\\ \end{aligned}[/latex]

For the deflection in the two meter to be same,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \theta _1 &=\theta _2\\ or, \;\; \frac{nBAI}{K} &= \frac{I^2}{K}\cdot \frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; nBA&=I\frac{dM}{d\theta }\\ or, \;\; I &=\frac{nBA}{\left ( \frac{dM}{d\theta } \right )} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} Given, \;\; n&= \text{number of turns}=100\\ B&= 0.2 Wb/m^2\\ A&=80mm^2=80 \times 10^{-6}m^2\\ \text{and}\;\; \frac{dM}{d\theta }&=0.5 mH/rad\\ &=0.5 \times 10^{-3}H/rad \\ \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the values in I, we get
[latex]\begin{aligned} I &=\left ( \frac{100 \times 0.2 \times 80 \times 10^{-6}}{0.5 \times 10^{-3}} \right ) A\\ &= \frac{1.6}{0.5}=3.2A \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Required value of current,
[latex]I=3.2Amp.[/latex]

2014-set-2.explanation_text: Let, A = Area of plates Let [latex]C_1= C_3[/latex] be the capacitance formed with dielectric having dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _1[/latex]. [latex]C_{eqv}[/latex] be the equivalent capacitance. [latex]C_2[/latex] be the capacitance formed with dielectic having dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _{r_2}[/latex]. Then,  [latex]C_1=C_3=\frac{\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}{\frac{d}{4}}=\frac{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}{d}[/latex] and [latex]C_2=\frac{\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2A}{\frac{d}{2}}=\frac{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2A}{d}[/latex] Also, equivalent capacitance [latex]= C_{eqv}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\;\frac{1}{C_{eqv}}&=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}+\frac{1}{C_3}=\frac{2}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2} \\ &(\because \;\;C_1=C_3)(C_1,C_2,C_3 \;\text{all in series}) \\ \frac{1}{C_{eqv}} &= \frac{2d}{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1d}+\frac{d}{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2d}\\ C_{eqv}&=\frac{2\varepsilon _1\varepsilon _2\varepsilon _0A}{d(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)} \end{aligned}[/latex] Given, [latex]V_{eqv}=[/latex] Total Voltage = 10 VOlt, [latex]V_1=V_3=2 [/latex] Volt We know that : [latex]C\propto \frac{1}{V}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} &\therefore \; \frac{C_{eqv}}{C_1}=\frac{V_1}{V_{eqv}}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &\frac{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1\varepsilon _2 A}{d(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)}\times \frac{d}{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &\frac{\varepsilon _2}{2(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &5\varepsilon _2=2\varepsilon _1+2\varepsilon _2 \\ &2\varepsilon _1 =3\varepsilon _2\\ &\varepsilon _1:\varepsilon _2=3:2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Let, A = Area of plates
Let [latex]C_1= C_3[/latex] be the capacitance formed with dielectric having dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _1[/latex].
[latex]C_{eqv}[/latex] be the equivalent capacitance.
[latex]C_2[/latex] be the capacitance formed with dielectic having dielectric constant [latex]\varepsilon _{r_2}[/latex].
Then, [latex]C_1=C_3=\frac{\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}{\frac{d}{4}}=\frac{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}{d}[/latex]
and [latex]C_2=\frac{\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2A}{\frac{d}{2}}=\frac{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2A}{d}[/latex]
Also, equivalent capacitance [latex]= C_{eqv}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \therefore \;\;\frac{1}{C_{eqv}}&=\frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}+\frac{1}{C_3}=\frac{2}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2} \\ &(\because \;\;C_1=C_3)(C_1,C_2,C_3 \;\text{all in series}) \\ \frac{1}{C_{eqv}} &= \frac{2d}{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1d}+\frac{d}{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _2d}\\ C_{eqv}&=\frac{2\varepsilon _1\varepsilon _2\varepsilon _0A}{d(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Given, [latex]V_{eqv}=[/latex] Total Voltage = 10 VOlt,
[latex]V_1=V_3=2 [/latex] Volt
We know that : [latex]C\propto \frac{1}{V}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} &\therefore \; \frac{C_{eqv}}{C_1}=\frac{V_1}{V_{eqv}}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &\frac{2\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1\varepsilon _2 A}{d(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)}\times \frac{d}{4\varepsilon _0\varepsilon _1A}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &\frac{\varepsilon _2}{2(\varepsilon _1+\varepsilon _2)}=\frac{1}{5} \\ &5\varepsilon _2=2\varepsilon _1+2\varepsilon _2 \\ &2\varepsilon _1 =3\varepsilon _2\\ &\varepsilon _1:\varepsilon _2=3:2 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-2.explanation_text: Impulse response of an LTI system = transfer function [latex]=\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}=H(s)[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{where, } y(t)&=e^{-3t}u(t)-e^{-5t}u(t) \\ \therefore \; Y(s) &=\frac{1}{(s+3)}-\frac{1}{(s+5)} \\ &=\frac{2}{(s+3)(s+5)} \\ \text{Also, } h(t)&=e^{-5t}u(t) \\ \therefore \; H(s) &=\frac{1}{(s+5)} \\ \text{Therefore, } X(s)&=\frac{Y(s)}{H(s)} \\ &=\frac{2}{(s+3)(s+5)} \times (s+5) \\ &= \frac{2}{(s+3)}\\ \therefore \; \text{Input}&=x(t)=2e^{-3t}u(t) \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Impulse response of an LTI system = transfer function [latex]=\frac{Y(s)}{X(s)}=H(s)[/latex]

2014-set-2.text:
The closed-loop transfer function of a system is [latex]T(s)=\frac{4}{(s^{2}+0.4s+4)}[/latex]. The steady
state error due to unit step input is _____.
2014-set-2.html: The closed-loop transfer function of a system is [latex]T(s)=\frac{4}{(s^{2}+0.4s+4)}[/latex]. The steady state error due to unit step input is _____.
2014-set-2.subject: Control Systems - Feedback Characteristics of Control Systems
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Closed loop transfer function, [latex]T(s)=\frac{4}{(s^2+0.4s+4)} [/latex] or, [latex]\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}[/latex] [latex]=\left ( \frac{4}{s^2+0.4s+4} \right )\;\;\;\;[H(s)=1] [/latex] or,  [latex](s^2+0.4s+4)=4+4G(s) [/latex] or,   [latex]G(s)=\frac{4}{s(s+0.4)} [/latex] =Open llop transfer function ( for unity feedback system) Given, input =u(t)=r(t) [latex]\therefore \;\;\; R(s)=1/s [/latex] Steady state error [latex]e_{ss}=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{sR(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)} \right ] [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{sR(s)}{1+G(s)} \right ]\;\;\; [For H(s)=1] [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{s \times \frac{1}{s}}{1+\frac{4}{s(s+0.4)}} \right ][/latex] [latex] \;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{s(s+0.4)}{s^2+0.4s+4} \right ]=0 [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex]  Steady state error for step input, [latex]e_{ss}=0[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Closed loop transfer function,
[latex]T(s)=\frac{4}{(s^2+0.4s+4)} [/latex]
or, [latex]\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)}[/latex]
[latex]=\left ( \frac{4}{s^2+0.4s+4} \right )\;\;\;\;[H(s)=1] [/latex]
or, [latex](s^2+0.4s+4)=4+4G(s) [/latex]
or, [latex]G(s)=\frac{4}{s(s+0.4)} [/latex]
=Open llop transfer function ( for unity feedback system)
Given, input =u(t)=r(t)
[latex]\therefore \;\;\; R(s)=1/s [/latex]
Steady state error
[latex]e_{ss}=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{sR(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)} \right ] [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{sR(s)}{1+G(s)} \right ]\;\;\; [For H(s)=1] [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{s \times \frac{1}{s}}{1+\frac{4}{s(s+0.4)}} \right ][/latex]
[latex] \;\;=\lim_{s \to 0}\left [ \frac{s(s+0.4)}{s^2+0.4s+4} \right ]=0 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Steady state error for step input, [latex]e_{ss}=0[/latex]

2014-set-2.text: The state transition matrix for the system [latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_{1}}\\ \dot{x_{2}} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u[/latex] is
2014-set-2.html:
The state transition matrix for the system
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_{1}}\\ \dot{x_{2}} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u[/latex]
is
2014-set-2.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given: [latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_1\\ \dot{x}_2 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u [/latex] or, [latex]\;\; \dot{x}(t)=Ax(t)+Bu [/latex] Here, [latex] [A]=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}, \;\;  B=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] State transition matric is given by, [latex]e^{At}=L^{-1}[sI-A]^{-1}[/latex] Now, [latex]  [sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 0 -1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]Adj[sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] and [latex] |sI-A|=(s-1)^2 [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; [sI-A]^{-1}=\frac{1}{|sI-A|}Adj[sI-A] [/latex] [latex][sI-A]^{-1}=\frac{1}{(s-1)^2}\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s-1} & \\ \frac{1}{(s-1)^2} & \frac{1}{s-1} \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; L^{-1}[sI-A]^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix} e^t & 0\\ te^t& e^t \end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex] \therefore[/latex]  State transition matrix[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} e^t & 0\\ te^t& e^t \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_1\\ \dot{x}_2 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u [/latex]
or, [latex]\;\; \dot{x}(t)=Ax(t)+Bu [/latex]
Here, [latex] [A]=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 1&1 \end{bmatrix}, \;\; B=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
State transition matric is given by,
[latex]e^{At}=L^{-1}[sI-A]^{-1}[/latex]
Now, [latex] [sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 0 -1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]Adj[sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
and [latex] |sI-A|=(s-1)^2 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; [sI-A]^{-1}=\frac{1}{|sI-A|}Adj[sI-A] [/latex]
[latex][sI-A]^{-1}=\frac{1}{(s-1)^2}\begin{bmatrix} s-1 & \\ 1 & s-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s-1} & \\ \frac{1}{(s-1)^2} & \frac{1}{s-1} \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; L^{-1}[sI-A]^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix} e^t & 0\\ te^t& e^t \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] State transition matrix[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} e^t & 0\\ te^t& e^t \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

2014-set-2.text:
The saw-tooth voltage waveform shown in the figure is fed to a moving iron
voltmeter. Its reading would be close to __________
2014-set-2.html: The saw-tooth voltage waveform shown in the figure is fed to a moving iron voltmeter. Its reading would be close to __________
2014-set-2.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Galvanometers, Voltmeters and Ammeters
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Moving iron voltmeter reads rms value of voltage and current. From the given waveform of voltage, [latex]\begin{aligned} V(t) &= \left\{\begin{matrix} 50000t, & 0 \lt t \lt 0.02s\\ 50000(t-0.02). & 0.02 \lt t \lt 0.04s \end{matrix}\right.\\ \therefore \; V_{rms} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}(V(T)^2 \; dt}\\ &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{0.04} \int_{0}^{0.02} (50000t)^2 \; dt +\int_{0.02}^{0.04}(50000(t-0.02))^2 \; dt}\\ &= 25000\sqrt{\left [ \frac{t^3}{3} \right ]_0^{0.02}+\left [ \frac{(t-0.02)^3}{3} \right ]_{0.02}^{0.04}}\\ &= 25000\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}\left [ (0.02)^3+(0.02)^3 \right ]}\\ &= 57.73 \text{Volt} \end{aligned} [/latex] [latex]\therefore [/latex]  Voltage reading by moving iron voltmeter =57.73 Volts
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Moving iron voltmeter reads rms value of voltage and current. From the given waveform of voltage,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V(t) &= \left\{\begin{matrix} 50000t, & 0 \lt t \lt 0.02s\\ 50000(t-0.02). & 0.02 \lt t \lt 0.04s \end{matrix}\right.\\ \therefore \; V_{rms} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}(V(T)^2 \; dt}\\ &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{0.04} \int_{0}^{0.02} (50000t)^2 \; dt +\int_{0.02}^{0.04}(50000(t-0.02))^2 \; dt}\\ &= 25000\sqrt{\left [ \frac{t^3}{3} \right ]_0^{0.02}+\left [ \frac{(t-0.02)^3}{3} \right ]_{0.02}^{0.04}}\\ &= 25000\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}\left [ (0.02)^3+(0.02)^3 \right ]}\\ &= 57.73 \text{Volt} \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore [/latex] Voltage reading by moving iron voltmeter =57.73 Volts

2014-set-2.explanation_text: In a [latex]3-\phi[/latex] induction motor, induced emf equation per phase is given by [latex]\begin{aligned} E_{{ph}_{1}} &=k_w \sqrt{2} \pi f \phi N_{ph}\approx V_1 \\ \text{where}\;\; \phi &=\text{flux per pole}=1.5\phi _m \\ \phi &\propto \frac{V}{f} \end{aligned} [/latex] Since V/f ratio is constant (to avoid over sluxing), therefore, [latex]\left ( \frac{V}{f} \right )_{\text{rated frequency}} \gt \left ( \frac{V}{f} \right )_{\text{reduced frequency}} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;\phi _{\text{rated}} \gt\phi _{\text{reduced}}[/latex]

2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given that, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K+1)\\X_2(K+1) \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} a & a-1\\ a+1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K)\\X_2(K) \end{bmatrix}[/latex] With initial conditions, [latex]X_1(0)=1,\;\;X_2(0)=0[/latex] For a=1, we can write, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K+1)\\X_2(K+1) \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K)\\X_2(K+) \end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \; X_1(K+1)=X_1(K) \;\;...(i)[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \; X_2(K+1)=2X_1(K)+X_2(k) \;\;...(ii)[/latex] Applying z-transform on equation (i), [latex]\begin{aligned} zX_1(z)-zX_1(0)&=X_1(z) \\ X_1(z)[z-1]&=zX_1(0) \\ X_1(z) =\frac{z}{z-1}\;\;&[Given, \; X_1(0)=1]...(iii) \\ \text{from equation (ii),}\\ zX_2(z)-zX_2(0)&=2X_1(z)+X_2(z)\\ X_2(z)[z-1]&=2X_1(z)+zX_2(0)\\ [Given,\;\; X_2(0)&=0]\\ \frac{X_2(z)}{X_1(z)}&=\frac{2}{z-1} \end{aligned}[/latex] Thus, transfer function, [latex]H(z)=\frac{2}{z-1}[/latex] Therefore, pole location is z=1.

For a=1, we can write,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K+1)\\X_2(K+1) \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} X_1(K)\\X_2(K+) \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; X_1(K+1)=X_1(K) \;\;...(i)[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; X_2(K+1)=2X_1(K)+X_2(k) \;\;...(ii)[/latex]
Applying z-transform on equation (i),
[latex]\begin{aligned} zX_1(z)-zX_1(0)&=X_1(z) \\ X_1(z)[z-1]&=zX_1(0) \\ X_1(z) =\frac{z}{z-1}\;\;&[Given, \; X_1(0)=1]...(iii) \\ \text{from equation (ii),}\\ zX_2(z)-zX_2(0)&=2X_1(z)+X_2(z)\\ X_2(z)[z-1]&=2X_1(z)+zX_2(0)\\ [Given,\;\; X_2(0)&=0]\\ \frac{X_2(z)}{X_1(z)}&=\frac{2}{z-1} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Thus, transfer function, [latex]H(z)=\frac{2}{z-1}[/latex]
Therefore, pole location is z=1.

2014-set-2.html: A 250 V dc shunt machine has armature circuit resistance of 0.6 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and field circuit resistance of 125 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. The machine is connected to 250 V supply mains. The motor is operated as a generator and then as a motor separately. The line current of the machine in both the cases is 50 A. The ratio of the speed as a generator to the speed as a motor is _____.
2014-set-2.subject: Electrical Machines - DC Machines
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given, [latex]V=250V, [/latex]  [latex]R_a=0.6\Omega , [/latex]  [latex]R_f=125\Omega , [/latex]  [latex]I_L=50A[/latex]  both for motor as well as generator action. Field current, [latex]I_f=\frac{V}{R_f}=\frac{250}{125}=2A [/latex] [latex]\text{For motor action:} [/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_m}&= V-I_aR_a\\ I_a&=I_l-I_f=50-2=48A \\ \therefore \; E_{a_m}&=250-48 \times 0.6 \\ &=221.2 V \\ \end{aligned} [/latex] [latex]\text{For generator action:} [/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_g} &=V+I_aR_a \\ I_a &= I_L+I_f=50+2=52A\\ \therefore \; E_{a_g} &=250+52 \times 0.6=281.2V \end{aligned} [/latex] For a DC shunt machine, [latex]E_a\propto \phi \omega _n [/latex] or   [latex] \;\; E_a\propto N  \;\text{(speed)}[/latex]    [latex] (\because \;\phi =constant)[/latex] [latex] \therefore \;\;\frac{E_{a_g}}{E_{a_m}}=\frac{N_g}{N_m} [/latex] [latex]\frac{N_g}{N_m}=\frac{281.2}{221.2}=1.271 [/latex] Therefore, ratio of the speed as a generator to the speed of motor=1.271
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]V=250V, [/latex] [latex]R_a=0.6\Omega , [/latex] [latex]R_f=125\Omega , [/latex] [latex]I_L=50A[/latex] both for motor as well as generator action.
Field current,
[latex]I_f=\frac{V}{R_f}=\frac{250}{125}=2A [/latex]
[latex]\text{For motor action:} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_m}&= V-I_aR_a\\ I_a&=I_l-I_f=50-2=48A \\ \therefore \; E_{a_m}&=250-48 \times 0.6 \\ &=221.2 V \\ \end{aligned} [/latex]
[latex]\text{For generator action:} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_g} &=V+I_aR_a \\ I_a &= I_L+I_f=50+2=52A\\ \therefore \; E_{a_g} &=250+52 \times 0.6=281.2V \end{aligned} [/latex]
For a DC shunt machine, [latex]E_a\propto \phi \omega _n [/latex]
or [latex] \;\; E_a\propto N \;\text{(speed)}[/latex] [latex] (\because \;\phi =constant)[/latex]
[latex] \therefore \;\;\frac{E_{a_g}}{E_{a_m}}=\frac{N_g}{N_m} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{N_g}{N_m}=\frac{281.2}{221.2}=1.271 [/latex]
Therefore, ratio of the speed as a generator to the speed of motor=1.271

2014-set-2.text: For a single phase, two winding transformer, the supply frequency and voltage are both increased by 10%. The percentage changes in the hysteresis loss and eddy current loss, respectively, are
2014-set-2.html: For a single phase, two winding transformer, the supply frequency and voltage are both increased by 10%. The percentage changes in the hysteresis loss and eddy current loss, respectively, are
2014-set-2.subject: Electrical Machines - DC Machines
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Eddy current loss, [latex]P_a\propto B_m^2 f^2[/latex] and Hysteresis loss, [latex]\begin{aligned} P_h &\propto B_m^x f\propto B_m^{1.6}f \\ \text{when}\;\; \frac{V}{f} &= \text{constant}, \\ P_e&\propto V^2 \\ \text{and}\;\; P_h &\propto \frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \\ \text{Given} \;\; V_2&=1.1V_1 \\ \text{and}\;\; f_2&= 1.1f_1 \\ \frac{P_{e_2}}{P_{e_1}}=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2\\ &=(1.1)^2=1.21\\ \frac{P_{e_2}-P_{e_1}}{P_{e_1}}&=0.21 \end{aligned} [/latex] Therefore, % increase in eddy current loss [latex]\begin{aligned} &= \left [ \frac{P_{e_2}-P_{e_1}}{P_{e_1}}\right ] \times 100\%=21\%\\ \text{also}\;\; \frac{P_{h_2}}{P_{h_1}}&= \left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=(1.1)^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{1}{1.1} \right )^{0.6}=1.1\\ \text{or}\;\; \frac{P_{h_2}-P_{h_1}}{P_{h_1}}&= 0.1 \end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, % increase in hysteresis loss [latex]=\left ( \frac{P_{h_2}-P_{h_1}}{P_{h_1}} \right ) \times 100\%=10\%[/latex] Thus, hysteresis loss increased by 10% and eddy current loss by 21%.
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Eddy current loss, [latex]P_a\propto B_m^2 f^2[/latex] and Hysteresis loss,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P_h &\propto B_m^x f\propto B_m^{1.6}f \\ \text{when}\;\; \frac{V}{f} &= \text{constant}, \\ P_e&\propto V^2 \\ \text{and}\;\; P_h &\propto \frac{V^{1.6}}{f^{0.6}} \\ \text{Given} \;\; V_2&=1.1V_1 \\ \text{and}\;\; f_2&= 1.1f_1 \\ \frac{P_{e_2}}{P_{e_1}}=\left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^2\\ &=(1.1)^2=1.21\\ \frac{P_{e_2}-P_{e_1}}{P_{e_1}}&=0.21 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Therefore, % increase in eddy current loss
[latex]\begin{aligned} &= \left [ \frac{P_{e_2}-P_{e_1}}{P_{e_1}}\right ] \times 100\%=21\%\\ \text{also}\;\; \frac{P_{h_2}}{P_{h_1}}&= \left ( \frac{V_2}{V_1} \right )^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{f_1}{f_2} \right )^{0.6}\\ &=(1.1)^{1.6} \times \left ( \frac{1}{1.1} \right )^{0.6}=1.1\\ \text{or}\;\; \frac{P_{h_2}-P_{h_1}}{P_{h_1}}&= 0.1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, % increase in hysteresis loss [latex]=\left ( \frac{P_{h_2}-P_{h_1}}{P_{h_1}} \right ) \times 100\%=10\%[/latex]
Thus, hysteresis loss increased by 10% and eddy current loss by 21%.

2014-set-2.text: A synchronous generator is connected to an infinite bus with excitation voltage [latex]E_f= 1.3[/latex] pu. The reactive power (Q) in pu supplied by the generator to the bus under this condition is _____.
2014-set-2.html: A synchronous generator is connected to an infinite bus with excitation voltage [latex]E_f= 1.3[/latex] pu. The generator has a synchronous reactance of 1.1 pu and is delivering real power (P) of 0.6 pu to the bus. Assume the infinite bus voltage to be 1.0 pu. Neglect stator resistance. The reactive power (Q) in pu supplied by the generator to the bus under this condition is _____.
2014-set-2.subject: Power Systems - Power System Stability
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given, [latex]E_f=1.3pu, X_s=1.1pu, V=1 pu, P=0.6pu[/latex] Neglecting stator resistance i.e. [latex]\theta _s=90^{\circ}[/latex] Output power delivered, [latex]\begin{aligned} P &=\frac{VE_f}{X_s}\sin \delta \\ \sin \delta &=\frac{PX_s}{VE_f} \\ &= \frac{0.6 \times 1.1}{1 \times 1.3}\approx 0.5\\ \therefore \;\; \delta &=30^{\circ}=\text{Power angle} \\ \therefore \;\; \cos \delta &= \cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex] Reactive power is given by, [latex]\begin{aligned} Q&=\left [ \frac{VE_f}{X_s} \cos \delta -\frac{V^2}{X_s} \right ]\\ &=\left [ \frac{1 \times 1.3}{1.1} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1^2}{1.1} \right ]\\ Q&=(1.023-0.909)=0.114pu\\ &\approx 0.11pu \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]E_f=1.3pu, X_s=1.1pu, V=1 pu, P=0.6pu[/latex]
Neglecting stator resistance i.e. [latex]\theta _s=90^{\circ}[/latex]
Output power delivered,
[latex]\begin{aligned} P &=\frac{VE_f}{X_s}\sin \delta \\ \sin \delta &=\frac{PX_s}{VE_f} \\ &= \frac{0.6 \times 1.1}{1 \times 1.3}\approx 0.5\\ \therefore \;\; \delta &=30^{\circ}=\text{Power angle} \\ \therefore \;\; \cos \delta &= \cos 30^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Reactive power is given by,
[latex]\begin{aligned} Q&=\left [ \frac{VE_f}{X_s} \cos \delta -\frac{V^2}{X_s} \right ]\\ &=\left [ \frac{1 \times 1.3}{1.1} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-\frac{1^2}{1.1} \right ]\\ Q&=(1.023-0.909)=0.114pu\\ &\approx 0.11pu \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-2.explanation_text: Let no-load frequency of generator-1 be 51.5 Hz and no-load frequency of generator-2 be 51 Hz. Given total load = 2.5 Mwand drop of both machines =1 Hz/MW Let machine-1 shares a load of [latex]P_1[/latex] MW them machine-2 will share a load of [latex](2.5-P_1)[/latex] MW Le the steady state frequency of the system be f. [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now, }\frac{51.5-f}{P_1}&=1=droop \\ P_1&= (51.5-f)\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Also, } \left ( \frac{51-f}{2.5-P_1} \right )&=1=droop \\ 51-f &=2.5-P_1 \\ P_1 &=f-48.5 \;\;...(ii) \\ \text{equating eq. }&\text{(i) and (ii), we get,} \\ 51.5-f &=f-48.5 \\ 2f&=100 \\ f&=50Hz \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-2.text: A three phase, 100 MVA, 25 kV generator has solidly grounded neutral. The positive, negative, and the zero sequence reactances of the generator are 0.2 pu, 0.2 pu and 0.05 pu, respectively, at the machine base quantities. If a bolted single phase to ground fault occurs at the terminal of the unloaded generator, the fault current in amperes immediately after the fault is_____.
2014-set-2.html: A three phase, 100 MVA, 25 kV generator has solidly grounded neutral. The positive, negative, and the zero sequence reactances of the generator are 0.2 pu, 0.2 pu and 0.05 pu, respectively, at the machine base quantities. If a bolted single phase to ground fault occurs at the terminal of the unloaded generator, the fault current in amperes immediately after the fault is_____.
2014-set-2.subject: Power Systems - Fault Analysis
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given, [latex]X_1=0.2pu, X_2=0.2pu, X_3=0.05pu[/latex] For a line-to-ground fault on generator, fault current is given by [latex]\begin{aligned} I_{f_{LG}}&=3I_{R_0} =3I_{R_1}=3I_{R_2}\\ &= \frac{3E}{Z_1+Z_2+Z_3}\\ &=\frac{3 \times 1}{0.2+0.2+0.05} \\ &= \frac{3}{0.45}=\frac{20}{3}pu \end{aligned}[/latex] Also, base MVA =100 Base KVA =25 Theerefore, Base current, [latex]I_b=\frac{100 \times 10^6}{\sqrt{3} \times 25 \times 10^3}=2.309kA[/latex] Actual fault current in ampere [latex]=(I_{f_{LG}})_{pu} \times I_b=\frac{20}{30} \times 2.309 \times 10^3[/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;I_f=15393 \text{ Ampere}[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]X_1=0.2pu, X_2=0.2pu, X_3=0.05pu[/latex]
For a line-to-ground fault on generator, fault current is given by
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{f_{LG}}&=3I_{R_0} =3I_{R_1}=3I_{R_2}\\ &= \frac{3E}{Z_1+Z_2+Z_3}\\ &=\frac{3 \times 1}{0.2+0.2+0.05} \\ &= \frac{3}{0.45}=\frac{20}{3}pu \end{aligned}[/latex]
Also, base MVA =100
Base KVA =25
Theerefore, Base current,
[latex]I_b=\frac{100 \times 10^6}{\sqrt{3} \times 25 \times 10^3}=2.309kA[/latex]
Actual fault current in ampere
[latex]=(I_{f_{LG}})_{pu} \times I_b=\frac{20}{30} \times 2.309 \times 10^3[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;I_f=15393 \text{ Ampere}[/latex]

2014-set-2.text: A system with the open loop transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s^{2}+2s+2)}[/latex] is connected in a negative feedback configuration with a feedback gain of unity. For the closed loop system to be marginally stable, the value of K is ______
2014-set-2.html:
A system with the open loop transfer function
[latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s^{2}+2s+2)}[/latex]
is connected in a negative feedback configuration with a feedback gain of unity. For the closed loop system to be marginally stable, the value of K is ______
2014-set-2.subject: Control Systems - Concepts of Stability
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s^2+2s+2)}[/latex] The characteristic equation of given unity-negative feedback control system is given by [latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0[/latex] or,  [latex] 1+\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s^3+2s+2)}=0 [/latex] or,  [latex]s(s+2)(s^3+2s+2)+K=0 [/latex] or,  [latex]s^4+4s^3+6s^2+4s+K=0 [/latex] Forming Routh' array as shown below For stability of the system, [latex]K \gt 0[/latex] and [latex]\frac{20-4K}{5} \gt 0 [/latex]or [latex]K\gt 5 [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex]  For stability,  [latex]0 \lt K \lt 5[/latex] For given system to be marginally stable K=5
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]G(s)=\frac{K}{s(s+2)(s^2+2s+2)}[/latex]

The characteristic equation of given unity-negative feedback control system is given by
[latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0[/latex]

2014-set-2.html:
The second order dynamic system
[latex]\frac{dX}{dt}=PX+Qu [/latex]
[latex] y=RX[/latex]
has the matrices P, Q and R as follows :
[latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0&-3 \end{bmatrix}\; Q=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \; R=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
The system has the following controllability and observability properties:
2014-set-2.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given: [latex]\dot{x}(t)=Px+Qu [/latex] [latex]y=Rx [/latex] [latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex],  [latex]Q=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex],   [latex] R=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] For controllability, [latex] Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} Q &PQ \end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex] [PQ]=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 1& -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;|Q_c|=-1\neq 0\Rightarrow \;\; controllable [/latex] Also, for observability, [latex] Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} R^T & P^TR^T \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\begin{bmatrix} P^T & R^T \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0\\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; |Q_0|=(0 \times -3 -0 \times 1)=0\Rightarrow \;\; non-observable[/latex] Since, [latex] Q_c\neq 0[/latex] and [latex]Q_0=0[/latex] [latex] \therefore[/latex]  System is controllable but not observable.
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Given: [latex]\dot{x}(t)=Px+Qu [/latex]
[latex]y=Rx [/latex]
[latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex], [latex]Q=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], [latex] R=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
For controllability,
[latex] Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} Q &PQ \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex] [PQ]=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &1 \\ 0& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 1& -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;|Q_c|=-1\neq 0\Rightarrow \;\; controllable [/latex]
Also, for observability,
[latex] Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} R^T & P^TR^T \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} P^T & R^T \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;Q_0=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0\\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; |Q_0|=(0 \times -3 -0 \times 1)=0\Rightarrow \;\; non-observable[/latex]
Since, [latex] Q_c\neq 0[/latex] and [latex]Q_0=0[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] System is controllable but not observable.

If resistors [latex]R_1 \; and \; R_2[/latex] have tolerance of 1% each, the equivalent resistor R for resistors [latex]R_1 = 300 \Omega[/latex] and [latex]R_2 = 200 \Omega[/latex] will have tolerance of
2014-set-2.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Measurement of Resistance and Potentiometers
2014-set-2.explanation_text: Given,[latex]R_1=300\Omega ,[/latex]  [latex] R_2=200\Omega [/latex] Equivalent resistance of parallel combination of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2} =\frac{300 \times 200}{500}\\ &= 120\Omega =R_T\\ \text{Given tolerance of} \; R_1&=1\% \\ \therefore \; R_1 &= 300 \pm 3\\ R_1 &= 303 \Omega \; \text{or} 297\Omega \\ \text{Tolerance of} \; R_2&=1\% \\ \therefore \; R_2 &= 200 \pm 2\\ R_2 &= 202 \Omega \; \text{or} 198\Omega \end{aligned} [/latex] Equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex] in high range is: [latex] R_H=\frac{303 \times 202}{303+202}=121.2\Omega [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex]  Tolerance for equivalent resistance R in high range of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex] is [latex]\begin{aligned} \varepsilon _R &=\left ( \frac{R_H-R}{R} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \left ( \frac{121.2-120}{120} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \frac{1.2}{120} \times 100\%=1\% \end{aligned} [/latex] Note: In low range of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex], [latex]R_L=\left ( \frac{297 \times 198}{495} \right )=118.8\Omega [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex]  Tolerance of equivalent resistance, R in low range is, [latex]\begin{aligned} \varepsilon _L &=\left ( \frac{R_L-R}{R} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \left ( \frac{118.8-120}{120} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= -1\% \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
Given,[latex]R_1=300\Omega ,[/latex] [latex] R_2=200\Omega [/latex]
Equivalent resistance of parallel combination of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\frac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2} =\frac{300 \times 200}{500}\\ &= 120\Omega =R_T\\ \text{Given tolerance of} \; R_1&=1\% \\ \therefore \; R_1 &= 300 \pm 3\\ R_1 &= 303 \Omega \; \text{or} 297\Omega \\ \text{Tolerance of} \; R_2&=1\% \\ \therefore \; R_2 &= 200 \pm 2\\ R_2 &= 202 \Omega \; \text{or} 198\Omega \end{aligned} [/latex]
Equivalent resistance of the parallel combination of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex] in high range is:
[latex] R_H=\frac{303 \times 202}{303+202}=121.2\Omega [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Tolerance for equivalent resistance R in high range of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex] is
[latex]\begin{aligned} \varepsilon _R &=\left ( \frac{R_H-R}{R} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \left ( \frac{121.2-120}{120} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \frac{1.2}{120} \times 100\%=1\% \end{aligned} [/latex]
Note: In low range of [latex]R_1[/latex] and [latex]R_2[/latex],
[latex]R_L=\left ( \frac{297 \times 198}{495} \right )=118.8\Omega [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Tolerance of equivalent resistance, R in low range is,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \varepsilon _L &=\left ( \frac{R_L-R}{R} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= \left ( \frac{118.8-120}{120} \right ) \times 100\% \\ &= -1\% \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-2.html: Two ammeters X and Y have resistances of 1.2 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and 1.5 [latex]\Omega[/latex] respectively and they give full-scale deflection with 150 mA and 250 mA respectively. The ranges have been extended by connecting shunts so as to give full scale deflection with 15 A. The ammeters along with shunts are connected in parallel and then placed in a circuit in which the total current flowing is 15 A. The current in amperes indicated in ammeter X is_____.
2014-set-2.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Galvanometers, Voltmeters and Ammeters
2014-set-2.explanation_text:
Given, [latex]R_{m_X}=1.2\Omega , [/latex] [latex]R_{m_Y}=1.5\Omega[/latex] [latex] I_{m_X}=0.15A, [/latex] [latex]I_{m_Y}=0.25A [/latex] and  [latex] I= [/latex] full scale deflection current=15A [latex]\therefore[/latex] Shunt multiplying factor for ammeter X is [latex]m_X=\frac{I}{I_{m_X}}=\frac{15}{0.15}=100[/latex] and shunt multiplier resistance, [latex]R_{{sh}_X}=\frac{R_{m_X}}{(m_X-1)}=\frac{12}{99}=0.012\Omega[/latex] Also, shunt multiplying factor for ammeteer Y is [latex]m_Y=\frac{I}{I_{m_Y}}=\frac{15}{0.25}=60 [/latex] and shunt multiplier resistance, [latex]R_{{sh}_Y}=\frac{R_{m_Y}}{(m_Y-1)}=\frac{1.5}{59}=0.025\Omega[/latex] when these ammeters are connected in parrelel as shown in the figure below, Let current in ammeter X be [latex]I_X[/latex] then, [latex]\begin{aligned}
R_X&=\left ( \frac{ R_{{sh}_X} \cdot R_{m_X}} { R_{{sh}_X}+R_{m_X}} \right )\\
 &= \left ( \frac{0.012 \times 1.2}{1.212} \right )\\ 
 &= 0.011 \Omega \\ 
R_Y &=\left ( \frac{R_{{sh}_Y}\cdot R_{m_Y}}{R_{{sh}_Y}+R_{m_Y}} \right )\\ 
 &= \left ( \frac{0.025 \times 1.5}{1.525} \right )\\ 
 &=0.024\Omega  \\ 
\therefore \; I_X &=\left (\frac{R_Y}{R_X+R_Y}   \right )\times 15 \\ 
 &=\left ( \frac{0.024}{0.035} \right ) \times 15 \\ 
 &= 10.28A
\end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]
\therefore[/latex]  Current in ammeter X=10.28A

when these ammeters are connected in parrelel as shown in the figure below,

The value of [latex]e^{\frac{\Delta t_{1}-\Delta t_{2}}{RC}}[/latex] will be ______.
2014-set-2.html:
An oscillator circuit using ideal op-amp and diodes is shown in the figure.

The time duration for +ve part of the cycle is [latex]\Delta t_{1}[/latex] and for -ve part is [latex]\Delta t_{2}[/latex]. The value of [latex]e^{\frac{\Delta t_{1}-\Delta t_{2}}{RC}}[/latex] will be ______.
2014-set-2.subject: Analog Electronics - Oscillators and Feedback Amplifiers
2014-set-2.explanation_text: This circuit is a stable multivibrator (or) free running oscillator. When [latex]V_0=+V_{sat} [/latex] [latex]V_{UPT}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +3k\Omega } = \frac{V_{sat}}{4} [/latex] When,   [latex] V_0=-V_{sat} [/latex] [latex]V_{LTP}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +1k\Omega }=\frac{-V_{sat}}{2}[/latex] [latex]V_c=V_{final}+(V_{inital}-V_{final})e^{-t/RC}[/latex] In time  [latex] t=\Delta t_1[/latex] [latex] V_c=V_{UTP}; [/latex] [latex]V_{initial}=V_{LTP};[/latex] [latex]V_{final}=+V_{sat}[/latex] [latex]V_{UTP}=V_{sat}+(V_{LTP}-V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex] [latex]\frac{V_{sat}}{4}=V_{sat}+\left ( -\frac{V_{sat}}{2}-V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex] [latex]V_{sat}\left ( -1+\frac{1}{4} \right )=-V_{sat}\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex] [latex]\left (1-\frac{1}{4} \right )=\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex] [latex]\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{2}e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}[/latex] [latex] e^{\Delta t_1/RC}=2\;\;....(i) [/latex] In time [latex] t=\Delta t_2 [/latex] [latex]V_c=V_{LTP};  [/latex]   [latex]V_{initial}=V_{UTP}; [/latex]  [latex]V_{final}=-V_{sat} [/latex] [latex]V_{LTP}=-V_{sat}+(V_{UTP}+V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex] [latex]-\frac{V_{sat}}{2}=-V_{sat}+\left ( \frac{V_{sat}}{4}+V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex] [latex]\left (1-\frac{1}{2} \right )V_{sat}=V_{sat}\left (1+ \frac{1}{4} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex] [latex]\frac{1}{2}= \frac{5}{4}e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex] [latex]e^{\Delta t_2/RC}=\frac{5}{2}\;\;....(ii)[/latex] From equation (i) and (ii), [latex]\frac{e^{\Delta t_1/RC}}{e^{\Delta t_2/RC}}[/latex] [latex]=e^{(\Delta t_1-\Delta t_2)/RC}[/latex] [latex]=\frac{2}{5/2}=\frac{4}{5}=0.8[/latex]
2014-set-2.explanation_html:
This circuit is a stable multivibrator (or) free running oscillator.
When [latex]V_0=+V_{sat} [/latex]
[latex]V_{UPT}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +3k\Omega } = \frac{V_{sat}}{4} [/latex]
When, [latex] V_0=-V_{sat} [/latex]
[latex]V_{LTP}=V_{sat}\times \frac{1k\Omega }{1k\Omega +1k\Omega }=\frac{-V_{sat}}{2}[/latex]

[latex]V_c=V_{final}+(V_{inital}-V_{final})e^{-t/RC}[/latex]
In time [latex] t=\Delta t_1[/latex]
[latex] V_c=V_{UTP}; [/latex] [latex]V_{initial}=V_{LTP};[/latex] [latex]V_{final}=+V_{sat}[/latex]
[latex]V_{UTP}=V_{sat}+(V_{LTP}-V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{V_{sat}}{4}=V_{sat}+\left ( -\frac{V_{sat}}{2}-V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]V_{sat}\left ( -1+\frac{1}{4} \right )=-V_{sat}\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\left (1-\frac{1}{4} \right )=\left ( \frac{1}{2}+1 \right )e^{-\Delta t_1/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{3}{4}=\frac{3}{2}e^{-\Delta t_1/RC}[/latex]
[latex] e^{\Delta t_1/RC}=2\;\;....(i) [/latex]

In time [latex] t=\Delta t_2 [/latex]
[latex]V_c=V_{LTP}; [/latex] [latex]V_{initial}=V_{UTP}; [/latex] [latex]V_{final}=-V_{sat} [/latex]
[latex]V_{LTP}=-V_{sat}+(V_{UTP}+V_{sat})e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]-\frac{V_{sat}}{2}=-V_{sat}+\left ( \frac{V_{sat}}{4}+V_{sat} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\left (1-\frac{1}{2} \right )V_{sat}=V_{sat}\left (1+ \frac{1}{4} \right )e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{1}{2}= \frac{5}{4}e^{-\Delta t_2/RC} [/latex]
[latex]e^{\Delta t_2/RC}=\frac{5}{2}\;\;....(ii)[/latex]
From equation (i) and (ii),
[latex]\frac{e^{\Delta t_1/RC}}{e^{\Delta t_2/RC}}[/latex]
[latex]=e^{(\Delta t_1-\Delta t_2)/RC}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{2}{5/2}=\frac{4}{5}=0.8[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} E_a & \simeq V=230 \text{volt} \\ \therefore \; \text{Torque} , \; T&= \frac{230 \times 8}{146.6}=12.55N-m\\ \therefore \; \text{Torque} , \; T&= 12.55N-m \end{aligned}[/latex]

Given, [latex]I_a=8A[/latex]

[latex]\therefore \;\;\omega _0=\frac{2 \pi}{60}\times N_0 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;= \frac{2 \pi}{60}\times 1400=146.6 \;red/s[/latex]
Power developed in the motor, [latex]P=E_aI_a[/latex]
Also Power, [latex]P=\text{Torque} \times \omega _0 [/latex]
or, [latex] \text{Torque} \;\; T=\frac{P}{\omega _0}=\frac{E_aI_a}{\omega _0} [/latex]
Since, armature resistance drop and brush drop are neglected therefore.
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_a & \simeq V=230 \text{volt} \\ \therefore \; \text{Torque} , \; T&= \frac{230 \times 8}{146.6}=12.55N-m\\ \therefore \; \text{Torque} , \; T&= 12.55N-m \end{aligned}[/latex]

The signal flow graph of a system is shown below. U(s) is the input and C(s) is
the output Assuming [latex]h_{1}=b_{1} \; and \;  h_{0}=b_{0}-b_{1}a_{1}[/latex], the input-output transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}[/latex] of the system is given by
2014-set-3.html:
The signal flow graph of a system is shown below. U(s) is the input and C(s) is the output

Assuming [latex]h_{1}=b_{1} \; and \; h_{0}=b_{0}-b_{1}a_{1}[/latex], the input-output transfer function [latex]G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}[/latex] of the system is given by
2014-set-3.subject: Control Systems - Mathematical Models of Physical Systems
2014-set-3.explanation_text: Using Mason's gain fomlula, Transfer function, [latex]G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{\Sigma P_k\Delta _k}{\Delta } [/latex] Forward paths are: [latex]P_1=\frac{h_0}{s^2} ,\; P_2=\frac{h_1}{s} [/latex] Individual loops are: [latex] L_1=\frac{-a_1}{s} , \; L_2=\frac{-a_0}{s^2} [/latex] Non-touching loops=zero [latex] \therefore \;\;\Delta _1=1, [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;\; \Delta _2=1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( 1+\frac{a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right ) [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;\;\Delta =1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s}-\frac{a_0}{s^2} \right )=\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{\Delta } [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;\;=\frac{\left ( \frac{h_0}{s^2} \right )\times 1+\left ( \frac{h_1}{s} \right )\times \left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right )}{\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2}} [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=\left [ \frac{h_0+h_1(s+a_1)}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right ] [/latex] Given:  [latex] h_1=b_1 [/latex] and [latex]h_0=b_0-b_1a_1[/latex] Thus,  [latex] G(s)=\frac{(b_0-b_1a_1)+b_1(s+a_1)}{(s^2+a_1s+a_0)} [/latex] [latex]G(s)=\left ( \frac{b_1s+b_0}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right )[/latex]
2014-set-3.explanation_html:
Using Mason's gain fomlula,
Transfer function,
[latex]G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{\Sigma P_k\Delta _k}{\Delta } [/latex]
Forward paths are:
[latex]P_1=\frac{h_0}{s^2} ,\; P_2=\frac{h_1}{s} [/latex]
Individual loops are:
[latex] L_1=\frac{-a_1}{s} , \; L_2=\frac{-a_0}{s^2} [/latex]
Non-touching loops=zero
[latex] \therefore \;\;\Delta _1=1, [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\; \Delta _2=1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( 1+\frac{a_1}{s} \right ) =\left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\;\Delta =1-\left ( \frac{-a_1}{s}-\frac{a_0}{s^2} \right )=\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; G(s)=\frac{C(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{\Delta } [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\;=\frac{\left ( \frac{h_0}{s^2} \right )\times 1+\left ( \frac{h_1}{s} \right )\times \left ( \frac{s+a_1}{s} \right )}{\frac{s^2+a_1s+a_0}{s^2}} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\left [ \frac{h_0+h_1(s+a_1)}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right ] [/latex]
Given: [latex] h_1=b_1 [/latex] and [latex]h_0=b_0-b_1a_1[/latex]
Thus, [latex] G(s)=\frac{(b_0-b_1a_1)+b_1(s+a_1)}{(s^2+a_1s+a_0)} [/latex]
[latex]G(s)=\left ( \frac{b_1s+b_0}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} \right )[/latex]

2014-set-3.text: The function [latex]f(x)=e^{x}-1[/latex] is to be solved using Newton-Raphson method. If the initial value of [latex]x_0[/latex] is taken as 1.0, then the absolute error observed at [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] iteration is _____.
2014-set-3.html: The function [latex]f(x)=e^{x}-1[/latex] is to be solved using Newton-Raphson method. If the initial value of [latex]x_0[/latex] is taken as 1.0, then the absolute error observed at [latex]2^{nd}[/latex] iteration is _____.
2014-set-3.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Numerical Methods
2014-set-3.explanation_text: Given, [latex]f(x)=e^x-1[/latex] or, [latex]f(x_K)=e^{x_K}-1[/latex] and [latex]x_0=1[/latex] In Newton-Raphson method, we have [latex]\begin{aligned} x_{K+1}&=\left [ x_K-\frac{f(x_K)}{f'(x_K)} \right ] \\ x_1&= \left [ x_0- \frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\right ]\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, } f(x_0)&=e^{x_0}-1=e^1-1=(e-1) \\ \text{and, } f'(x)&=e6x \\ \therefore \;\; f'(x_0) &=e^1=e \end{aligned}[/latex] Putting the values, we get: [latex]\begin{aligned} x_1&=\left [ 1-\frac{e-1}{e} \right ]=\left [ \frac{e-e+1}{e} \right ]=e^{-1}\\ \text{Also, }x_2&=\left [ x_1-\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)} \right ]\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now, }x_1&=\frac{1}{e}=e^{-1} \text{ and } f(x_1)=(e^{e^{-1}}-1)\\ f'(x_1)&=e^{e^{-1}} \end{aligned}[/latex] Putting the value, we get: [latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{e^{-1}}-1)}{e^{e^{-1}}} \right ]\\ &=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{0.37}-1)}{e^{0.37}} \right ]=0.06 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-3.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]f(x)=e^x-1[/latex]
or, [latex]f(x_K)=e^{x_K}-1[/latex] and [latex]x_0=1[/latex]
In Newton-Raphson method, we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_{K+1}&=\left [ x_K-\frac{f(x_K)}{f'(x_K)} \right ] \\ x_1&= \left [ x_0- \frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\right ]\;\;...(i)\\ \text{Now, } f(x_0)&=e^{x_0}-1=e^1-1=(e-1) \\ \text{and, } f'(x)&=e6x \\ \therefore \;\; f'(x_0) &=e^1=e \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the values, we get:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1&=\left [ 1-\frac{e-1}{e} \right ]=\left [ \frac{e-e+1}{e} \right ]=e^{-1}\\ \text{Also, }x_2&=\left [ x_1-\frac{f(x_1)}{f'(x_1)} \right ]\;\;...(ii)\\ \text{Now, }x_1&=\frac{1}{e}=e^{-1} \text{ and } f(x_1)=(e^{e^{-1}}-1)\\ f'(x_1)&=e^{e^{-1}} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting the value, we get:
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{e^{-1}}-1)}{e^{e^{-1}}} \right ]\\ &=\left [ e^{-1}-\frac{(e^{0.37}-1)}{e^{0.37}} \right ]=0.06 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Also, [latex] Z=|Z|\angle \tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{X_L-X_C}{R} \right ] \;\;...(ii)[/latex]
Comparing equation (i) and (ii), we have:

[latex] \frac{\omega _1}{\omega _2^2C}-\frac{1}{\omega _1C}=-30 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{1 \times 10^3}{4 \times 10^6 C}-\frac{1}{10^3C}=-30 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{10^{-3}}{4C}-\frac{10^{-3}}{C}=-30 [/latex]

Substituting the value of C in equation (iv), we get,
[latex]L=\frac{1}{\omega _2^2C}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{(2 \times 10^3)^2 \times 25 \times 10^{-6}}[/latex]
[latex]\;\; =\frac{1}{100}=10mH[/latex]
Therefore, values are:
[latex]R=50\Omega , [/latex]
[latex]L=10mH, [/latex]
[latex]C=25\mu F[/latex]

Hence, the angle of the voltage behind the synchronous reactance =Power angle [latex](\delta ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\; \delta =33.49[/latex]

drawing an armature current of 2 A. The armature resistance is 0.5 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and leakage inductance is 0.01 H. When loaded, the armature current is 15 A. Then, the speed in rpm is _____.
2014-set-3.html: A separately excited 300 V DC shunt motor under no load runs at 900 rpm drawing an armature current of 2 A. The armature resistance is 0.5 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and leakage inductance is 0.01 H. When loaded, the armature current is 15 A. Then, the speed in rpm is _____.
2014-set-3.subject: Electrical Machines - DC Machines
2014-set-3.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given,}\;\; V &= 300 \text{volt, no load speed} \\ &=900 \text{rpm, no load current}\\ I_{a_0}&=2A \\ &\therefore \; \text{No load induced emf}\\ E_{a_0}&=V-I_{a_0}R\\ &=300-2 \times 0.5\\ &=299 \text{volt}\\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Also, full load armature current, [latex]I_{a_f}=15A [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] induced emf in armature at load, [latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_f}&=V-I_{a_f}R_a \\ &= 300-15 \times 0.5\\ &= 292.5 \text{volt} \end{aligned} [/latex] Let the speed of motor during loaded condition be N. We know that: [latex]\begin{aligned} E_a &\propto \phi N \\ \text{or} \;\; E_a&\propto N\;\;(\phi =\text{constant}) \\ \therefore \; \frac{N}{N_0} &=\frac{E_{a_f}}{E_{a_0}} \\ N&= \frac{E_{a_f}}{E_{a_0}} N_0\\ &= \frac{292.5}{299} \times 900\\ N&=880.43 \text{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Also, full load armature current,

[latex]\begin{aligned} E_{a_f}&=V-I_{a_f}R_a \\ &= 300-15 \times 0.5\\ &= 292.5 \text{volt} \end{aligned} [/latex]
Let the speed of motor during loaded condition be N.

For a 400 km long transmission line, the series impedance is [latex](0.0+j0.5)\Omega /km[/latex]
and the shunt admittance is[latex](0.0+j5.0)\mu mho /km[/latex]. The magnitude of the series

2014-set-3.html: For a 400 km long transmission line, the series impedance is [latex](0.0+j0.5)\Omega /km[/latex] and the shunt admittance is[latex](0.0+j5.0)\mu mho /km[/latex]. 2014-set-3.subject: Power Systems - Performance of Transmission Lines, Line Parameters and Corona
2014-set-3.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} z &=(0+j0.5)\Omega /km \\ Z &=zl = (0+j200) \Omega\\ y&= (0+j5)\mu \Omega/km\\ Y&=yl=(0+j5) \times 10^{-6} \times 400\\ &=(0+j2 \times 10^{-3})\Omega \\ \gamma l &=\sqrt{ZY}=\sqrt{(200 \times 2 \times 10^{-3})} \\ \gamma l &= j0.6324 \\ &= \alpha l+j\beta l=0+j\beta l\\ Z_c&=\sqrt{\frac{Z}{Y}}=\sqrt{\frac{200}{2 \times 10^{-3}}} \\ &= 316.22\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex] Equivalent [latex]\pi[/latex]-network: [latex]\begin{aligned} Z &=Z_C \sin \gamma l \\ &= Z_C \sinh (\alpha l+j\beta l)\\ &=Z_C ( \sinh \alpha l\cdot \cos \beta l+j \cos \alpha l \sin \beta l) \\ &=316.22[\sin (0) \times \cos \beta l+j \cosh(0)] \\ & \sin \left ( 0.6324 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \right ) \\ &=187\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

Equivalent [latex]\pi[/latex]-network:

[latex]\begin{aligned} Z &=Z_C \sin \gamma l \\ &= Z_C \sinh (\alpha l+j\beta l)\\ &=Z_C ( \sinh \alpha l\cdot \cos \beta l+j \cos \alpha l \sin \beta l) \\ &=316.22[\sin (0) \times \cos \beta l+j \cosh(0)] \\ & \sin \left ( 0.6324 \times \frac{180}{\pi} \right ) \\ &=187\Omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

where, [latex]1 kW \leq P1 \leq 1.5 kW[/latex] and
[latex]0.5 kVAR \leq Q_1 \leq 1 kVAR[/latex].
A compensating shunt capacitor is chosen such that [latex]|Q| \leq 0.25 kVAR[/latex], where Q is the net reactive power consumed by the capacitor load combination. The reactive power (in kVAR) supplied by the capacitor is ____.
2014-set-3.subject: Power Systems - Compensation Techniques and Voltage Profile Control
2014-set-3.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given, }S_{load}&=P_1+jQ_1 \\ 1kW \leq P_1 &\leq1.5 kW \\ 0.5 \text{ kVAR} \leq Q_1 &\leq 1\text{ kVAR} \end{aligned}[/latex] Shunt capacitor will only supply reactive power and the total reactive power consumed by the load and the capacitor together will be less than 0.25 kVAR i.e.  [latex]Q \leq 0.25\text{ kVAR}[/latex] Therefore, reactive power supplied by the capacitor will be [latex]Q _C=(1-0.25)=0.75 \text{ kVAR (lagging)}[/latex]
2014-set-3.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Given, }S_{load}&=P_1+jQ_1 \\ 1kW \leq P_1 &\leq1.5 kW \\ 0.5 \text{ kVAR} \leq Q_1 &\leq 1\text{ kVAR} \end{aligned}[/latex]
