2014-set-3.text:
The figure shows the single line diagram of a single machine infinite bus system. The inertia constant of the synchronous generator H = 5 MW-s/MVA. Frequency
is 50 Hz. Mechanical power is 1 pu. The system is operating at the stable equilibrium point with rotor angle [latex]\delta[/latex] equal to 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. A three phase short circuit fault occurs at a certain location on one of the circuits of the double circuit transmission line. During fault, electrical power in pu is  [latex]P_{max} \sin \delta[/latex] . If the values of [latex] \delta \; and \; d\delta/dt [/latex] at the instant of fault clearing are 45[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] and 3.762 radian/s respectively, then  [latex]P_{max}[/latex] (in pu) is ______.
2014-set-3.html:
The figure shows the single line diagram of a single machine infinite bus system.

The inertia constant of the synchronous generator H = 5 MW-s/MVA. Frequency is 50 Hz. Mechanical power is 1 pu. The system is operating at the stable equilibrium point with rotor angle [latex]\delta[/latex] equal to 30[latex]^{\circ}[/latex]. A three phase short circuit fault occurs at a certain location on one of the circuits of the double circuit transmission line. During fault, electrical power in pu is [latex]P_{max} \sin \delta[/latex] . If the values of [latex] \delta \; and \; d\delta/dt [/latex] at the instant of fault clearing are 45[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] and 3.762 radian/s respectively, then [latex]P_{max}[/latex] (in pu) is ______.
2014-set-3.subject: Power Systems - Power System Stability
2014-set-3.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{2H}{\omega _s}\frac{d^2\delta }{dt^2}&=(P_m-P_e) \\ \text{Let, } \omega _r&=\frac{d\delta }{dt} \\ \frac{2H}{\omega _s}\frac{d\omega _r }{dt} &=(P_m-P_e) \\ \text{Multiplying with } &\omega _r \text{ in both side}\\ \frac{H}{\omega _s}\left ( 2\omega _r \frac{d\omega _r }{dt}\right )&= (P_m-P_e)\frac{d\delta }{dt}\\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{H}{\omega _s} 2d(\omega _r)^2&=(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{H}{\omega _s}\int_{\omega _{r_1}}^{\omega _{r_2}}d(\omega _r^2) &= \int_{\delta _1}^{\delta _2}(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \text{where, } & \\ \omega _{r_1}&=\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{d\delta }{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{\delta =\delta _1} =\omega (\delta =\delta _1)-\omega _s\\ \omega _{r_2}&=\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{d\delta }{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{\delta =\delta _2} =\omega (\delta =\delta _2)-\omega _s\\ \frac{H}{\omega _s}(\omega _{r_2}^2 -\omega _{r_1}^2)&=\int_{\delta _1}^{\delta _2}(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \text{In problem, }&\\ \frac{d\delta }{dt}=0, &\frac{d\delta }{dt}=3.762\\ \frac{5}{314}(3.762^2-0^2)&=\int_{30^{\circ}}^{45^{\circ}}(1-P_{max} \sin \delta )d\delta \\ \Rightarrow \;\; P_{max}&=0.23p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]
2014-set-3.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{2H}{\omega _s}\frac{d^2\delta }{dt^2}&=(P_m-P_e) \\ \text{Let, } \omega _r&=\frac{d\delta }{dt} \\ \frac{2H}{\omega _s}\frac{d\omega _r }{dt} &=(P_m-P_e) \\ \text{Multiplying with } &\omega _r \text{ in both side}\\ \frac{H}{\omega _s}\left ( 2\omega _r \frac{d\omega _r }{dt}\right )&= (P_m-P_e)\frac{d\delta }{dt}\\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{H}{\omega _s} 2d(\omega _r)^2&=(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{H}{\omega _s}\int_{\omega _{r_1}}^{\omega _{r_2}}d(\omega _r^2) &= \int_{\delta _1}^{\delta _2}(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \text{where, } & \\ \omega _{r_1}&=\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{d\delta }{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{\delta =\delta _1} =\omega (\delta =\delta _1)-\omega _s\\ \omega _{r_2}&=\left.\begin{matrix} \frac{d\delta }{dt} \end{matrix}\right|_{\delta =\delta _2} =\omega (\delta =\delta _2)-\omega _s\\ \frac{H}{\omega _s}(\omega _{r_2}^2 -\omega _{r_1}^2)&=\int_{\delta _1}^{\delta _2}(P_m-P_e)d\delta \\ \text{In problem, }&\\ \frac{d\delta }{dt}=0, &\frac{d\delta }{dt}=3.762\\ \frac{5}{314}(3.762^2-0^2)&=\int_{30^{\circ}}^{45^{\circ}}(1-P_{max} \sin \delta )d\delta \\ \Rightarrow \;\; P_{max}&=0.23p.u. \end{aligned}[/latex]

2014-set-3.html:
Consider the system described by following state space equations
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_{1}}\\ \dot{x_{2}} \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1& -1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u; [/latex] [latex] y=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_{1}\\ x_{2} \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
If u is unit step input, then the steady state error of the system is
2014-set-3.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2014-set-3.explanation_text: Given [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix}, [/latex] [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, [/latex][latex]C=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] Transfer function of the given system is given by [latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=C(sI-A)^{-1}B [/latex] Now, [latex] (sI-A)=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=\begin{bmatrix} s & -1\\ 1&s+1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex](sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{|sI-A|}(Adj[A]) [/latex] [latex]|sI-A|=s(s+1)+1=(s^2+s+1) [/latex] and [latex] Adj[A]=\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;(sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] Transfer function, [latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right \} [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} (s+1) & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right \}[/latex] [latex] \;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \times 1 [/latex] [latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} [/latex] Given, input=unit step [latex] \therefore \;\;  U(s)=\frac{1}{s} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; Y(s)=\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}=\frac{1}{s(s^2+s+1)} [/latex] [latex]\therefore[/latex] Final Value [latex]\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}[sY(s)][/latex] [latex]=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \right ]=1 [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;[/latex] Error=Final value -Initial value [latex]e_{ss}=0[/latex]
2014-set-3.explanation_html:
Given [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix}, [/latex] [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, [/latex][latex]C=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
Transfer function of the given system is given by
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=C(sI-A)^{-1}B [/latex]
Now, [latex] (sI-A)=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1&-1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\begin{bmatrix} s & -1\\ 1&s+1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex](sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{|sI-A|}(Adj[A]) [/latex]
[latex]|sI-A|=s(s+1)+1=(s^2+s+1) [/latex]
and [latex] Adj[A]=\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;(sI-A)^{-1}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Transfer function,
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} s+1 & 1\\ -1&s \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \right \} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}\left \{ \begin{bmatrix} (s+1) & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right \}[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \times 1 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{U(s)}=\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} [/latex]
Given, input=unit step
[latex] \therefore \;\; U(s)=\frac{1}{s} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; Y(s)=\frac{1}{s}\frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)}=\frac{1}{s(s^2+s+1)} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] Final Value
[latex]\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}[sY(s)][/latex]
[latex]=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{1}{(s^2+s+1)} \right ]=1 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;[/latex] Error=Final value -Initial value
[latex]e_{ss}=0[/latex]

2014-set-3.explanation_text: From the given Bode plot, it is clear that corner frequencies, [latex]\omega _{c1}=\frac{1}{3}[/latex] and [latex]\omega _{c2}=1[/latex] [latex] \therefore[/latex]  Transfer function of given system is given by [latex]T(s)=\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\left [ \frac{1+3s}{1+s} \right ]=\left [ \frac{1+Ts}{1+\alpha Ts} \right ] [/latex] Here, [latex]T=3[/latex] and  [latex]\alpha T=1,[/latex] [latex] \alpha =\frac{1}{3}[/latex] As  [latex] \alpha \lt 1[/latex], therefore the transfer function T(s) represents a lead compensator having [latex]\alpha =\frac{1}{3}[/latex] [latex] \therefore[/latex]   Maximum phase shift, [latex]\phi _{m}=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1-\alpha }{2\sqrt{\alpha }} \right ][/latex] [latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1-\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}} \right ][/latex] [latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{2}{3}\times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right ][/latex] [latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right ]=30^{\circ} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; \phi _m=30^{\circ}[/latex] Also, [latex]T(j\omega )=\frac{1+j3\omega }{1+j\omega } [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;  |T(j\omega )|=\frac{\sqrt{1+9\omega ^2}}{\sqrt{1+\omega ^2}} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; Gain G_m[/latex] in dB [latex]=20log |T(j\omega )| [/latex] [latex]=20 log_{10}\left [ \frac{\sqrt{1+9\omega ^2_m}}{1+\omega ^2_m} \right ][/latex] Now, [latex] \omega _m=\frac{1}{T\sqrt{\alpha }}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; G_m=20 log_{10}\left [ \sqrt{\frac{1+9\times \left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right )^2}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right )^2}} \right ][/latex] [latex]=20 log_{10}\left [ \sqrt{\frac{1+3}{1+\frac{1}{3}}} \right ]=20 log_{10}\sqrt{3} [/latex] [latex]G_m=4.77dB[/latex]
2014-set-3.explanation_html:
From the given Bode plot, it is clear that corner frequencies,
[latex]\omega _{c1}=\frac{1}{3}[/latex] and [latex]\omega _{c2}=1[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Transfer function of given system is given by
[latex]T(s)=\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\left [ \frac{1+3s}{1+s} \right ]=\left [ \frac{1+Ts}{1+\alpha Ts} \right ] [/latex]
Here, [latex]T=3[/latex] and [latex]\alpha T=1,[/latex]
[latex] \alpha =\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
As [latex] \alpha \lt 1[/latex], therefore the transfer function T(s) represents a lead compensator having [latex]\alpha =\frac{1}{3}[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] Maximum phase shift,
[latex]\phi _{m}=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1-\alpha }{2\sqrt{\alpha }} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1-\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{2}{3}\times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=tan^{-1}\left [ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right ]=30^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; \phi _m=30^{\circ}[/latex]
Also,
[latex]T(j\omega )=\frac{1+j3\omega }{1+j\omega } [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; |T(j\omega )|=\frac{\sqrt{1+9\omega ^2}}{\sqrt{1+\omega ^2}} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; Gain G_m[/latex] in dB [latex]=20log |T(j\omega )| [/latex]
[latex]=20 log_{10}\left [ \frac{\sqrt{1+9\omega ^2_m}}{1+\omega ^2_m} \right ][/latex]
Now, [latex] \omega _m=\frac{1}{T\sqrt{\alpha }}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; G_m=20 log_{10}\left [ \sqrt{\frac{1+9\times \left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right )^2}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right )^2}} \right ][/latex]
[latex]=20 log_{10}\left [ \sqrt{\frac{1+3}{1+\frac{1}{3}}} \right ]=20 log_{10}\sqrt{3} [/latex]
[latex]G_m=4.77dB[/latex]

Residue theorem says, [latex]\frac{1}{2 \pi j}\oint _Cf(z)dz=[/latex]Residue of those poles which are inside C. 2012.text: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation [latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex], is
2012.html: With initial condition x(1)=0.5, the solution of the differential equation [latex]t\frac{dx}{dt}+x=t[/latex], is
2012.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2012.explanation_text: The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as  [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex] Which is a linear differential equation [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex] Where,  [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1 Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex] Solution  is [latex]\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2012.explanation_html:
The given differential equation is [latex]\frac{tdx}{dt}+x=t[/latex] with initial condition [latex]x(t)=\frac{1}{2}[/latex] which is same as [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{x}{t}=1[/latex]
Which is a linear differential equation
[latex]\frac{dx}{dt}+P{x}=Q[/latex]
Where, [latex]P=\frac{1}{t}[/latex] and Q=1
Integrating factor [latex]=e^{\int P\;dt}=e^{\int \frac{1}{t}dt}=e^{\log _{e}t}=t[/latex]
Solution is
[latex]\begin{aligned} x\cdot (IF) &=\int Q\cdot (IF)dt +C\\ x\cdot t&= \int 1\cdot t\cdot dt+C\\ xt&= \frac{t^2}{2}+C\\ x&= \frac{t}{2}+\frac{C}{t}\\ \text{Put } x(1)&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; \frac{1}{2}+\frac{C}{1}&=\frac{1}{2} \\ \Rightarrow \; C&=0 \\ \text{So, }x&=\frac{t}{2}\text{ is the solution.} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2012.explanation_text: [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -5 & -3\\ 2& 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex]I=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Characteristic equation of A is [latex]\begin{bmatrix} -5-\lambda & -3\\ 2& 0-\lambda \end{bmatrix}=0[/latex] [latex] (-5-\lambda )(-\lambda )+6=0 [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \lambda ^2+5\lambda +6=0 [/latex] [latex]\text{So,  } A^2+5A+6I=0 [/latex] (by Cayley Hamilton theorem) [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; A^2=-5A-6I [/latex] Multiplying by A on both sides, we have, [latex]A^3=-5A^2-6A[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \;\; A^3=-5(-5A-6I)-6A=19A+30I[/latex]

2012.text: The maximum value of [latex]f(x)=x^{3}-9x^{2}+24x+5[/latex] in the interval [1,6] is

2012.explanation_text: We need absolute maximum of [latex]f(x)=x^3-9x^2+24x+5[/latex] in the interval of [1,6] First find local maximum if any by putting f'(x)=0. [latex]\begin{aligned} f'(x) &=3x^2-18x+24=0 \\ x^2-6x+8&=0 \\ x&=2,4 \\ \text{Now } f''(x) &=6x-18 \\ f''(2)&=12-18=-6 \lt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=2 \text{ is a point of local maximum)} \\ f''(4)&=24-18=+6 \gt 0 \\ \text{(So } x&=4 \text{ is a point of local minimum)} \\ \end{aligned}[/latex] Now tabulate the value of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below [latex]\begin{matrix} x& f(x)\\ 1& 21\\ 2 & 25\\ 6& 41 \end{matrix}[/latex] Clearly the absolute maxima is at x=6 and absolute maximum value is 41.
2012.explanation_html:
We need absolute maximum of
[latex]f(x)=x^3-9x^2+24x+5[/latex] in the interval of [1,6]

Now tabulate the value of f at end point of interval and at local maximum point, to find absolute maximum in given range, as shown below

2012.text: The Fourier transform of a signal h(t) is [latex]H(j \omega)=(2\cos\omega)(\sin 2 \omega)/\omega[/latex]. The value of h(0) is

2012.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Transform
2012.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} H(j\omega )&=\cos \omega \cdot \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega }\\ &=\frac{e^{j\omega}+e^{-j\omega}}{2}\cdot \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega }\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\left [ e^{j\omega}\left ( \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \right )+e^{-j\omega}\left ( \frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \right ) \right ]\\ \text{Let, }X(\omega )&=\frac{2 \sin 2\omega }{\omega } \\ \text{Then, }x(t)&=\left\{\begin{matrix} 1 & -2 \lt t \lt 2\\ 0 & \text{ otherwise} \end{matrix}\right. \\ &\text{By time shifting property}\\ h(t)&=\frac{1}{2}(x(t+1)+x(t-1))\\ \therefore \; h(0)&=\frac{1}{2}[x(1)+x(-1)]=\frac{1}{2}[1+1]=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2012.text: The input x(t) and output y(t) of a system are related as [latex]y(t)=\int^{t}_{-\infty }x(\tau ) cos (3\tau )d\tau[/latex]. The system is

2012.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} y&=\int_{-\infty }^{t}x{\tau } \cos (3\tau )d\tau \\ y(t-t_0)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t-t_0}x{\tau } \cos (3\tau )d\tau\\ y(t) & \text{ for input }x(t-t_0) \text{ is}\\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t}x{\tau -t_0} \cos (3\tau )d\tau\\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{t-t_0}x{\tau} \cos 3(\tau +t_0 )d\tau\\ y'(t) &\neq y(t-t_0) \end{aligned}[/latex] So, system is not time invariant for input [latex]x{\tau } =\cos (3\tau )[/latex] bounded input [latex]y(t)=\int_{-\infty }^{t} \cos ^2 (3\tau )d\tau \rightarrow \infty \; as \; t \rightarrow \infty[/latex] So, for bounded input, output is not bounded therefore system is not stable.

2011.html:
Consider the following statement

(1) The compensating coil of a low power factor wattmeter compensates the effect of the impedance of the current coil.
(2) The compensating coil of a low power factor wattmeter compensates the effect of the impedance of the voltage coil circuit.
2011.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Measurement of Energy and Power
2011.explanation_text: The current coil carries a current of [latex]I +I_P[/latex] and produces a filed corresponding to this current. The compensating coil is connected in series with the pressure coil circuit and is made as nearly as possible identical and coincident with the current coil. It is so connected that it  opposes the field of the current coil. The compensating coil carries a current [latex]I_P[/latex] and produces a field corresponding to this current.  This field acts as in opposition to the current coil field. Thus the resultant field is due to current [latex]I[/latex] only. Hence the error caused by the pressure coil current flowing in the current coil is neutralized.

2011.html:
The open loop transfer function G(s) of a unity feedback control system is given as

[latex]G(s)=\frac{k(s+\frac{2}{3})}{s^{2}(s+2)}[/latex]

From the root locus, at can be inferred that when k tends to positive infinity,
2011.subject: Control Systems - Root Locus Techniques
2011.explanation_text: [latex]G(s)=\frac{k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )}{s^2(s+2)}[/latex] and [latex] H(s)=1 [/latex] Characteristic equation,  [latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0 [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; 1+\frac{k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )}{s^2(s+2)}=0 [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; s^3+2s^2+k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )=0 [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; s^3+2s^2+ks+\frac{2k}{3}=0[/latex] Routh array: As [latex]k \gt 0[/latex], there is no sign change in the 1st column of routh array. So the system is stable and all the three roots lie on LHS of s-plane. For [latex]k \gt 0(k\neq 0)[/latex], none of the row of Routh array becomes zero. So root loci does not cross the [latex]j\omega[/latex]-axis. Number of Zero = Z = 1 Number of poles= P =3 Number of branches terminating at infinity = P-Z = 3-1 =2 Angle of asymptotes [latex]=\frac{(2k+1) \times 180^{\circ}}{P-Z} [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=\frac{(2k+1) \times 180^{\circ}}{2} [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=(2k+1) \times 90^{\circ} [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=90^{\circ} \; and \; 270^{\circ}[/latex] [latex] Centroid=\frac{\Sigma poles-\Sigma zero}{P-Z} [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{0+0-2-\left ( -\frac{2}{3} \right )}{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[/latex] Since, all the three branches terminates at [latex]R_e(s)=-\frac{2}{3}[/latex]. So, all the three roots have nearly equal real parts.
2011.explanation_html:
[latex]G(s)=\frac{k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )}{s^2(s+2)}[/latex]
and [latex] H(s)=1 [/latex]
Characteristic equation, [latex]1+G(s)H(s)=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; 1+\frac{k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )}{s^2(s+2)}=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; s^3+2s^2+k\left ( s+\frac{2}{3} \right )=0 [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; s^3+2s^2+ks+\frac{2k}{3}=0[/latex]
Routh array:

As [latex]k \gt 0[/latex], there is no sign change in the 1st column of routh array. So the system is stable and all the three roots lie on LHS of s-plane.
For [latex]k \gt 0(k\neq 0)[/latex], none of the row of Routh array becomes zero. So root loci does not cross the [latex]j\omega[/latex]-axis.
Number of Zero = Z = 1
Number of poles= P =3
Number of branches terminating at infinity = P-Z = 3-1 =2
Angle of asymptotes [latex]=\frac{(2k+1) \times 180^{\circ}}{P-Z} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\frac{(2k+1) \times 180^{\circ}}{2} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=(2k+1) \times 90^{\circ} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=90^{\circ} \; and \; 270^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex] Centroid=\frac{\Sigma poles-\Sigma zero}{P-Z} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{0+0-2-\left ( -\frac{2}{3} \right )}{2}=-\frac{2}{3}[/latex]

Since, all the three branches terminates at [latex]R_e(s)=-\frac{2}{3}[/latex]. So, all the three roots have nearly equal real parts.

2011.html: The matrix [latex][A]=\begin{bmatrix} 2 &1 \\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is decomposed into a product of a lower triangular matrix [L] and an upper triangular matrix [U]. The properly decomposed [L] and [U] matrices respectively are

2011.explanation_text: Let us try Dolittle's decomposition by putting [latex]l_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]l_{22}=1[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ l_{21}& 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12}\\ 0&u_{22} \end{bmatrix} \\ u_{11}&=2, u_{12}=1 \\ l_{21}u_{11}&=4 \\ l_{21} &=\frac{4}{2}=2 \\ l_{21}u_{12}+u_{22} &= -1\\ \Rightarrow \; 2 \times 1+u_{22} &=-1 \\ u_{22} &=-3 \end{aligned}[/latex] So one possible breakdown is [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2& 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0&-3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] But this is not any of the choises given. So let us do Crout's decomposition, by putting [latex]u_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]u_{22}=1[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0\\ l_{21}& l_{22} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & u_{12}\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\ l_{11} &=2,l_{11}u_{12} =1\\ \Rightarrow \; u_{12}&=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \\ l_{21}&=4,l_{21}u_{12}+l_{22}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \; 4 \times \frac{1}{2}+l_{22} &=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \;l_{22} &=-3 \\ So\;\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4 &-1 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 4& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.5\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2011.explanation_html:
Let us try Dolittle's decomposition by putting [latex]l_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]l_{22}=1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ l_{21}& 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} u_{11} & u_{12}\\ 0&u_{22} \end{bmatrix} \\ u_{11}&=2, u_{12}=1 \\ l_{21}u_{11}&=4 \\ l_{21} &=\frac{4}{2}=2 \\ l_{21}u_{12}+u_{22} &= -1\\ \Rightarrow \; 2 \times 1+u_{22} &=-1 \\ u_{22} &=-3 \end{aligned}[/latex]
So one possible breakdown is
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 2& 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 0&-3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
But this is not any of the choises given.
So let us do Crout's decomposition, by putting [latex]u_{11}=1[/latex] and [latex]u_{22}=1[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4& -1 \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} l_{11} & 0\\ l_{21}& l_{22} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & u_{12}\\ 0&1 \end{bmatrix} \\ l_{11} &=2,l_{11}u_{12} =1\\ \Rightarrow \; u_{12}&=\frac{1}{2}=0.5 \\ l_{21}&=4,l_{21}u_{12}+l_{22}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \; 4 \times \frac{1}{2}+l_{22} &=-1 \\ \Rightarrow \;l_{22} &=-3 \\ So\;\; \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1\\ 4 &-1 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 4& -3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0.5\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2011.html: The response h(t) of a linear time invariant system to an impulse [latex]\delta (t)[/latex], under initially relaxed condition is [latex]h(t)=e^{-t}+e^{-2t}[/latex]. The response of this system for a unit step input u(t) is

2011.explanation_text: Transafer function of system is impulse response of the system with zero initial conditions. Transfer function=[latex]H(s)=L(e^{-t}+e^{-2t}) [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+2} [/latex] [latex]H(s)=\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\left ( \frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) [/latex] [latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s} [/latex]   (step input) [latex]C(s)=R(s)\cdot H(s)=\frac{1}{s}\left ( \frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) [/latex] [latex]C(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)}+\frac{1}{s(s+2)} [/latex] [latex]C(s)=\left ( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1} \right )+\frac{1}{2}\left ( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) [/latex] [latex]C(s)=\frac{1.5}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{0.5}{s+2} [/latex] [latex]Response=C(t)=L^{-1}[C(s)] [/latex] [latex]C(t)=L^{-1}\left [ \frac{1.5}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{0.5}{s+2} \right ] [/latex] [latex]C(t)=(1.5-e^{-t}-0.5e^{-2t})u(t)[/latex]
2011.explanation_html:
Transafer function of system is impulse response of the system with zero initial conditions.
Transfer function=[latex]H(s)=L(e^{-t}+e^{-2t}) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+2} [/latex]
[latex]H(s)=\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\left ( \frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s} [/latex] (step input)
[latex]C(s)=R(s)\cdot H(s)=\frac{1}{s}\left ( \frac{1}{s+1}+\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]C(s)=\frac{1}{s(s+1)}+\frac{1}{s(s+2)} [/latex]
[latex]C(s)=\left ( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1} \right )+\frac{1}{2}\left ( \frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s+2} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]C(s)=\frac{1.5}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{0.5}{s+2} [/latex]
[latex]Response=C(t)=L^{-1}[C(s)] [/latex]
[latex]C(t)=L^{-1}\left [ \frac{1.5}{s}-\frac{1}{s+1}-\frac{0.5}{s+2} \right ] [/latex]
[latex]C(t)=(1.5-e^{-t}-0.5e^{-2t})u(t)[/latex]

2010.text: The zero-sequence circuit of the three phase transformer shown in the figure
2010.html: The zero-sequence circuit of the three phase transformer shown in the figure
2010.subject: Power Systems - Fault Analysis
2010.explanation_text: Equivalent circuit for the zero sequence network depends upon the impedances met by the zero sequence currents flowing through the three phases and their sum, [latex]3I_{a0}[/latex], flowing through the neutral impedance and returning through the ground or a neutral conductor. If there is no complete path for zero sequence currents in a circuit, the zero sequence impedance is infinite. Thus a Y-connected circuit with ungrounded neutral has infinite impedance to zero sequence currents. A delta-connected circuit provides no path for zero sequence currents flowing in the line. The zero sequence currents being single phase, circulate within the winding. Hence viewed from its terminals its zero sequence impedance is infinite.
2010.explanation_html:
Equivalent circuit for the zero sequence network depends upon the impedances met by the zero sequence currents flowing through the three phases and their sum, [latex]3I_{a0}[/latex], flowing through the neutral impedance and returning through the ground or a neutral conductor.
If there is no complete path for zero sequence currents in a circuit, the zero sequence impedance is infinite.
Thus a Y-connected circuit with ungrounded neutral has infinite impedance to zero sequence currents.
A delta-connected circuit provides no path for zero sequence currents flowing in the line. The zero sequence currents being single phase, circulate within the winding. Hence viewed from its terminals its zero sequence impedance is infinite.

2010.text: An eigenvector of [latex]P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1&0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0&0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}[/latex] is
2010.html: An eigenvector of [latex]P=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1&0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0&0 & 3 \end{pmatrix}[/latex] is
2010.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
2010.explanation_text: Given, [latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 &0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0& 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] P is triangular. So eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves. Eigen values are therefore, [latex]\lambda _1=1,\lambda _2=2,\lambda _3=3.[/latex] Now, the eigen value problem is [latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex] [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda &1 &0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 2\\ 0& 0 &3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Putting [latex]\lambda _1=1[/latex], we get the eigen vector corresponding to this eigen value, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 0&1 &0 \\ 0 & 1& 2\\ 0& 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Which gives the equations [latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=0 \\ x_2+2x_3&=0 \\ 2x_3 &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] The solution is [latex]x_2=0, x_3=0, x_1=k[/latex] So, one eigen vector is [latex]\hat{x_1}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=k:0:0[/latex] Since, none of the eigen vectors given in choises matches with this, ratio we need to proceed further and find the other eigen vectors corresponding to the other eigen values. Now, corresponding to [latex]\lambda _2=2,[/latex] we get by substituting [latex]\lambda =2,[/latex], in the eigen value problem, the following set of equations, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} -1&1 &0 \\ 0 & 0& 2\\ 0& 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Which gives the equations, [latex]\begin{aligned} -x_1+x_2&=0 \\ 2x_3&=0 \\ x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] Solution is [latex]x_3=0, x_1=k, x_2=k[/latex] [latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_2}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:1:0[/latex] Since none of the eigen vectors given in the choises is of this ratio, we need to proceed further and find 3rd eigen vector also. By putting  [latex]\lambda =3,[/latex] in the eigen value problem, we get [latex]\begin{bmatrix} -2&1 &0 \\ 0 & -1& 2\\ 0& 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} -2x_1+x_2&=0 \\ -x_2+2x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex] putting [latex]x_1=k[/latex], we get, [latex]x_2=2k[/latex] and [latex]x_3=k[/latex] [latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_3}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 2k\\ k \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:2:1[/latex] Only the eigen vector geven in choise [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is in this ratio.
2010.explanation_html:
Given, [latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 &0 \\ 0& 2 & 2\\ 0& 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
P is triangular. So eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves. Eigen values are therefore, [latex]\lambda _1=1,\lambda _2=2,\lambda _3=3.[/latex]
Now, the eigen value problem is [latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1-\lambda &1 &0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda & 2\\ 0& 0 &3-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Putting [latex]\lambda _1=1[/latex], we get the eigen vector corresponding to this eigen value,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 0&1 &0 \\ 0 & 1& 2\\ 0& 0 &2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_2&=0 \\ x_2+2x_3&=0 \\ 2x_3 &=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
The solution is [latex]x_2=0, x_3=0, x_1=k[/latex]
So, one eigen vector is [latex]\hat{x_1}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=k:0:0[/latex]
Since, none of the eigen vectors given in choises matches with this, ratio we need to proceed further and find the other eigen vectors corresponding to the other eigen values.
Now, corresponding to [latex]\lambda _2=2,[/latex] we get by substituting [latex]\lambda =2,[/latex], in the eigen value problem, the following set of equations,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -1&1 &0 \\ 0 & 0& 2\\ 0& 0 &1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations,
[latex]\begin{aligned} -x_1+x_2&=0 \\ 2x_3&=0 \\ x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Solution is [latex]x_3=0, x_1=k, x_2=k[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_2}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:1:0[/latex]
Since none of the eigen vectors given in the choises is of this ratio, we need to proceed further and find 3rd eigen vector also.
By putting [latex]\lambda =3,[/latex] in the eigen value problem, we get
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} -2&1 &0 \\ 0 & -1& 2\\ 0& 0 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} -2x_1+x_2&=0 \\ -x_2+2x_3&=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
putting [latex]x_1=k[/latex], we get, [latex]x_2=2k[/latex] and [latex]x_3=k[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \hat{X_3}=\begin{bmatrix} k\\ 2k\\ k \end{bmatrix}\;i.e.\; x_1:x_2:x_3=1:2:1[/latex]
Only the eigen vector geven in choise [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is in this ratio.

2010.html: For the differential equation [latex]\frac{d^{2}x}{dt^{2}}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+8x=0[/latex] with initial conditions x(0) = 1 and [latex]\frac{dx}{dt}|_{t=0}=0[/latex], the solution is
2010.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Differential Equations
2010.explanation_text:
[latex]\begin{aligned}
\text{Given,  }\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}+6\frac{dx}{dt}+8x=0\\
x(0)=1\text{  and   }\left.\begin{matrix}
\frac{dx}{dt}
\end{matrix}\right|_{t=0}=0\\
D^2+6D+8=0\\
(D+4)(D+2)=0\\
D=-2, D=-4\\
\therefore \;\;\text{ Solution is }\\
x=C_1e^{-2t}+C_2e^{-4t}\\
\text{Since,   }x(0)=1\\
\text{We have  }C_1+C_2=1\;\;...(i)\\
\frac{dx}{dt}=-2C_1e^{-2t}-4C_2e^{-4t}\\

-2C_1-4C_2=0\;\;\;...(ii)\\
\text{Solving (i) and (ii) we have } \\ C_1=2 \; and \;C_2=-1\\

x(t)=2e^{-2t}-e^{-4t}

2010.text: The system [latex]\dot{x}=Ax+Bu[/latex] with [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0&2 \end{bmatrix},B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is
2010.html: The system [latex]\dot{x}=Ax+Bu[/latex] with [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0&2 \end{bmatrix},B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is
2010.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2010.explanation_text: [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex] B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex][sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]=\begin{bmatrix} s+1 &-2 \\ 0 & s-2 \end{bmatrix} [sI-A]^{-1}[/latex] [latex]=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s-1 &2 \\ 0 & s+1 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+1)(s+2)}\;\;...(i)[/latex] Transfer function [latex]= C[sI-A]^{-1}B[/latex] So, denominator of equation (i) gives pole of the system. [latex](s+1)(s-2)=0 [/latex] [latex]s=-1 \; and \; 2 [/latex] One pole lies in RHS of s-plane. Hence, system is unstable. For controllability, [latex]Q_c[/latex] is defined as [latex]Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} B\; : & AB \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]AB=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]Q_C=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] [latex]|Q_c|\neq 0[/latex] Hence the system is controllable.
2010.explanation_html:
[latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] and [latex] B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex][sI-A]=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]=\begin{bmatrix} s+1 &-2 \\ 0 & s-2 \end{bmatrix} [sI-A]^{-1}[/latex]
[latex]=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s-1 &2 \\ 0 & s+1 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+1)(s+2)}\;\;...(i)[/latex]
Transfer function [latex]= C[sI-A]^{-1}B[/latex]
So, denominator of equation (i) gives pole of the system.
[latex](s+1)(s-2)=0 [/latex]
[latex]s=-1 \; and \; 2 [/latex]
One pole lies in RHS of s-plane. Hence, system is unstable.
For controllability, [latex]Q_c[/latex] is defined as
[latex]Q_c=\begin{bmatrix} B\; : & AB \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]AB=\begin{bmatrix} -1 &2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]Q_C=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &2 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} [/latex]
[latex]|Q_c|\neq 0[/latex]
Hence the system is controllable.

Number of zeros=Z=1 zero at -2
Number of poles = P= 3 poles at 0, -1 and -3
Number of branches terminating at infinity
[latex]= P-Z = 3-1 =2[/latex]
Angle of asymptotes
[latex]=\frac{(2k+1)\times 180^{\circ}}{P-Z} [/latex]

Breakaway point lies in the range [latex]-1 \lt Re[s] \lt 0[/latex] and two branches terminates at infinityalong the asymptotes [latex]Re(s)=-1[/latex].

2009.explanation_text: Let resistance of a single incandescent lamp=R. Power consumed by a single lamp, P=200W. When connected across voltage, V=220V. So, [latex]P=\frac{V^2}{R}\; \Rightarrow \; 200=\frac{220^2}{R} [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \; R=242\Omega [/latex] Let, n number of lamps are connected in series across voltage V=200V. So total resistance of lamps [latex] R_{eq.}=nR=242n[/latex] Total power consumed, [latex]P=\frac{V^2}{R_{eq.}} [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \; 100=\frac{220^2}{242n} \Rightarrow \; n=2[/latex]

Let, n number of lamps are connected in series across voltage V=200V.
So total resistance of lamps

Total power consumed,
[latex]P=\frac{V^2}{R_{eq.}} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; 100=\frac{220^2}{242n} \Rightarrow \; n=2[/latex]

2009.subject: Electrical Machines - Transformers
2009.explanation_text: Mutual inductance is where the flux of two or more coils are linked so that voltage is induced in one coil proportional to the rate of change of current in another. The mutual inductance that exist between the coils can be greatly increased by positioning them on a common soft iron core or by increasing the number of turns of either coil. Consider: The changing flux on coil 1 is proportional to changing current in coil 2. [latex]\begin{aligned} N_1 \frac{d\phi _{12}}{dt}&=M_{12}\frac{dI_2}{dt} \\ \Rightarrow \;\;M_{12} &=N_1 \frac{\phi _{12}}{I_2} \end{aligned}[/latex] Similarly time rate of change of magnetic flux [latex]\phi _{21}[/latex] in coil 2 is proportional to time rate of change of current in coil 1 [latex]\begin{aligned} N_2 \frac{d\phi _{21}}{dt}&=M_{21}\frac{dI_1}{dt} \\ \Rightarrow \;\;M_{21} &=N_2 \frac{\phi _{21}}{I_1}\\ \text{Also} \;\; M_{12}&=M_{21}=M \end{aligned} [/latex] We can observe that none of the parameters changes due to placing of coils on horizontal arms. Hence, mutual inductance will remain unchanged.
2009.explanation_html:
Mutual inductance is where the flux of two or more coils are linked so that voltage is induced in one coil proportional to the rate of change of current in another.
The mutual inductance that exist between the coils can be greatly increased by positioning them on a common soft iron core or by increasing the number of turns of either coil.
Consider:
The changing flux on coil 1 is proportional to changing current in coil 2.
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_1 \frac{d\phi _{12}}{dt}&=M_{12}\frac{dI_2}{dt} \\ \Rightarrow \;\;M_{12} &=N_1 \frac{\phi _{12}}{I_2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Similarly time rate of change of magnetic flux [latex]\phi _{21}[/latex] in coil 2 is proportional to time rate of change of current in coil 1
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_2 \frac{d\phi _{21}}{dt}&=M_{21}\frac{dI_1}{dt} \\ \Rightarrow \;\;M_{21} &=N_2 \frac{\phi _{21}}{I_1}\\ \text{Also} \;\; M_{12}&=M_{21}=M \end{aligned} [/latex]
We can observe that none of the parameters changes due to placing of coils on horizontal arms. Hence, mutual inductance will remain unchanged.

At [latex]\omega =3[/latex] rad/sec, slope changes by 20 dB/dec from -60 dB/dec to -40 dB/dec. Hence the corresponding term of the transfer function is [latex]\left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )[/latex]. At [latex]\omega =25[/latex] rad/sec, slope changes by -20 dB/dec from -40 dB/dec to -60 dB/dec. [latex]G(s)=\frac{k\left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )}{s^2\left ( 1+\frac{s}{2} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{25} \right )}[/latex] At  [latex] \omega =0.1(\omega \leq 2 \;rad/sec)[/latex] [latex] Gain(dB)=20 \log k-40 \log \omega [/latex] [latex]80=20 \log k-40 \log 0.1 [/latex] [latex]20 \log k=40 [/latex] [latex]k=100 [/latex] [latex]G(s)=\frac{100 \left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )}{s^2\left ( 1+\frac{s}{2} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{25} \right )} =\frac{1000(s+5)}{s^2(s+2)(s+25)}[/latex]

At [latex]\omega =2[/latex] rad/sec, slope changes by -20 dB/dec from -40 dB/dec to -60 dB/dec. Hence the corresponding term of the transfer function is [latex]\frac{1}{\left ( 1+\frac{s}{2} \right )}[/latex].

At [latex]\omega =3[/latex] rad/sec, slope changes by 20 dB/dec from -60 dB/dec to -40 dB/dec. Hence the corresponding term of the transfer function is [latex]\left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )[/latex].

At [latex]\omega =25[/latex] rad/sec, slope changes by -20 dB/dec from -40 dB/dec to -60 dB/dec. Hence the corresponding term of the transfer function is [latex]\frac{1}{\left ( 1+\frac{s}{25} \right )}[/latex].

[latex]G(s)=\frac{k\left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )}{s^2\left ( 1+\frac{s}{2} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{25} \right )}[/latex]
At [latex] \omega =0.1(\omega \leq 2 \;rad/sec)[/latex]
[latex] Gain(dB)=20 \log k-40 \log \omega [/latex]
[latex]80=20 \log k-40 \log 0.1 [/latex]
[latex]20 \log k=40 [/latex]
[latex]k=100 [/latex]
[latex]G(s)=\frac{100 \left ( 1+\frac{s}{5} \right )}{s^2\left ( 1+\frac{s}{2} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{25} \right )} =\frac{1000(s+5)}{s^2(s+2)(s+25)}[/latex]

Put, [latex] s=j\omega [/latex]

[latex] -\frac{\pi}{2}-0.1\omega_{pc}=-\pi [/latex]

[latex]|e^{-0.1\omega}|[/latex] is always 1 for any value of [latex]\omega[/latex]
[latex] |G(j\omega)|=\frac{1}{\omega }[/latex]
Gain at [latex]\omega_{pc}[/latex] ( phase-cross frequency)
[latex] |G(j\omega)|_{\omega_{pc}=5 \pi}=\frac{1}{5 \pi }[/latex]
Gain margin [latex]=20 log \frac{1}{|G(j\omega_{pc}|} [/latex]

2009.text: The Fourier Series coefficients of a periodic signal x(t), expressed as [latex]x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty }a_{k}e^{j2 \pi kt/T}[/latex] are given by [latex]a_{-2}=2-j1[/latex], [latex]a_{-1}=0.5+j0.2[/latex], [latex]a_{0}=j2[/latex], [latex]a_{1}=0.5-j0.2[/latex], [latex]a_{2}=2+j1[/latex] and [latex]a_{k}=0[/latex] for [latex]|k| \gt 2[/latex] Which of the following is true ?
2009.html: The Fourier Series coefficients of a periodic signal x(t), expressed as [latex]x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty }^{\infty }a_{k}e^{j2 \pi kt/T}[/latex] are given by [latex]a_{-2}=2-j1[/latex], [latex]a_{-1}=0.5+j0.2[/latex], [latex]a_{0}=j2[/latex], [latex]a_{1}=0.5-j0.2[/latex], [latex]a_{2}=2+j1[/latex] and [latex]a_{k}=0[/latex] for [latex]|k| \gt 2[/latex] Which of the following is true ?
2009.subject: Signals and Systems - Fourier Series
2009.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} x(t)&=a_{-2}e^{-j2\omega _0t}+a_{-1}e^{-j\omega _0t}\\ &+a_{1}e^{j\omega _0t} +a_{2}e^{j2\omega _0t}\\ &=(2-j)e^{-j2\omega _0t}+(2+j)e^{j2\omega _0t}\\ &+(0.5+j0.2)e^{-j\omega _0t}+(0.5-j0.2)e^{j\omega _0t}+2j\\ &=2(e^{-j2\omega _0t}+e^{j2\omega _0t})+j(e^{j2\omega _0t}-e^{-j2\omega _0t})\\ &+0.5(e^{j\omega _0t}+e^{-j\omega _0t})-j0.2(e^{j\omega _0t}-e^{-j\omega _0t})+2j\\ &=4 \cos 2\omega _0t-2 \sin 2\omega _0t+ \cos \omega _0t \\ &+0.4 \sin \omega _0t+2j\\ &=\text{Real}[x(t)]+j\text{Img}[x(t)]\\ &\text{where,}\\ \text{Real}[x(t)]&=4 \cos 2\omega _0t-2 \sin 2\omega _0t+ \cos \omega _0t \\ &+0.4 \sin \omega _0t\\ &= \text{neither even nor odd signal}\\ \text{Img}[x(t)]&=2=\text{constant} \end{aligned}[/latex]

It is applied to a system, with a transfer function  [latex]H(z) =3z^{-1}-2[/latex].

2009.html: The z-transform of a signal x[n] is given by [latex]4z^{-3}+3z^{-1}+2-6z^{2}+2z^{3}[/latex]. It is applied to a system, with a transfer function [latex]H(z) =3z^{-1}-2[/latex]. Let the output be y(n). Which of the following is true ?
2009.subject: Signals and Systems - Z-Transform
2009.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} y[n] &=x[n]*H[n] \\ y[z]&= x[z]H[z]\\ y[z]&=(4z^{-3}+3z^{-1}+2-6z^{2}+2z^{3}) (3z^{-1}-2)\\ &=12z^{-4}+9z^{-2}+6z^{-1}-18z+6z^{2} \\ &-8z^{-3}-6z^{-1}-4+12z^{2}-4z^{3} \\ &= -4z^3+18z^2-18z+12z^{-4}+9z^{-2}-4-8z^{-3}\\ y[n]&\neq 0 \; \text{ for }n \lt 0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Therefore, it is noncausal with finite support.

Thyristor pairs [latex]T_1,T_2 \text{ and }T_3,T_4[/latex] are alternatively switches to obtain a nearly square wave load current. 2009.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2009.explanation_text: Selecting [latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] as state variable, [latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{x}_1(t)&=\frac{dx_1(t)}{dt} \\&=-3x_1(t)+x_2(t)+2u(t)  \\ \dot{x}_2(t)&=\frac{dx_2(t)}{dt} =-2x_2(t)+u(t)  \\ \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_1(t)\\ \dot{x}_2(t) \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1(t)\\ x_2(t) \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u(t)  \\ \dot{x}&=AX+BU \\ \text{So, } A&=\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix}, \; B=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}  \\ y(t)&=x_1(t)  \\ y(t)&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1(t)\\ x_2(t) \end{bmatrix}  \\ y&=CX+DU \\ \text{So, } C&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix} \text{ and } D=0 \\  [sI-A]&=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} s+3 &-1\\ 0& s+2 \end{bmatrix}  \\ [sI-A]^{-1}&=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 &1\\ 0& s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)} \\ &\text{Transfer function} \\ &=C[sI-A]^{-1}B+D  \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 &1\\ 0& s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)}\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}+0  \\ &=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2(s+2)+1\\ s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)}  \\ &=\frac{2s+5}{(s+2)(s+3)}=\frac{2s+5}{s^2+5s+6}\end{aligned}[/latex]

Selecting [latex]x_1(t)[/latex] and [latex]x_2(t)[/latex] as state variable,
[latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{x}_1(t)&=\frac{dx_1(t)}{dt} \\&=-3x_1(t)+x_2(t)+2u(t) \\ \dot{x}_2(t)&=\frac{dx_2(t)}{dt} =-2x_2(t)+u(t) \\ \begin{bmatrix} \dot{x}_1(t)\\ \dot{x}_2(t) \end{bmatrix}&=\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1(t)\\ x_2(t) \end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}u(t) \\ \dot{x}&=AX+BU \\ \text{So, } A&=\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix}, \; B=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\ y(t)&=x_1(t) \\ y(t)&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1(t)\\ x_2(t) \end{bmatrix} \\ y&=CX+DU \\ \text{So, } C&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix} \text{ and } D=0 \\ [sI-A]&=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} -3 &1\\ 0& -2 \end{bmatrix} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} s+3 &-1\\ 0& s+2 \end{bmatrix} \\ [sI-A]^{-1}&=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 &1\\ 0& s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)} \\ &\text{Transfer function} \\ &=C[sI-A]^{-1}B+D \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 &1\\ 0& s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)}\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}+0 \\ &=\frac{\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2(s+2)+1\\ s+3 \end{bmatrix}}{(s+2)(s+3)} \\ &=\frac{2s+5}{(s+2)(s+3)}=\frac{2s+5}{s^2+5s+6}\end{aligned}[/latex]

2008.explanation_text: First of all we will check for causality, [latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{-2t}x(\tau ) d\tau \\ \text{So for }t&=2 \\ y(-2)&=\int_{-\infty }^{4}x(\tau ) d\tau \end{aligned}[/latex] So, output depends on future values of input along with past and present values of input, so system is non-casual. Let us find output for shifted input [latex]x(t-t_0)[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{-2t}x(\tau -t_0) d\tau \\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{2(t-t_0)}x(\tau ) d\tau\;\;...(i) \end{aligned}[/latex] Now, shift the output by [latex]t_0[/latex] then, [latex]y(t-t_0)=\int_{-\infty }^{2(t-t_0)}x(\tau ) d\tau \;\;...(ii)[/latex] so from eq. (i) and (ii), [latex] y'(t) \neq y(t-t_0)[/latex] Therefore system is time varient. Non-causal and time variant is present only in option (D).
2008.explanation_html:
First of all we will check for causality,
[latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{-2t}x(\tau ) d\tau \\ \text{So for }t&=2 \\ y(-2)&=\int_{-\infty }^{4}x(\tau ) d\tau \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, output depends on future values of input along with past and present values of input, so system is non-casual.
Let us find output for shifted input [latex]x(t-t_0)[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} y(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{-2t}x(\tau -t_0) d\tau \\ y'(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{2(t-t_0)}x(\tau ) d\tau\;\;...(i) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Now, shift the output by [latex]t_0[/latex]
then,
[latex]y(t-t_0)=\int_{-\infty }^{2(t-t_0)}x(\tau ) d\tau \;\;...(ii)[/latex]
so from eq. (i) and (ii),
[latex] y'(t) \neq y(t-t_0)[/latex]
Therefore system is time varient.
Non-causal and time variant is present only in option (D).

2008.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Calculus
2008.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x) &=(x^2-4)^2 \\ f'(x)&=2(x^2-4) \times 2x \\ &= 4x(x^2-4)=0\\ & x=0, \; x=2 \; \text{and} \; x=-2 \\ & \text{are the stationary points}\\ f''(x)&=4[x(2x)+(x^2-4) \times 1] \\ &= 4[2x^2+x^2-4]\\ &= 12x^2-16\\ f''(0)&=-16 \lt 0\; \text{ maxima at } x=0 \\ f'(2)&=(12)2^2-16 \\ &= 32 \gt 0\text{ minima at } x=2\\ f'(-2)&=12(-2)^2-16 \\ &= 32 \gt 0\text{ minima at } x=-2 \end{aligned}[/latex] Therefore, there is only one maxima and only two minima for this function.

2008.explanation_text: Here, [latex]\begin{aligned} f(x)&=e^x-1\\ f(x)&=e^x \end{aligned}[/latex] The newton raphson iterative equation is [latex]\begin{aligned} x_{i+1}&=x_i-\frac{f(x_i)}{f'(x_i)}\\ f(x_i)&=e^{xi}-1\\ f'(x_i)&=e^{xi}\\ \therefore \;\; x_{i+1}&=x_i-\frac{e^{x_i}-1}{e^{x_i}}\\ i.e.\;\;x_{i+1}&=\frac{x_ie^{x_i}-(e^{x_i}-1)}{e^{x_i}}\\ &=\frac{e^{x_i}(x_i-1)+1}{e^{x_i}}\\ \text{Now put }i&=0\\ x_1&=\frac{e^{x_0}(x_0-1)+1}{e^{x_0}}\\ \text{put, }x_0&=-1 \text{ as given,}\\ x_1&=[e^{-1}(-2)+1]/e^{-1}\\ &=0.71828 \end{aligned}[/latex]

For minimum cost analysis

Solving equation (i) and (ii),

If the firing pulses are suddenly removed, the steady state voltage ([latex]v_0[/latex]) waveform of the converter will become
2008.subject: Power Electronics - Phase Controlled Rectifiers
2008.explanation_text: Single phase half controlled converter. As load is highly inductive, it means laod current is continuous and almost constant. [latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{During,}\\ &0 \lt \omega t \lt \alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_2D_1, V_0=0\\ &\alpha \lt \omega t \lt \pi \\ &T_1D_1 \text{ conducts }V_0=V_s\\ &\pi \lt \omega t \lt \pi+\alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_1D_2, V_0=0\\ &\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi \\ &T_2D_2 \text{ conducts }V_0=-V_s\\ &T_1 \text{ is again triggered at }2 \pi+\alpha \end{aligned}[/latex] So, during [latex]2\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 3\pi , T_1D_1[/latex] conducts. Now, if firing pulses are removed after [latex]T_1[/latex] is triggered at [latex]2 \pi+\alpha[/latex]. At [latex]\omega t=3 \pi+\alpha[/latex], no firing pulse will be available to trigger [latex]T_2[/latex]. So, load current will flow through [latex]T_1D_2[/latex] as load current is continuos. So during [latex]3 \pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 4 \pi,\;\; T_1D_2[/latex] will continue to conduct and  [latex]V_0=0[/latex]. At [latex]\omega t=4 \pi,\; D_1[/latex] will become forward biassed and [latex]D_2[/latex] will become reverse biased. So, [latex]D_1[/latex] will conduct and [latex]T_1[/latex] is already conducting. So, load current will flow through [latex]T_1D_1[/latex] and [latex]V_0=V_s[/latex].
2008.explanation_html:
Single phase half controlled converter.
As load is highly inductive, it means laod current is continuous and almost constant.

[latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{During,}\\ &0 \lt \omega t \lt \alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_2D_1, V_0=0\\ &\alpha \lt \omega t \lt \pi \\ &T_1D_1 \text{ conducts }V_0=V_s\\ &\pi \lt \omega t \lt \pi+\alpha \\ &\text{freewheeling by }T_1D_2, V_0=0\\ &\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi \\ &T_2D_2 \text{ conducts }V_0=-V_s\\ &T_1 \text{ is again triggered at }2 \pi+\alpha \end{aligned}[/latex]
So, during [latex]2\pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 3\pi , T_1D_1[/latex] conducts.
Now, if firing pulses are removed after [latex]T_1[/latex] is triggered at [latex]2 \pi+\alpha[/latex].
At [latex]\omega t=3 \pi+\alpha[/latex], no firing pulse will be available to trigger [latex]T_2[/latex]. So, load current will flow through [latex]T_1D_2[/latex] as load current is continuos. So during [latex]3 \pi+\alpha \lt \omega t \lt 4 \pi,\;\; T_1D_2[/latex] will continue to conduct and [latex]V_0=0[/latex].
At [latex]\omega t=4 \pi,\; D_1[/latex] will become forward biassed and [latex]D_2[/latex] will become reverse biased. So, [latex]D_1[/latex] will conduct and [latex]T_1[/latex] is already conducting.
So, load current will flow through [latex]T_1D_1[/latex] and [latex]V_0=V_s[/latex].

2008.subject: Electrical Machines - Three Phase Induction Machines
2008.explanation_text: If the three phase supply is given to the rotor winding through an autotransformer, the three phase rotor current will generate a rotating field in the air-gap, rotating at the synchronous speed woth respect to rotor. If the rotor is kept stationary, this rotating field will also rotate in the gap at the synchronous speed voltage and current will be induced in the stator winding and a torque will be developed. If rotor is allowed to move, it will rotate as per the Lenz's law, opposing the rotation of the rotating field decreasing the induced voltage in the stator winding. Thus at a particular speed, the frequency of the stator circuit will correspond to the slip speed. Synchronous speed, [latex]N_s=\frac{120f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500 \; \text{rpm} [/latex] Rotor speed, [latex]N_r=1410 \; \text{rpm} [/latex] [latex]\text{Slip}=\frac{N_s-N_r}{N_s}[/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{1500-1410}{1500}=0.06 [/latex] Slip frequency induced in stator [latex]sf=0.06 \times 50=3 Hz[/latex] Slip speed [latex]= \frac{120 \times 3}{4}=90\; \text{rpm}[/latex] As stator magnetic field rotates 90 rpm in the opposite direction of the rotation of rotor, therefore, speed of the stator field with respect to rotor [latex]=1410+90=1500 rpm[/latex]
2008.explanation_html:
If the three phase supply is given to the rotor winding through an autotransformer, the three phase rotor current will generate a rotating field in the air-gap, rotating at the synchronous speed woth respect to rotor. If the rotor is kept stationary, this rotating field will also rotate in the gap at the synchronous speed voltage and current will be induced in the stator winding and a torque will be developed. If rotor is allowed to move, it will rotate as per the Lenz's law, opposing the rotation of the rotating field decreasing the induced voltage in the stator winding. Thus at a particular speed, the frequency of the stator circuit will correspond to the slip speed.
Synchronous speed,
[latex]N_s=\frac{120f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500 \; \text{rpm} [/latex]
Rotor speed,

Slip frequency induced in stator
[latex]sf=0.06 \times 50=3 Hz[/latex]
Slip speed [latex]= \frac{120 \times 3}{4}=90\; \text{rpm}[/latex]
As stator magnetic field rotates 90 rpm in the opposite direction of the rotation of rotor, therefore, speed of the stator field with respect to rotor [latex]=1410+90=1500 rpm[/latex]

The state space equation of a system is described by

[latex]\dot{x}=Ax+Bu[/latex],
[latex]y=Cx[/latex]

where [latex]x[/latex] is state vector, u is input, y is output and [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], [latex]B=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], [latex]C=[1 \; \; 0][/latex]

The transfer function G(s) of this system will be
2008.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2008.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{x}&=Ax+Bu \\ \text{and   }y&=Cx \\ \text{where, }  A&=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix} \\ B&=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\ C&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\ \text{ and  } D&=0 \\ [sI-A]&=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix}\\ &=\begin{bmatrix} s &-1 \\ 0 &s+2 \end{bmatrix} \\  [sI-A]^{-1}&=\frac{1}{s(s+2)}\begin{bmatrix} s+2 & 1\\ 0& s \end{bmatrix} \\ & \text{Transfer function} \\ &=C[sI-A]^{-1}B+D  \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 & 1\\ 0& s \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}{s(s+2)} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ s \end{bmatrix}}{s(s+2)} \\ &=\frac{1}{s(s+2)} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2008.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} \dot{x}&=Ax+Bu \\ \text{and }y&=Cx \\ \text{where, } A&=\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix} \\ B&=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\ C&=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\ \text{ and } D&=0 \\ [sI-A]&=\begin{bmatrix} s & 0\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix} 0 &1 \\ 0 &-2 \end{bmatrix}\\ &=\begin{bmatrix} s &-1 \\ 0 &s+2 \end{bmatrix} \\ [sI-A]^{-1}&=\frac{1}{s(s+2)}\begin{bmatrix} s+2 & 1\\ 0& s \end{bmatrix} \\ & \text{Transfer function} \\ &=C[sI-A]^{-1}B+D \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} s+2 & 1\\ 0& s \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}}{s(s+2)} \\ &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 \end{bmatrix}\frac{\begin{bmatrix} 1\\ s \end{bmatrix}}{s(s+2)} \\ &=\frac{1}{s(s+2)} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2008.subject: Electrical Machines - DC Machines
2008.explanation_text: Before plugging Current through field winding, [latex]\begin{aligned} I_f &=\frac{V_t}{R_f} =\frac{240}{80}=3A\\ I_L &=I_f+I_a \end{aligned}[/latex] Current through armature [latex]\begin{aligned} I_a &=I_L-I_f\\ &= 15-3=12A\\ \text{Back emf}&=E_a=V_t-I_aR_a\\ &=240-12 \times 0.5\\ &=234V \end{aligned}[/latex]In plugging, the connection of armature winding is reversed. A strong baking torque is achieved by maintaining the supply voltage to the armature with connections reversed. So, the net voltage across the armature resistance at the time of plugging [latex]E_a+V=240+234=474V[/latex]

Before plugging

Current through field winding,

Current through armature

The system [latex]\frac{900}{s(s+1)(s+9)}[/latex] is to be compensated such that its gain-crossover frequency
becomes same as its uncompensated phase crossover frequency and provides a 45[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] phase margin. To achieve this, one may use
2007.html: The system [latex]\frac{900}{s(s+1)(s+9)}[/latex] is to be compensated such that its gain-crossover frequency becomes same as its uncompensated phase crossover frequency and provides a 45[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] phase margin. To achieve this, one may use
2007.subject: Control Systems - Design of Control Systems
2007.explanation_text: Let uncompensated syatem, [latex]T(s)=\frac{900}{s(s+1)(s+9)} [/latex] Phase crossover frequency of uncompensated system [latex]=(\omega _{pc})[/latex], at this frequency phase of [latex]T(j \omega )[/latex] is [latex]-180^{\circ}[/latex] Put   [latex] s=j\omega \text{ in }  T(s) [/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} T(j\omega )&=\frac{900}{j\omega (j\omega +1)(j\omega +9)} \\ \angle T(j\omega )&=-90^{\circ}-tan ^{-1}\omega -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right ) \\ \text{At, } & (\omega _{pc})_1,\angle T(j\omega )=-180^{\circ}\\ -180^{\circ}&=-90^{\circ}-tan^{-1}(\omega _{pc})_1 -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9} \right )\\ -90^{\circ}&=tan^{-1}\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1+\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9}}{1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}} \\ \Rightarrow 1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow (\omega _{pc})_1&= 3 \text{ rad/sec}   \end{aligned}[/latex] Gain cross frequency of compensated system, [latex](\omega _{gc})_2[/latex]= phase cross frequency of uncompensated system, [latex](\omega _{pc})_1[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\;(\omega _{gc})_2=(\omega _{gc})_1=\; 3[/latex]  rad/sec Phase-margin   [latex]=180^{\circ}+\angle T(j\omega )|_{\omega =(\omega _{gc})_2} [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \; \; \;  45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}+\angle T(j\omega )|_{\omega =(\omega _{pc})_2} [/latex] At     [latex] (\omega _{gc})_2=3[/latex] rad/sec, phase angle of [latex]\angle T(j\omega )[/latex] is [latex] -135^{\circ}[/latex] and phase of uncompensated systen is [latex]-180^{\circ}[/latex] at 3 rad/sec. Therefore, the compensator provides phase lead of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex] at the frequency of 3 rad/sec. Let X dB is the gain provided by the compensator, so at gain cross frequency, [latex]|T(j\omega )|_{com}[/latex]=1 or 0 dB. Gain of uncompensated system [latex]=|T(j\omega )|_{un-com} =\frac{100}{\omega \sqrt{1+\omega ^2}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}} [/latex] [latex]|T(j\omega )|_{un-com}[/latex] in dB [latex]\;=40-20 \log \omega -20 \log \sqrt{1+\omega ^2} -20 \log \sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}[/latex] Gain of compensated system, [latex]|T(j\omega )|_{com}=X+|T(j\omega )_{un-com}| [/latex] [latex]|T(j\omega )|_{com}[/latex] must be zero at gain cross frequency [latex](\omega _{gc})_2[/latex] [latex] |T(j\omega_{gc} )_2|_{com}=X+40-20 \log (\omega _{gc})_2 -20 \log \sqrt{1+(\omega _{gc})^2_2}-20 \log \sqrt{1+\frac{(\omega _{gc})^2}{9^2}}=0 [/latex] [latex]X+40-20 \log 3-20 \log \sqrt{1+3^2}-20 \log \sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{3}{9} \right )^2}=0 [/latex] [latex]X=-20dB[/latex] So, the compensator provides an attenuation od 20dB. Hence option (D) is correct.
2007.explanation_html:
Let uncompensated syatem,
[latex]T(s)=\frac{900}{s(s+1)(s+9)} [/latex]
Phase crossover frequency of uncompensated system [latex]=(\omega _{pc})[/latex], at this frequency phase of [latex]T(j \omega )[/latex] is [latex]-180^{\circ}[/latex]
Put [latex] s=j\omega \text{ in } T(s) [/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} T(j\omega )&=\frac{900}{j\omega (j\omega +1)(j\omega +9)} \\ \angle T(j\omega )&=-90^{\circ}-tan ^{-1}\omega -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right ) \\ \text{At, } & (\omega _{pc})_1,\angle T(j\omega )=-180^{\circ}\\ -180^{\circ}&=-90^{\circ}-tan^{-1}(\omega _{pc})_1 -tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9} \right )\\ -90^{\circ}&=tan^{-1}\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1+\frac{(\omega _{pc})_1}{9}}{1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}} \\ \Rightarrow 1-\frac{(\omega _{pc})^2_1}{9}&=0 \\ \Rightarrow (\omega _{pc})_1&= 3 \text{ rad/sec} \end{aligned}[/latex]
Gain cross frequency of compensated system, [latex](\omega _{gc})_2[/latex]= phase cross frequency of uncompensated system, [latex](\omega _{pc})_1[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\;(\omega _{gc})_2=(\omega _{gc})_1=\; 3[/latex] rad/sec
Phase-margin [latex]=180^{\circ}+\angle T(j\omega )|_{\omega =(\omega _{gc})_2} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; \; \; 45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}+\angle T(j\omega )|_{\omega =(\omega _{pc})_2} [/latex]
At [latex] (\omega _{gc})_2=3[/latex] rad/sec,
phase angle of [latex]\angle T(j\omega )[/latex] is [latex] -135^{\circ}[/latex] and phase of uncompensated systen is [latex]-180^{\circ}[/latex] at 3 rad/sec.
Therefore, the compensator provides phase lead of [latex]45^{\circ}[/latex] at the frequency of 3 rad/sec.
Let X dB is the gain provided by the compensator, so at gain cross frequency, [latex]|T(j\omega )|_{com}[/latex]=1 or 0 dB. Gain of uncompensated system [latex]=|T(j\omega )|_{un-com} =\frac{100}{\omega \sqrt{1+\omega ^2}\sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}} [/latex]
[latex]|T(j\omega )|_{un-com}[/latex] in dB
[latex]\;=40-20 \log \omega -20 \log \sqrt{1+\omega ^2} -20 \log \sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{\omega }{9} \right )^2}[/latex]
Gain of compensated system,
[latex]|T(j\omega )|_{com}=X+|T(j\omega )_{un-com}| [/latex]
[latex]|T(j\omega )|_{com}[/latex] must be zero at gain cross frequency [latex](\omega _{gc})_2[/latex]
[latex] |T(j\omega_{gc} )_2|_{com}=X+40-20 \log (\omega _{gc})_2 -20 \log \sqrt{1+(\omega _{gc})^2_2}-20 \log \sqrt{1+\frac{(\omega _{gc})^2}{9^2}}=0 [/latex]
[latex]X+40-20 \log 3-20 \log \sqrt{1+3^2}-20 \log \sqrt{1+\left ( \frac{3}{9} \right )^2}=0 [/latex]
[latex]X=-20dB[/latex]
So, the compensator provides an attenuation od 20dB. Hence option (D) is correct.

 C_1&=\frac{2}{j\pi}e^{j\pi/4}=\frac{2}{\pi}e^{-j\pi/4} =\frac{2}{\pi}\left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{j}{\sqrt{2}} \right )\\ 
 &\text{Comparing it with} \\

\end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\omega _0=\frac{2 \pi}{T_0}=\frac{2 \pi}{2T}=\frac{\pi}{T}[/latex]
Now,
[latex]C_1=[/latex] (exponential series coefficient for k=1)
[latex]\begin{aligned} C_1 &=\frac{1}{T_0}\int _{T_0}x(t)e^{-j\omega _0t}dt \\ C_1 &=\frac{1}{T_0}\left [ \int_{-T/4}^{3T/4} e^{-j\omega _0t}dt+\int_{3T/4}^{7T/4} -1e^{-j\omega _0t}dt \right ] \\ C_1 &=\frac{1}{j 2\pi}[2e^{j\pi/4}+2e^{j\pi/4}] \\ C_1&=\frac{2}{j\pi}e^{j\pi/4}=\frac{2}{\pi}e^{-j\pi/4} =\frac{2}{\pi}\left ( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{j}{\sqrt{2}} \right )\\ &\text{Comparing it with} \\ C_1 &=\frac{a_1}{2}-\frac{jb_1}{2} \\ a_1&=\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}\pi}, b_1=\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}\pi} \\ \therefore \; & \text{fundamental fourier term will be}\\ &= a_1 \cos \omega _0 t+b_1 \sin \omega _0 t \\ &= \frac{4}{\sqrt{2}\pi} \cos \left ( \frac{\pi}{T}t \right )+\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}\pi} \sin \left ( \frac{\pi}{T}t \right )\\ &=\frac{4}{\pi}\cos \left [\frac{\pi}{T}t-\frac{\pi}{4} \right ] \end{aligned}[/latex]

There are two forward paths:
[latex]P_1=1 \times c_0 \times \frac{1}{s}\times \frac{1}{s}\times P=\frac{c_0P}{s^2} [/latex]

All the loop touch forward paths
[latex]\Delta _1=\Delta _2=1 [/latex]
[latex]\Delta =1-(L_1+L_2+L_3+L_4) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=1+\frac{a_0}{s^2}+\frac{a_1}{s}-\frac{b_0P}{s^2}-\frac{b_1P}{s} [/latex]
Using Masson's gain formula
[latex]\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{s} [/latex]

[latex]\frac{C(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{xyP}{1-yzP} \;\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
Comparing equation (i) and (ii), we get
[latex]xy=\frac{c_0+c_1s}{s^2+a_1s+a_0} [/latex]
[latex]yz=\frac{b_0+b_1s}{s^2+a_1s+a_0}[/latex]
Hence, Option (D)is correct.

harmonic distortion is defined as [latex]THD=\frac{\sqrt{V^{2}_{rms}-V_{1}^{2}}}{V_{1}} \times 100[/latex], where  [latex]V_1[/latex] is the rms value of the fundamental component of the output voltage. The THD of output ac voltage waveform is
2007.html: A single-phase voltages source inverter is controlled in a single pulse-width modulated mode with a pulse width of 150[latex]^{\circ}[/latex] in each half cycle. Total harmonic distortion is defined as [latex]THD=\frac{\sqrt{V^{2}_{rms}-V_{1}^{2}}}{V_{1}} \times 100[/latex], where [latex]V_1[/latex] is the rms value of the fundamental component of the output voltage. The THD of output ac voltage waveform is
2007.subject: Power Electronics - Inverters
2007.explanation_text: Pulse width [latex]=2d=150^{\circ}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \; d&=75^{\circ} \\ V_{rms}&=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\pi/2-d}^{\pi/2+d}V_s^2 d (\omega t)} \\ &= V_s\sqrt{\frac{2d}{\pi}}=V_s\sqrt{\frac{5}{6}}=0.913V_s \end{aligned}[/latex] Output voltage in fourier series, [latex]V_0=\sum_{n=1,3,5}^{\infty }\frac{4V_s}{n \pi} \sin \frac{n \pi}{2} \sin nd \sin n\omega t [/latex] RMS value of fundamental component of output voltage, [latex]V_1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left [ \frac{4V_s}{\pi} \sin 75^{\circ} \right ]=0.87V_s [/latex] Total harmonic Distortion, [latex]\begin{aligned} THD &=\sqrt{\frac{V_{rms}^2-V_1^2}{V_1^2} } \times 100 \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{(0.913V_s)^2-(0.87V_s)^2}{(0.87V_s)^2}} \times 100\\ &= 31.83 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]
2007.explanation_html:
Pulse width [latex]=2d=150^{\circ}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \; d&=75^{\circ} \\ V_{rms}&=\sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\pi/2-d}^{\pi/2+d}V_s^2 d (\omega t)} \\ &= V_s\sqrt{\frac{2d}{\pi}}=V_s\sqrt{\frac{5}{6}}=0.913V_s \end{aligned}[/latex]
Output voltage in fourier series,
[latex]V_0=\sum_{n=1,3,5}^{\infty }\frac{4V_s}{n \pi} \sin \frac{n \pi}{2} \sin nd \sin n\omega t [/latex]
RMS value of fundamental component of output voltage,
[latex]V_1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left [ \frac{4V_s}{\pi} \sin 75^{\circ} \right ]=0.87V_s [/latex]
Total harmonic Distortion,
[latex]\begin{aligned} THD &=\sqrt{\frac{V_{rms}^2-V_1^2}{V_1^2} } \times 100 \\ &= \sqrt{\frac{(0.913V_s)^2-(0.87V_s)^2}{(0.87V_s)^2}} \times 100\\ &= 31.83 \% \end{aligned}[/latex]

2007.html: A three-phase, 440 V, 50 Hz ac mains fed thyristor bridge is feeding a 440 V dc, 15 kW, 1500 rpm separately excited dc motor with a ripple free continuos current in the dc link under all operating conditions, Neglecting the losses, the power factor of the ac mains at half the rated speed is
2007.subject: Power Electronics - Electrical Drives
2007.explanation_text: For a separately excited dc motor back emf [latex]=E_a=V_0-I_aR_a[/latex] Since, losses are neglected [latex]R_a[/latex] can be neglected So, [latex]\begin{aligned} E_a&=V_0 \\ V_0&=E_a =k_a\phi N \;\;...(i)\\ V_0&\propto N \end{aligned}[/latex] At rated voltage [latex]V_0=440V[/latex] and N=1500rpm, so, at half the rated speed [latex]\left ( \frac{N}{2} =750 \;rpm\right )[/latex] output voltage of the bridge  ([latex]V_0[/latex]) is 220V. if [latex]I_a[/latex] is the average value of armature current rms value of supply current will be [latex]I_s=I_a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}[/latex] Power delivered to the motor [latex]P_0=V_0I_a[/latex] Input VA to the thyristor bridge [latex]S_{in}=\sqrt{3}V_sI_s[/latex] Input power factor [latex]=\frac{P_0}{S_{in}}=\frac{V_0I_a}{\sqrt{3}V_sI_s}=\frac{220 \times I_a}{\sqrt{3} \times 440 \times I_a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}}=0.345[/latex]
2007.explanation_html:
For a separately excited dc motor
back emf [latex]=E_a=V_0-I_aR_a[/latex]
Since, losses are neglected [latex]R_a[/latex] can be neglected
So,
[latex]\begin{aligned} E_a&=V_0 \\ V_0&=E_a =k_a\phi N \;\;...(i)\\ V_0&\propto N \end{aligned}[/latex]
At rated voltage [latex]V_0=440V[/latex] and N=1500rpm, so, at half the rated speed [latex]\left ( \frac{N}{2} =750 \;rpm\right )[/latex] output voltage of the bridge ([latex]V_0[/latex]) is 220V.
if [latex]I_a[/latex] is the average value of armature current rms value of supply current will be
[latex]I_s=I_a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}[/latex]
Power delivered to the motor
[latex]P_0=V_0I_a[/latex]
Input VA to the thyristor bridge
[latex]S_{in}=\sqrt{3}V_sI_s[/latex]
Input power factor
[latex]=\frac{P_0}{S_{in}}=\frac{V_0I_a}{\sqrt{3}V_sI_s}=\frac{220 \times I_a}{\sqrt{3} \times 440 \times I_a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}}=0.345[/latex]

2007.subject: Power Electronics - Phase Controlled Rectifiers
2007.explanation_text: Input to the converter, [latex]V_s=\left ( \frac{1}{4} \right )230=57.5V[/latex] Diode conducts when [latex]V_s\geq E[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} V_m \sin \theta _1&=E \\ 57.5\sqrt{2} \sin \theta _1&= 12\\ \theta _1=8.486^{\circ} \; or &\; 0.148 \; rad \end{aligned}[/latex] Charging current flows during [latex]\theta _1 \leq \omega t \leq \pi-\theta _1[/latex] and can be expressed as, [latex]\begin{aligned} I_0&= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2 \pi}i_0 d\omega t\\ &=\frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{\theta _1}^{\pi-\theta _1}\left ( \frac{V_m \sin \omega t-E}{R} \right )\\ I_0&=\frac{1}{2 \pi R}[2V_m \cos \theta _1-E(\pi-2\theta _1)] \\ &=\frac{1}{2 \pi \times 19.04}[2 \times 57.5\sqrt{2} \times \cos 8.486^{\circ}\\ &-12 \times (\pi-2 \times 0.148)] \\ &=1.06\approx 1A \end{aligned}[/latex]

Charging current flows during [latex]\theta _1 \leq \omega t \leq \pi-\theta _1[/latex] and can be expressed as,

2007.explanation_text: In two winding transformer [latex]\begin{aligned} V_1 &=500V \\ V_2&= 250V\\ I_1 &=\frac{50 \times 10^3}{500}=100A \\ I_2&= \frac{50 \times 10^3}{250}=200A\\ \eta &= \frac{x S \cos \phi }{xS \cos \phi + \text{losses}}\\ \text{Full load}& \\ x&=1,\; \text{upf}, \; \cos \phi =1, \; S=50 \\ 0.95&= \frac{1 \times 50 \times 1}{1 \times 50 \times 1+ \text{losses}}\\ \text{losses} &= 2.63\\ \text{losses}&= \text{Iron loss}+ \text{Copper loss} \end{aligned}[/latex] When two winding transformer is connected as step up autotransformer [latex]I_2=200,\;\; V_2=750 [/latex] kVA rating of auto transformer [latex]\begin{aligned} S_{auto} &=V_2I_2 \\ &=750 \times 200 \\ &= 150kVA \end{aligned} [/latex] As current through windings and voltage across winding are equal in two-winding transformer and autotransformer. 2007.explanation_text: Taking [latex]V_{AN}[/latex] as the reference [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{AN}&=230\angle 0^{\circ} V\\ V_{BN}&=230\angle -120^{\circ}V \\ V_{CN}&=230\angle 120^{\circ}V \\ I_A&= \frac{P}{V_{AN} \cos \phi }\\ &= \frac{4 \times 10^3}{230 \times 1}\\ &=17.4\angle 0^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex] If an pure inductor is present in phase B, then [latex]I_B[/latex] lags [latex]V_{BN}[/latex] by [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex]. If a pure capacitor is present in phase C, then [latex]I_C[/latex] leads [latex]V_{CN}[/latex] by [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex]. If current through neutral is to be zero. [latex]\begin{aligned} I_B \sin 30^{\circ} &=I_C \sin 30^{\circ} \\ \Rightarrow \; I_B &=I_C=I \\ I_A&=I_B \cos 30^{\circ} +I_C \cos 30^{\circ} \\ &=2I \cos 30^{\circ}=\sqrt{3}I \\ |I_B|&=|I_C|=|I|=\frac{|I_A|}{\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \frac{17.04}{\sqrt{3}}=10.05\\ |I_B|&=\frac{|V_{BN}|}{\omega L} \\ 10.05 &=\frac{230}{2 \pi \times 50 \times L} \\ L&=72.847 mH \\ |I_C| &=|V_{CN}| \cdot \omega C\\ 10.05&=230 \times 2 \times \pi \times 50 \times C \\ C&=139.087 \mu F \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned}
u(t+1)*r(t-1)&=\int_{-\infty }^{\infty }r(\tau -2)u(t+1-\tau )d\tau \\
z(t)&=\int_{-\infty }^{(t+1)}r(\tau -2)d\tau \\

&=\frac{1}{2}[\tau ^2-4\tau ]_2^{(t+1)}\\

[latex]X(z) = 1 - 3z^{-1}[/latex], [latex]Y(z) = 1 + 2z^{-2}[/latex] are Z transforms of two signals x[n],y[n] respectively. A linear time invariant system has the impulse response h[n] defined by these two signals as
h[n] = x[n-1] * y[n]
where * denotes discrete time convolution. Then the output of the system for the input [latex]\delta[/latex][n-1]
2007.subject: Signals and Systems - Z-Transform
2007.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} X(z)&=(1-3z^{-1})\\ Y(z)&=(1+2z^{-2})\\ h[n]&=x(n-1)*y[n]\\ \Rightarrow \; H[z]&=z^{-1}X(z)\cdot Y(z)\\ \Rightarrow \; H[z]&=z^{-1}(1-3z^{-1})(1+2z^{-2})\\ \Rightarrow \; H[z]&=z^{-1}(1+2z^{-2}-3z^{-1}-6z^{-3})\\ \Rightarrow \; H[z]&=(z^{-1}-3z^{-2}+2z^{-3}-6z^{-4})\\ &\text{when input,}\\ I(n)&=\delta [n-1]\; \text{ then }, I[z]=z^{-1}\\ &\text{Therefore output,}\\ P(n)&=h[n]*I[n]\\ \Rightarrow \; P(z)&=H(z)I(z)\\ P(z)&=(z^{-1}-3z^{-2}+2z^{-3}-6z^{-4}) \times z^{-1}\\ P(z)&=z^{-2}-3z^{-3}+2z^{-4}-6z^{-5}\\ \therefore \; P(z)&=\delta [n-2]-3\delta [n-3]\\&+2\delta [n-4]-6\delta [n-5] \end{aligned}[/latex]

2007.explanation_text: At [latex]t=0^-,v_c=V_s, i_c=0\; and \; i_{T1}=I_0[/latex] At t=0, [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex] is triggered, a resonant current [latex]i_c[/latex] designs to flow from C through [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex],  L and back to C. This resonant current is given by [latex]i_c=-V_s\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \sin \omega _0 t[/latex] [latex]i_c=-I_P \sin \omega _0 t[/latex] after half a cycle of [latex]i_c\left \{ t_1=\frac{\pi}{\omega _0} \right \}[/latex];  [latex]i_c=0, v_c=-V_s \; and \; i_{T1}=I_0[/latex]. As [latex]i_c[/latex] tends to reverse, [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex] is turned off. When [latex]v_c=-V_s[/latex] right hand plate has positive polarity, resonant current [latex]i_c[/latex] now builds up through C, L, D and [latex]Th_m[/latex]. As this current [latex]i_c[/latex] grows opposite to forward thyristor current of [latex]Th_m[/latex], net forward current [latex]i_m=I_0-i_c[/latex] begins to decrease. Finalyy when [latex]i_c[/latex] in the reversed direction attains the value [latex]I_0, i_m[/latex] is reduced to zero and [latex]Th_m[/latex] is turned off. [latex]i_m=I_0-i_c=I_0-I_p \sin \omega _0\Delta t=0[/latex] [latex]\Delta t=\frac{1}{\omega _0}\sin ^{-1}\left ( \frac{I_0}{I_p} \right )[/latex] So, [latex]Th_m[/latex]is turned off between [latex]t_1 \lt t \lt t_1+\Delta t[/latex] [latex]t_1 =\frac{\pi}{\omega _0}= \pi \sqrt{LC}=\pi \times \sqrt{10 \times 25.28}=50\mu sec[/latex] Since commutation of [latex]Th_m[/latex] starts from [latex]t_1=50\mu sec[/latex].

At [latex]t=0^-,v_c=V_s, i_c=0\; and \; i_{T1}=I_0[/latex]
At t=0, [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex] is triggered, a resonant current [latex]i_c[/latex] designs to flow from C through [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex], L and back to C.
This resonant current is given by
[latex]i_c=-V_s\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \sin \omega _0 t[/latex]
[latex]i_c=-I_P \sin \omega _0 t[/latex]
after half a cycle of [latex]i_c\left \{ t_1=\frac{\pi}{\omega _0} \right \}[/latex]; [latex]i_c=0, v_c=-V_s \; and \; i_{T1}=I_0[/latex]. As [latex]i_c[/latex] tends to reverse, [latex]Th_{aux}[/latex] is turned off.
When [latex]v_c=-V_s[/latex] right hand plate has positive polarity, resonant current [latex]i_c[/latex] now builds up through C, L, D and [latex]Th_m[/latex]. As this current [latex]i_c[/latex] grows opposite to forward thyristor current of [latex]Th_m[/latex], net forward current [latex]i_m=I_0-i_c[/latex] begins to decrease. Finalyy when [latex]i_c[/latex] in the reversed direction attains the value [latex]I_0, i_m[/latex] is reduced to zero and [latex]Th_m[/latex] is turned off.
[latex]i_m=I_0-i_c=I_0-I_p \sin \omega _0\Delta t=0[/latex]
[latex]\Delta t=\frac{1}{\omega _0}\sin ^{-1}\left ( \frac{I_0}{I_p} \right )[/latex]
So, [latex]Th_m[/latex]is turned off between
[latex]t_1 \lt t \lt t_1+\Delta t[/latex]
[latex]t_1 =\frac{\pi}{\omega _0}= \pi \sqrt{LC}=\pi \times \sqrt{10 \times 25.28}=50\mu sec[/latex]
Since commutation of [latex]Th_m[/latex] starts from [latex]t_1=50\mu sec[/latex].

2007.explanation_text: Assuming rated torque [latex]=T_{rated}[/latex] Starting torque [latex]T_s=150\% \; \text{of} \; T_{rated}=1.5T_{rated}[/latex] Maximum torque, [latex]T_m=300\% \; \text{of} \; T_{rated}=3.0T_{rated}[/latex] as we know, [latex]\begin{aligned} T_s &=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{V^2R'_2}{{R'_2}^2+{X'_2}^2}\\ T_m &=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{0.5V^2}{X'_2} \\ \frac{T_m}{T_s}&= \frac{0.5}{X'_2} \frac{{R'_2}^2 \times {X'_2}^2}{R'_2}\\ &= 0.5\left [ \frac{(R_2/X'_2)^2 +1}{(R'_2/X'_2)} \right ] \end{aligned} [/latex] as we know, maximum torque occurs at [latex]\begin{aligned} s_m &=\frac{R'_2}{X'_2} \\ \frac{T_m}{T_s} &= 0.5\left ( \frac{{s_m}^2 +1}{s_m} \right )\\ \frac{3T_{rated}}{1.5T_{rated}}&=0.5 \left ( \frac{{s_m}^2 +1}{s_m} \right ) \\ {s_m}^2 -4s_m +1&=0 \\ s_m&= 3.73 \; \text{or} \; 0.2679 \end{aligned} [/latex] [latex]s_m=3.73[/latex] is rejected, as for this value of slip motor works in braking mode.
