2007.explanation_text: [latex]x_1=\omega L_1 [/latex] and  [latex] x_4=\frac{1}{\omega C_4} [/latex] [latex]z_1=R_1+jx_1=R_1+j\omega L_1 [/latex] [latex]z_2=R_2 [/latex] [latex]z_3=R_3 [/latex] [latex]z_4=R_4-jx_4=R_4-\frac{j}{\omega C_4} [/latex] Under balanced condition [latex]z_1z_4=z_2z_3[/latex] [latex] (R_1+j\omega L_1)(R_4-jx_4)=R_2R_3 [/latex] [latex]\left ( R_1R_4+\frac{L_1}{C_4} \right )+j\left ( \omega L_1R_4-\frac{R_1}{\omega C_4} \right )=R_2R_3[/latex] Equating real and imaginary terms, we obtain [latex]R_1R_4+\frac{L_1}{C_4} =R_2R_3 [/latex] [latex]\omega L_1R_4-\frac{R_1}{\omega C_4}=0[/latex] Solving above equations, we get [latex]L_1=\frac{R_2R_3C_4}{1+\omega ^2C_4^2R_4^2} [/latex] and [latex]R_2=\frac{\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2}{1+\omega ^2C_4^2R_4^2} [/latex] Q-factor of the coil [latex]Q=\frac{\omega L_1}{R_1}=\frac{1}{\omega C_4R_4} [/latex] Therefore, [latex]L_1=\frac{R_2R_3C_4}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{Q} \right )^2}\;\;...(i) [/latex] [latex]R_1=\frac{\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{Q} \right )^2}\;\;...(ii)[/latex] For a value of a greater than 10, the term [latex](1/Q)^2[/latex] will be smaller than 1/1000 and can be neglected. Therefore equation (i) and (ii) reduces to [latex]L_1=R_2R_3C_4 \;\;...(iii) [/latex] [latex]R_1=\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2\;\;...(iv)[/latex] [latex] R_4[/latex] appears only in equation (iv) and [latex]R_2[/latex] appears in both equation (iii) and (iv). So first [latex]R_2[/latex] is adjusted and then [latex]R_4[/latex] is adjusted.
2007.explanation_html:
[latex]x_1=\omega L_1 [/latex] and [latex] x_4=\frac{1}{\omega C_4} [/latex]
[latex]z_1=R_1+jx_1=R_1+j\omega L_1 [/latex]
[latex]z_2=R_2 [/latex]
[latex]z_3=R_3 [/latex]
[latex]z_4=R_4-jx_4=R_4-\frac{j}{\omega C_4} [/latex]
Under balanced condition
[latex]z_1z_4=z_2z_3[/latex]
[latex] (R_1+j\omega L_1)(R_4-jx_4)=R_2R_3 [/latex]
[latex]\left ( R_1R_4+\frac{L_1}{C_4} \right )+j\left ( \omega L_1R_4-\frac{R_1}{\omega C_4} \right )=R_2R_3[/latex]
Equating real and imaginary terms, we obtain
[latex]R_1R_4+\frac{L_1}{C_4} =R_2R_3 [/latex]
[latex]\omega L_1R_4-\frac{R_1}{\omega C_4}=0[/latex]
Solving above equations, we get
[latex]L_1=\frac{R_2R_3C_4}{1+\omega ^2C_4^2R_4^2} [/latex]
and [latex]R_2=\frac{\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2}{1+\omega ^2C_4^2R_4^2} [/latex]
Q-factor of the coil [latex]Q=\frac{\omega L_1}{R_1}=\frac{1}{\omega C_4R_4} [/latex]
Therefore, [latex]L_1=\frac{R_2R_3C_4}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{Q} \right )^2}\;\;...(i) [/latex]
[latex]R_1=\frac{\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2}{1+\left ( \frac{1}{Q} \right )^2}\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
For a value of a greater than 10, the term [latex](1/Q)^2[/latex] will be smaller than 1/1000 and can be neglected. Therefore equation (i) and (ii) reduces to
[latex]L_1=R_2R_3C_4 \;\;...(iii) [/latex]
[latex]R_1=\omega ^2R_2R_3R_4C_4^2\;\;...(iv)[/latex]
[latex] R_4[/latex] appears only in equation (iv) and [latex]R_2[/latex] appears in both equation (iii) and (iv).
So first [latex]R_2[/latex] is adjusted and then [latex]R_4[/latex] is adjusted.

[latex]\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \; A^2 &=-3A-2I \\ AA^4&=A^2 \times A^2 \\ &= (-3A-2I)(-3A-2I)\\ &=9A^2+12A+4I \\ &= 9(-3A-2I)+12A+4I\\ &= -15A-14I\\ A^8&=A^4 \times A^4 \\ &= (-15A-14I)(-15A-14I)\\ &=225A^2+420A+156I \\ &=225(-3A-2I)+420A+196I \\ &=-225A-254I \\ A^9&=A \times A^8 \\ &=A(-255A-254I) \\ &=-255A^2-254A \\ &=-255(-3A-2I)-254A \\ &= 511A+510I \end{aligned}[/latex]

2007.explanation_text: [latex]G(z)=\alpha z^{-1}+\beta z^{-3}[/latex] For, low frequency [latex](z=1)\rightarrow G(1)=\alpha +\beta \;\;...(i)[/latex] For, high frequency [latex](z=-1)\rightarrow G(-1)=-(\alpha +\beta) \;\;...(ii)[/latex] For now, [latex]g(n)=\{0,\alpha ,0, \beta\}[/latex] For linear phase FIR filter, g(n) should be either even symmetric or odd symmetric about virtual y-axis. To, satisfy the above condition. CASE: (i) [latex]\alpha =- \beta[/latex] ( odd symmetric about virtual y-axis) But in this case, G(1)=G(-1)=0 i.e. at low frequency [latex]\Rightarrow \; G(z)=0[/latex] and at high frequency [latex]\Rightarrow \; G(z)=0[/latex] Thus in this case filter will be band-pass. CASE: (ii) [latex]\alpha = \beta[/latex] ( even symmetric about virtual y-axis) In this case, At low frequency [latex]\Rightarrow \; G(z)=2\alpha [/latex] and at high frequency [latex]\Rightarrow \; G(-1)=-2\alpha [/latex] Filter will be either all pass or band-stop. Now, [latex]\begin{aligned} G(e^{j\omega })&=\alpha (e^{-j\omega }+e^{-j 3 \omega }) \\ &=\alpha e^{-j2\omega }(e^{j\omega }+e^{-j\omega }) \\ &= 2\alpha e^{-j2\omega } \cos \omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

2006.explanation_text: Circuit model in open-circuit test: In open-circuit test, the transformer draws only exciting current. This is represnted by [latex]I_m[/latex] lagging the induced emf by [latex]90^{\circ}[/latex]. However, the presence of eddy-current, and hysteresis, both demad the flow of active power into the system and as a consequence the exciting current [latex]I_0[/latex] has another component [latex]I_i[/latex] in phase with [latex]E_1[/latex]. 2006.explanation_text: For a [latex]3-\phi[/latex] induction motor, stator voltage per phase is given by [latex]\begin{aligned} V_1 &=\sqrt{2}\pi f_1 N_{pn_1}\phi K_{\omega 1} \\ \phi &\propto \frac{V_1}{f_1} \end{aligned}[/latex] To keep the [latex]\phi[/latex] constant, constant V/f control is applied and voltage ([latex]V_1[/latex]) varies linearly with frequency ([latex]f_1[/latex]). For frequency above 50 Hz, such control is not possible because voltage can not be increased above rated voltage. Therefore, for frequency above 50 Hz, voltage is kept constant, During this control induction motor is said to be working in field weakling mode.

At rated frequency of 50 Hz and rated voltage of 400 V its speed is 1440 rpm. Find the speed at 30 Hz, if the load torque is constant
2006.subject: Electrical Machines - Three Phase Induction Machines
2006.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} N_{s_1} &=\frac{120f_1}{P} \\ &= \frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500\; \text{rpm}\\ s_1 &=\frac{N_{s_1}-N_{R_1}}{N_{s_1}} \\ &= \frac{1500-1440}{1500}=0.04\\ \text{as}\;\;\frac{V}{f} &=\text{Constant} \\ \frac{V_1}{f_1}&=\frac{V_2}{f_2} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; V_2&=V_1\left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right ) \\ &= 400 \times \frac{30}{50}=240V \end{aligned}[/latex] Torque developed in induction motor [latex]T=\frac{3}{\omega _s}\frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2 +{X'_2}^2} [/latex] In stable region, slip is very low, so  [latex]\frac{R'_2}{s} \gt \gt X'_2[/latex] So, T can be approximated as [latex]\begin{aligned} T &=\frac{3}{\omega _s}\frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2} \\ &=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{8V^2}{R'_2} \\ T&\propto \frac{sV^2}{f} \\ \frac{T_1}{T_2}&= \frac{s_1}{s_2}\left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 \times \frac{f_2}{f_1} \end{aligned} [/latex] as load torque is constant, [latex]T_1=T_2[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} s_2 &=s_1 \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 \times \frac{f_2}{f_1}\\ &= 0.04 \times \left ( \frac{400}{240} \right )^2 \times \left ( \frac{30}{50} \right )\\ &= 0.067\\ N_{s2} &=\frac{120f_2}{P} \\ &= \frac{120 \times 30}{4}=900 \; \text{rpm}\\ &\text {Rotor speed,}\\ N_{r2}&=N_{s2(1-s_2)} \\ &= 900(1-0.067)\\ &\approx 840 \; \text{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} N_{s_1} &=\frac{120f_1}{P} \\ &= \frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500\; \text{rpm}\\ s_1 &=\frac{N_{s_1}-N_{R_1}}{N_{s_1}} \\ &= \frac{1500-1440}{1500}=0.04\\ \text{as}\;\;\frac{V}{f} &=\text{Constant} \\ \frac{V_1}{f_1}&=\frac{V_2}{f_2} \\ \Rightarrow \;\; V_2&=V_1\left ( \frac{f_2}{f_1} \right ) \\ &= 400 \times \frac{30}{50}=240V \end{aligned}[/latex]

In stable region, slip is very low, so [latex]\frac{R'_2}{s} \gt \gt X'_2[/latex]
So, T can be approximated as
[latex]\begin{aligned} T &=\frac{3}{\omega _s}\frac{V^2R'_2/s}{(R'_2/s)^2} \\ &=\frac{3}{\omega _s} \frac{8V^2}{R'_2} \\ T&\propto \frac{sV^2}{f} \\ \frac{T_1}{T_2}&= \frac{s_1}{s_2}\left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 \times \frac{f_2}{f_1} \end{aligned} [/latex]
as load torque is constant, [latex]T_1=T_2[/latex]
[latex] \begin{aligned} s_2 &=s_1 \left ( \frac{V_1}{V_2} \right )^2 \times \frac{f_2}{f_1}\\ &= 0.04 \times \left ( \frac{400}{240} \right )^2 \times \left ( \frac{30}{50} \right )\\ &= 0.067\\ N_{s2} &=\frac{120f_2}{P} \\ &= \frac{120 \times 30}{4}=900 \; \text{rpm}\\ &\text {Rotor speed,}\\ N_{r2}&=N_{s2(1-s_2)} \\ &= 900(1-0.067)\\ &\approx 840 \; \text{rpm} \end{aligned}[/latex]

on a toroidal core. When it carries a current of 160 A on the primary, the ratio
and phase errors of the CT are found to be -0.5% and 30 minutes respectively.
If the number of secondary turns is reduced by 1 new ratio-error(%) and phaseerror(
min) will be respectively
2006.html: A 200/1 Current transformer (CT) is wound with 200 turns on the secondary on a toroidal core. When it carries a current of 160 A on the primary, the ratio and phase errors of the CT are found to be -0.5% and 30 minutes respectively. If the number of secondary turns is reduced by 1 new ratio-error(%) and phaseerror( min) will be respectively
2006.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Instrument Transformers
2006.explanation_text: Nominal ratio [latex]=k_n=\frac{200}{1}=200 [/latex] Primary current [latex]=I_P=160A [/latex] Actual ratio [latex]= R_1=n_1\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(i)[/latex] [latex] \% \text{Ratio error} [/latex]  [latex]=\frac{k_n - R_1}{R_1}\times 100[/latex] [latex] -0.5=\frac{200-R_1}{R_1} \times 100 [/latex] Actual ratio [latex]=R_1=201 [/latex] [latex]n_1=\text{turn ratio}=200 [/latex] [latex]R_1=200\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(ii)[/latex] when number of secondary is reduced by 1 [latex]\begin{aligned} N_s &= 199\\ n_2&=199 \\ R_2&=n_2\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right ) \\ &= 199\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(iii) \end{aligned} [/latex] Dividing equation (ii) and (iii), [latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{R_1}{R_2} &=\frac{200}{199} \\ \Rightarrow \;R_2 &= R_1 \times \left ( \frac{200}{199} \right )\\ &=201 \times \frac{200}{199}\approx 200 \\ \% \text{Ratio error} &=\frac{k_n-R_2}{R_2} \times 100\\ &= \frac{200-200}{200}\times 100=0 \end{aligned} [/latex] Phase angle error [latex]=\theta =\frac{180}{\pi}\left ( \frac{I_m}{I_P} \right ) [/latex] Reduction of one or two turns of the secondary winding, no doubt, reduces the ration error, but it has no effect on the phase angle error.
2006.explanation_html:
Nominal ratio [latex]=k_n=\frac{200}{1}=200 [/latex]
Primary current [latex]=I_P=160A [/latex]
Actual ratio [latex]= R_1=n_1\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(i)[/latex]
[latex] \% \text{Ratio error} [/latex] [latex]=\frac{k_n - R_1}{R_1}\times 100[/latex]
[latex] -0.5=\frac{200-R_1}{R_1} \times 100 [/latex]
Actual ratio [latex]=R_1=201 [/latex]
[latex]n_1=\text{turn ratio}=200 [/latex]
[latex]R_1=200\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
when number of secondary is reduced by 1
[latex]\begin{aligned} N_s &= 199\\ n_2&=199 \\ R_2&=n_2\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right ) \\ &= 199\left ( 1+\frac{I_e}{I_P} \right )\;\;...(iii) \end{aligned} [/latex]
Dividing equation (ii) and (iii),
[latex]\begin{aligned} \frac{R_1}{R_2} &=\frac{200}{199} \\ \Rightarrow \;R_2 &= R_1 \times \left ( \frac{200}{199} \right )\\ &=201 \times \frac{200}{199}\approx 200 \\ \% \text{Ratio error} &=\frac{k_n-R_2}{R_2} \times 100\\ &= \frac{200-200}{200}\times 100=0 \end{aligned} [/latex]
Phase angle error [latex]=\theta =\frac{180}{\pi}\left ( \frac{I_m}{I_P} \right ) [/latex]
Reduction of one or two turns of the secondary winding, no doubt, reduces the ration error, but it has no effect on the phase angle error.

2006.explanation_text: In double layer winding No. of coil = No. of slots =48 Each coil has 10 turns Total no. of turns [latex]=48 \times 10=480[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} T_{ph} &=\text{No. of turns/phase} \\ &= \frac{480}{3}=160 \end{aligned} [/latex] Slots/pole/phase [latex]=m=\frac{48}{4 \times 3}=4 [/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} \gamma &= \text{slot angle}\\ &=\frac{180 \times \text{poles}}{\text{slots}} \\ &= \frac{180 \times 4}{48}=15^{\circ}\\ &\text{Distribution factor,}\\ k_d&=\frac{\sin \frac{m\gamma }{2}}{m \sin \frac{\gamma }{2}} \\ &= \frac{\sin \left ( \frac{4 \times 15}{2} \right )}{2 \sin \left ( \frac{15}{2} \right )}\\ &= 0.957\\ & \text{Short-pitching angle,}\\ \alpha &=36^{\circ} \end{aligned} [/latex] For the [latex]n^{th}[/latex] harmonic, pitch factor, [latex]k_p=\cos \frac{n\alpha }{2}[/latex] pitch factor due to fundamental component [latex]\begin{aligned} k_p&=\cos \frac{\alpha }{2}=\cos 18^{\circ}=0.951 \\ &\text{Winding factor,} \\ k_w&=k_dk_p \\ &=0.957 \times 0.951=0.910 \\ &\text{Induced emf per phase,} \\ E_{ph}&= 4.44 k_w f T_{ph}\phi \\ &=4.44 \times 0.91 \times 50 \times 160 \times 0.025 \\ &\approx 808\\ \Rightarrow \;\; E_{line} &=\sqrt{3} E_{ph}=1400V \end{aligned}[/latex]

For the [latex]n^{th}[/latex] harmonic, pitch factor,
[latex]k_p=\cos \frac{n\alpha }{2}[/latex]
pitch factor due to fundamental component
[latex]\begin{aligned} k_p&=\cos \frac{\alpha }{2}=\cos 18^{\circ}=0.951 \\ &\text{Winding factor,} \\ k_w&=k_dk_p \\ &=0.957 \times 0.951=0.910 \\ &\text{Induced emf per phase,} \\ E_{ph}&= 4.44 k_w f T_{ph}\phi \\ &=4.44 \times 0.91 \times 50 \times 160 \times 0.025 \\ &\approx 808\\ \Rightarrow \;\; E_{line} &=\sqrt{3} E_{ph}=1400V \end{aligned}[/latex]

2006.explanation_text: Initially, main thyristor (m) and auxiliary thyristor (A) are off and capacitor is  assumed charged to voltage V with upper plate positive. When 'm' is turned on at t=0, source voltage V  is applied across load and load current [latex]I_0[/latex] begins to flow which is assumed to remain constant. With 'm' ON at t=0, anotheroscillatory circuit consisting of C, m, L and D is formed where the capacitor current is given by [latex]i_c=V\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \sin \omega _0 t=I_p \sin \omega _0 t[/latex] When, [latex]\omega _0 t=\pi, i_c=0[/latex] Between [latex]0 \\lt t \\lt \frac{\pi}{\omega _0}, i_{T1}=I_0+I_P \sin \omega _0 t[/latex] capacitor voltage charges from [latex]+V_s \; to \; -V_s[/latex] sinusoidally and the lower plate becomes positive. At [latex]\omega _0 t=\pi, i_c=0, i_{T1}=I_0 \text{ and }V_c=-V_s[/latex] At [latex]t_1[/latex], thyristor A is turned on and capacitor voltage V applies a reverse voltage across thyristor in and SCR 'm' is turned off. The load current is now carried by C and SCR A. So, minimum time for which SCR 'm' should be ON. [latex]\begin{aligned} T_{min}&=\frac{\pi}{\omega _0}=\pi\sqrt{LC} \\ &= \pi\sqrt{2 \times 10^{-3} \times 1 \times 10^{-6}}=140\mu s \end{aligned}[/latex]
2006.explanation_html:
Initially, main thyristor (m) and auxiliary thyristor (A) are off and capacitor is assumed charged to voltage V with upper plate positive. When 'm' is turned on at t=0, source voltage V is applied across load and load current [latex]I_0[/latex] begins to flow which is assumed to remain constant.
With 'm' ON at t=0, anotheroscillatory circuit consisting of C, m, L and D is formed where the capacitor current is given by
[latex]i_c=V\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} \sin \omega _0 t=I_p \sin \omega _0 t[/latex]

When, [latex]\omega _0 t=\pi, i_c=0[/latex]
Between [latex]0 \\lt t \\lt \frac{\pi}{\omega _0}, i_{T1}=I_0+I_P \sin \omega _0 t[/latex] capacitor voltage charges from [latex]+V_s \; to \; -V_s[/latex] sinusoidally and the lower plate becomes positive.
At [latex]\omega _0 t=\pi, i_c=0, i_{T1}=I_0 \text{ and }V_c=-V_s[/latex]
At [latex]t_1[/latex], thyristor A is turned on and capacitor voltage V applies a reverse voltage across thyristor in and SCR 'm' is turned off. The load current is now carried by C and SCR A.
So, minimum time for which SCR 'm' should be ON.
[latex]\begin{aligned} T_{min}&=\frac{\pi}{\omega _0}=\pi\sqrt{LC} \\ &= \pi\sqrt{2 \times 10^{-3} \times 1 \times 10^{-6}}=140\mu s \end{aligned}[/latex]

2005.explanation_text: At f = 100Hz [latex]|V_R|=|V_L| [/latex] as R and L are series connected, current through R and L is same, so [latex]\begin{aligned}IR&=IX_L=I\omega L  \\ \Rightarrow \; R&=X_L=\omega L  \\ I&=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}}  \\ &=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+R^2}}=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{2}R}  \\ V_R&=u_{rms}=IR  \\ V_R&=\left ( \frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{2}R} \right ) \times R=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{2}}  \\ V_{in}&=\sqrt{2}u_{rms}\;\;...(i)  \\  f&=50 Hz  \\ X_l & \propto f \\ \text{So, }  X'_L&=X_L \times \frac{50}{100} \\ &=\frac{X_L}{2}=\frac{R}{2}  \\ I'&=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+(X'_L)^2}}  \\ &=\frac{V_{in}}{\sqrt{R^2+\left ( \frac{R}{2} \right )^2}}  \\ &=\frac{2V_{in}}{\sqrt{5}R}  \\ V'_R&=I'R \\ &=\left ( \frac{2V_{in}}{\sqrt{5}R} \right )R  \\ &=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}V_{in} \\  &\text{From equation (i), }\\ V'_R&=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \times (\sqrt{2}u_{rms}) \\  &=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{5}}u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{8}{5}}u_{rms}\end{aligned}[/latex]

2005.explanation_text: Using signal flow graph, Forward path gains [latex]P_{1}=\left ( -1 \right )\times \frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{-2}{s+2}[/latex]  and [latex]P_2=\frac{3}{s}\frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{6}{s(s+2)} [/latex] Individual loop, [latex]L_1=-1 \times \frac{3}{s}\times \frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{-6}{s(s+2)}[/latex] Loop touches forward paths, therefore, [latex]\Delta _1=1 \text{ and } \Delta _2=1 [/latex] [latex]D=1-L_1 =1+\frac{6}{s(s+2)}=\frac{s(s+2)+6}{s(s+2)} [/latex] Using Mason's gain formula, [latex] \frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{\Delta } =\frac{-\frac{2}{s+2}\times 1+\frac{6}{s(s+2)}\times 1}{\frac{s(s+2)+6}{s(s+2)}} [/latex] [latex]\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} [/latex] For unit step input, [latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} Y(s)&=R(s)\cdot \left ( \frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ) \\ Error&=E(s)=R(s)-Y(s) \\&=R(s)-R(s)\left (\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ) \\ &=R(s)\left [ 1-\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ]\\ E(s)&=\frac{1}{s}\left [ \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ] \end{aligned}[/latex] Steady state value of error, using final value theoram, [latex]\begin{aligned}e_{ss}&=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}sE(s) \\ &=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}s\left [ \frac{1}{s}\cdot \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ] \\ &=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ]=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
2005.explanation_html:
Using signal flow graph,



Forward path gains
[latex]P_{1}=\left ( -1 \right )\times \frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{-2}{s+2}[/latex] and
[latex]P_2=\frac{3}{s}\frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{6}{s(s+2)} [/latex]
Individual loop,
[latex]L_1=-1 \times \frac{3}{s}\times \frac{2}{s+2}=\frac{-6}{s(s+2)}[/latex]
Loop touches forward paths, therefore,
[latex]\Delta _1=1 \text{ and } \Delta _2=1 [/latex]
[latex]D=1-L_1 =1+\frac{6}{s(s+2)}=\frac{s(s+2)+6}{s(s+2)} [/latex]
Using Mason's gain formula,
[latex] \frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{P_1\Delta _1+P_2\Delta _2}{\Delta } =\frac{-\frac{2}{s+2}\times 1+\frac{6}{s(s+2)}\times 1}{\frac{s(s+2)+6}{s(s+2)}} [/latex]
[latex]\frac{Y(s)}{R(s)}=\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} [/latex]
For unit step input, [latex]R(s)=\frac{1}{s}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} Y(s)&=R(s)\cdot \left ( \frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ) \\ Error&=E(s)=R(s)-Y(s) \\&=R(s)-R(s)\left (\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ) \\ &=R(s)\left [ 1-\frac{6-2s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ]\\ E(s)&=\frac{1}{s}\left [ \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ] \end{aligned}[/latex]
Steady state value of error, using final value theoram,
[latex]\begin{aligned}e_{ss}&=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}sE(s) \\ &=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}s\left [ \frac{1}{s}\cdot \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ] \\ &=\lim_{s\rightarrow 0}\left [ \frac{s^2+4s}{s^2+2s+6} \right ]=0 \end{aligned}[/latex]

2005.text: For the matrix [latex]p=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2&2 \\ 0& -2 & 1\\ 0 &0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] one of the eigen values is equal to -2. Which of the following is an eigen vector ?
2005.html:
For the matrix
[latex]p=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2&2 \\ 0& -2 & 1\\ 0 &0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
one of the eigen values is equal to -2. Which of the following is an eigen vector ?
2005.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
2005.explanation_text:
Since matrix is triangular, the eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves namely [latex]\lambda =3, -2[/latex] and 1. Corresponding to eigen value [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] let us find the eigen vector [latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex] [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 3-\lambda & -2 & 2\\ 0 & -2-\lambda & 1\\ 0& 0 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Putting  [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] in above equation we get, [latex]\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0& 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] Which gives the equations, [latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\\ 3x_3&=0 \;\;...(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex] Since equation (ii) and (iii) are same we have [latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex]
Putting [latex]x_2=k[/latex], we get [latex]x_3=0, x_2=k[/latex] and [latex]5x_1-2k+2 \times 0=0[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;x_1=2/5 \;k[/latex] Eigen vectors are of the form [latex]\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2/5 k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} x_1:x_2:x_3&=2/5k:k:0\\ &=2/5:1:0\\ &=2:5:0 \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\;\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 5\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is an eigen vector of matrix p.
2005.explanation_html:
Since matrix is triangular, the eigen values are the diagonal elements themselves namely [latex]\lambda =3, -2[/latex] and 1.
Corresponding to eigen value [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] let us find the eigen vector
[latex][A-\lambda I]\hat{x}=0[/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 3-\lambda & -2 & 2\\ 0 & -2-\lambda & 1\\ 0& 0 & 1-\lambda \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Putting [latex]\lambda = -2[/latex] in above equation we get,
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} 5 & -2 & 2\\ 0 & 0 & 1\\ 0& 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
Which gives the equations,
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\\ 3x_3&=0 \;\;...(iii) \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since equation (ii) and (iii) are same we have
[latex]\begin{aligned} 5x_1-2x_2+2x_3&=0 \;\;...(i)\\ x_3 &=0 \;\;...(ii)\end{aligned}[/latex] Putting [latex]x_2=k[/latex], we get
[latex]x_3=0, x_2=k[/latex] and [latex]5x_1-2k+2 \times 0=0[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;x_1=2/5 \;k[/latex]
Eigen vectors are of the form
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2/5 k\\ k\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} x_1:x_2:x_3&=2/5k:k:0\\ &=2/5:1:0\\ &=2:5:0 \end{aligned}[/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\;\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2\\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix} 2\\ 5\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex] is an eigen vector of matrix p.

2005.text: If [latex]R=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0&-1 \\ 2& 1 & -1\\ 2&3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], then top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex] is
2005.html: If [latex]R=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0&-1 \\ 2& 1 & -1\\ 2&3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}[/latex], then top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex] is
2005.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Linear Algebra
2005.explanation_text:
[latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2& 3& 2 \end{bmatrix} \\ R^{-1} &=\frac{adj(R)}{|R|}=\frac{[\text{cofator }(R)]^T}{|R|} \\ |R|&=\begin{vmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2 & 3& 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=1(2+3)-0(4+2)-1(6-2) \\ &= 5-4=1 \end{aligned}[/latex] Since we need only the top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex], we need to find only first column of (R) which after transpose will become first row of Adj(A). [latex]\begin{aligned}
 \text{co-factor of (1,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix}
1 &-1 \\ 
3 & 2
\end{vmatrix} \\ 
 &=2+3=5 \\ 
 \text{co-factor of (2,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix}
0 &-1 \\ 
1 & -1
\end{vmatrix}=-3 \\ 
\text{co-factor of (3,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix}
0 &-1 \\ 
1 & -1
\end{vmatrix}=+1\\
\therefore \;\text{ co-factor of (A)} &= \begin{bmatrix}
5 &-  &- \\ 
-3 & - &- \\ 
 1& - & -
\end{bmatrix}\\ 
 Adj(A)&= [cof.(A)]^T\\ 
 &= \begin{bmatrix}
5 &-3  &1 \\ 
- & - &- \\ 
 -& - & -
\end{bmatrix}\\ 
\text{Dividing by |R|} &= 1 \text{ gives}\\ 
 R^{-1}&= \begin{bmatrix}
5 &-3  &1 \\ 
- & - &- \\ 
 -& - & -
\end{bmatrix}\\ 
 \therefore \;\; \text{top row of }R^{-1}&=[5\;-3\;1]
\end{aligned}[/latex]
2005.explanation_html:
[latex]\begin{aligned} R &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2& 3& 2 \end{bmatrix} \\ R^{-1} &=\frac{adj(R)}{|R|}=\frac{[\text{cofator }(R)]^T}{|R|} \\ |R|&=\begin{vmatrix} 1 &0 &-1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\\ 2 & 3& 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=1(2+3)-0(4+2)-1(6-2) \\ &= 5-4=1 \end{aligned}[/latex]
Since we need only the top row of [latex]R^{-1}[/latex], we need to find only first column of (R) which after transpose will become first row of Adj(A).
[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{co-factor of (1,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 1 &-1 \\ 3 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \\ &=2+3=5 \\ \text{co-factor of (2,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 0 &-1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}=-3 \\ \text{co-factor of (3,1)}&=+\begin{vmatrix} 0 &-1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}=+1\\ \therefore \;\text{ co-factor of (A)} &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &- &- \\ -3 & - &- \\ 1& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ Adj(A)&= [cof.(A)]^T\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &-3 &1 \\ - & - &- \\ -& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ \text{Dividing by |R|} &= 1 \text{ gives}\\ R^{-1}&= \begin{bmatrix} 5 &-3 &1 \\ - & - &- \\ -& - & - \end{bmatrix}\\ \therefore \;\; \text{top row of }R^{-1}&=[5\;-3\;1] \end{aligned}[/latex]

2005.text:
A fair coin is tossed three times in succession. If the first toss produces a head,
then the probability of getting exactly two heads in three tosses is
2005.html: A fair coin is tossed three times in succession. If the first toss produces a head, then the probability of getting exactly two heads in three tosses is
2005.subject: Engineering Mathematics - Probability and Statistics
2005.explanation_text: [latex]\begin{aligned} P(A|B)&=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ \therefore \; &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses }| \text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{P(\text{3 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})}{P(\text{ first toss is head})}\\ &=P(\text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\\ &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})\\ &=P(HHT)+P(HTH)\\ &=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} =\frac{1}{4}\\ \therefore \;&\text{ Required probability}=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2005.explanation_html: [latex]\begin{aligned} P(A|B)&=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\\ \therefore \; &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses }| \text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{P(\text{3 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})}{P(\text{ first toss is head})}\\ &=P(\text{ first toss is head})\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\\ &P(\text{2 heads in 3 tosses and first toss is head})\\ &=P(HHT)+P(HTH)\\ &=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} =\frac{1}{4}\\ \therefore \;&\text{ Required probability}=\frac{1/4}{1/2}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Now, } f''(x) &= e^{-x}(2-2x)+(2x-x^2)(-e^{-x})\\ &= e^{-x}(2-2x-(2x-x^2))\\ &= e^{-x}(x^2-4x+2)\\ At\;x=0& \\ f''(0)&= e^{-0}(0-0+2)=2 \end{aligned}[/latex] Since [latex]f''(x)=2[/latex] is [latex]\gt 0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] we have a minima. Now at [latex]x=2[/latex] [latex] \begin{aligned} f''(2)&=e^{-2}(2^2-4\times 2 +2) \\ &=-2e^{-2} \lt 0 \end{aligned} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; At \;\; x=2[/latex] we have a maxima.

[latex] x =0 [/latex] or [latex] x=2[/latex] are the stationary points.

Since [latex]f''(x)=2[/latex] is [latex]\gt 0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] we have a minima.

2005.explanation_text: Torque in induction motor is given by, [latex]\begin{aligned} T &=\frac{3}{\omega _s}(I'_2)\frac{R'_2}{s} \\ & \text{Full load torque}\\ T_{fl} &= \frac{2}{\omega _s}(I'_{2fl})^2 \frac{R'_2}{S_{fl}}\\ & \text{At starting,}\\ s &= 1\\ & \text{Starting torque}\\ T_{st}&= \frac{3}{\omega _s}(I'_{2st})^2 R'_2\\ \frac{T_{st}}{T_{fl}}&=\left ( \frac{I'_{2st}}{I'_{2fl}} \right )^2 S_{fl} \\ &= 6^2 \times 0.04=1.44 \end{aligned}[/latex]

Determine the correctness or otherwise of the following assertion[A] and the reason[R].

Assertion [A] : Under V/f control of induction motor, the maximum value of the developed torque remains constant over a wide range of speed in the subsynchronous region.

Reason [R] : The magnetic flux is maintained almost constant at the rated value by keeping the ration V/f constant over the considered speed range.
2005.subject: Electrical Machines - Three Phase Induction Machines
2005.explanation_text: The resultant air-gap flux per pole is given by [latex]\phi _r=\frac{1}{4.44k_{\omega _1}N_{pn_1}}\left ( \frac{V}{f} \right ) [/latex] [latex]\phi _r\propto \left ( \frac{V}{f} \right )[/latex] Therefore, in order to avoid saturation in stator and rotor cores which would cause sharp increase in magnetization current, the flux [latex]f_p[/latex] must be kept constant. To achieve this, [latex]\frac{V}{f}[/latex] ratio must be kept constant. Let, [latex]V_0=[/latex] Nominal voltage [latex]f_0=[/latex] Nominal frequency [latex]X'_{20}=[/latex] Nominal rotor standstill reactance reffered to stator then at any frequency f. Then at any frequency f, [latex]\begin{aligned} V &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right ) V_0\\ X'_2 &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right ) X'_{20} \\ \omega _s &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )\omega _{20} \\ T_{max}&= \frac{3}{\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )\omega _{s_0}}\left [ \frac{0.5 \left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )^2 V_0^2}{\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )X'_{20}} \right ]\\ &= \frac{3}{\omega _{s_0}}\frac{0.5V_0^2}{X'_{20}}\\ &=\text{constant, independent of f} \end{aligned}[/latex]
2005.explanation_html:
The resultant air-gap flux per pole is given by
[latex]\phi _r=\frac{1}{4.44k_{\omega _1}N_{pn_1}}\left ( \frac{V}{f} \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\phi _r\propto \left ( \frac{V}{f} \right )[/latex]
Therefore, in order to avoid saturation in stator and rotor cores which would cause sharp increase in magnetization current, the flux [latex]f_p[/latex] must be kept constant. To achieve this, [latex]\frac{V}{f}[/latex] ratio must be kept constant.
Let, [latex]V_0=[/latex] Nominal voltage
[latex]f_0=[/latex] Nominal frequency
[latex]X'_{20}=[/latex] Nominal rotor standstill reactance reffered to stator then at any frequency f.
Then at any frequency f,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right ) V_0\\ X'_2 &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right ) X'_{20} \\ \omega _s &=\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )\omega _{20} \\ T_{max}&= \frac{3}{\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )\omega _{s_0}}\left [ \frac{0.5 \left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )^2 V_0^2}{\left ( \frac{f}{f_0} \right )X'_{20}} \right ]\\ &= \frac{3}{\omega _{s_0}}\frac{0.5V_0^2}{X'_{20}}\\ &=\text{constant, independent of f} \end{aligned}[/latex]

Where [latex]P_1 \; and \; P_2[/latex] are the generation in MW of [latex]G_{1}[/latex] and [latex]G_{2}[/latex], respectively. For most economic generation to meet 300 MW of load [latex]P_1 \; and \; P_2[/latex] respectively, are
2005.subject: Power Systems - Economic Power Generation and Load Dispatch
2005.explanation_text: Fuel-cost curve of generating station 1 [latex]F_1=a+bP_1+cP_1^2 \; \text{Rs/hour}[/latex] Fuel-cost curve of generating station 2 [latex]F_2=a+bP_2+2cP_2^2 \; \text{Rs/hour}[/latex] The slope of the fuel-cost curve i.e. [latex]\frac{dF_i}{dP_i}[/latex] is called the incremental fuel-cost (IC) and is expressed in Rs/MWh. [latex]\begin{aligned} IC_1&=\frac{dF_1}{dP_1}=b+2cP_1 \\ IC_2&=\frac{dF_2}{dP_2}=b42cP_2 \end{aligned}[/latex] For economic generation [latex]\begin{aligned} IC_1&=IC_2\\ b+2cP_1&=b+4cP_2\\ P_1&=2P_2\;\;...(i) \\ &\text{To meet 300 MW of load}\\ P_1+P_2&=300\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{Solving eq. (i) and (ii)}\\ P_1&=200MW\\ P_2&=100MW \end{aligned}[/latex]
2005.explanation_html:
Fuel-cost curve of generating station 1
[latex]F_1=a+bP_1+cP_1^2 \; \text{Rs/hour}[/latex]
Fuel-cost curve of generating station 2
[latex]F_2=a+bP_2+2cP_2^2 \; \text{Rs/hour}[/latex]
The slope of the fuel-cost curve i.e. [latex]\frac{dF_i}{dP_i}[/latex] is called the incremental fuel-cost (IC) and is expressed in Rs/MWh.
[latex]\begin{aligned} IC_1&=\frac{dF_1}{dP_1}=b+2cP_1 \\ IC_2&=\frac{dF_2}{dP_2}=b42cP_2 \end{aligned}[/latex]
For economic generation
[latex]\begin{aligned} IC_1&=IC_2\\ b+2cP_1&=b+4cP_2\\ P_1&=2P_2\;\;...(i) \\ &\text{To meet 300 MW of load}\\ P_1+P_2&=300\;\;...(ii)\\ &\text{Solving eq. (i) and (ii)}\\ P_1&=200MW\\ P_2&=100MW \end{aligned}[/latex]

2005.text:
The figure shows the voltage across a power semiconductor device and the
current through the device during a switching transitions. Is the transition a
turn ON transition or a turn OFF transition ? What is the energy lost during
the transition ?
2005.html: The figure shows the voltage across a power semiconductor device and the current through the device during a switching transitions. Is the transition a turn ON transition or a turn OFF transition ? What is the energy lost during the transition ?
2005.subject: Power Electronics - Power Semiconductor Devices and Commutation Techniques
2005.explanation_text: During interval [latex]t_2[/latex], voltage starts decreasing and becomes zero and current starts increasing and becomes constant (I), so transition is turn on. During [latex]t_1[/latex] interval: Power loss [latex]=vi[/latex] [latex]E_1=\text{Energy loss}=\int vi\; dt=V\int i\; dt[/latex] V is constant during this period v=V [latex]\int i\; dt[/latex] represents area under i-t curve [latex]\int i\; dt=\frac{1}{2} \times I \times t_1[/latex] [latex]E_1=V\int i\; dt=\frac{1}{2} V I t_1\;\;...(i)[/latex] During [latex]t_2[/latex] interval: Power loss = vi [latex]E_2=\text{Energy loss}=\int vi\; dt=I\int v\; dt[/latex] i is constant during this period i=I [latex]\int v\; dt[/latex] represents area under v-t curve [latex]\int v\; dt=\frac{1}{2} VIt_2[/latex] [latex]E_2=I\int v\; dt=\frac{1}{2} V I t_2\;\;...(ii)[/latex] Total energy lost during the transition [latex]E=E_1+E_2[/latex] [latex]E=\frac{1}{2}VIt_1+\frac{1}{2}VIt_2[/latex]
2005.explanation_html:
During interval [latex]t_2[/latex], voltage starts decreasing and becomes zero and current starts increasing and becomes constant (I), so transition is turn on.

During [latex]t_1[/latex] interval:
Power loss [latex]=vi[/latex]
[latex]E_1=\text{Energy loss}=\int vi\; dt=V\int i\; dt[/latex]
V is constant during this period v=V
[latex]\int i\; dt[/latex] represents area under i-t curve
[latex]\int i\; dt=\frac{1}{2} \times I \times t_1[/latex]
[latex]E_1=V\int i\; dt=\frac{1}{2} V I t_1\;\;...(i)[/latex]
During [latex]t_2[/latex] interval:
Power loss = vi
[latex]E_2=\text{Energy loss}=\int vi\; dt=I\int v\; dt[/latex]
i is constant during this period i=I
[latex]\int v\; dt[/latex] represents area under v-t curve
[latex]\int v\; dt=\frac{1}{2} VIt_2[/latex]
[latex]E_2=I\int v\; dt=\frac{1}{2} V I t_2\;\;...(ii)[/latex]
Total energy lost during the transition
[latex]E=E_1+E_2[/latex]
[latex]E=\frac{1}{2}VIt_1+\frac{1}{2}VIt_2[/latex]

2004.explanation_text:
Impedance of the load [latex]=Z_L=R+j\omega L=|Z|\angle \theta _L[/latex] where, [latex]\theta _L=\tan ^{-1}\left ( \frac{\omega L}{R} \right )[/latex] Voltages of [latex]3-\phi[/latex] supply [latex]\begin{aligned}
 V_a&=V_m \sin \omega t \\ 
 V_b&=V_m \sin (\omega t-120^{\circ}) \\ 
V_c &=V_m \sin (\omega t+120^{\circ}) \\ 
 I_a&=\frac{V_a}{Z_L}=\frac{V_m \sin \omega t}{|Z|\angle \theta _L} \\ 
 &= I_M \sin (\omega t-\theta _L)\\ 
\text{where, } I_m&=\frac{V_m}{|Z|}\\
 \text{Similarly,}&\\
I_b&=I_m \sin (\omega t-120-\theta _L)\\
I_c&=I_m \sin (\omega t+120-\theta _L)\\
& \text{Instantaneous power}\\
&=P=V_aI_a+V_bI_b+V_cI_c\\
P&=V_mI_m[\sin \omega t\cdot \sin (\omega t-\theta _L)\\

&=\frac{V_mI_m}{2}[(\cos \theta _L -\cos(2\omega t-\theta _L) ) \\
&+(\cos \theta _L -\cos(2\omega t-240-\theta _L) )\\
&+(\cos \theta _L -\cos(2\omega t+240-\theta _L) )]\\
P&=\frac{3V_mI_m}{2}\cos \phi = \text{constant}
\end{aligned}[/latex]

2004.text:
The armature resistance of a permanent magnet dc motor is 0.8 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. At no load,
the motor draws 1.5 A from a supply voltage of 25 V and runs at 1500 rpm.
The efficiency of the motor while it is operating on load at 1500 rpm drawing a
current of 3.5 A from the same source will be
2004.html: The armature resistance of a permanent magnet dc motor is 0.8 [latex]\Omega[/latex]. At no load, the motor draws 1.5 A from a supply voltage of 25 V and runs at 1500 rpm. The efficiency of the motor while it is operating on load at 1500 rpm drawing a current of 3.5 A from the same source will be
2004.subject: Electrical Machines - DC Machines
2004.explanation_text: At no load, [latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a0} &= 1.5A\\ \text{supply voltage} &= V_t=250V\\ &\text{Back emf at no load,}\\ E_{b0}&=V_t-I_{a0}R_a \\ &= 25-1.5 \times 0.8\\ &= 23.8V\\ &\text{Power developed by the motor} \\ P_0=E_{b0}I_{a0} &=23.8 \times 1.5 \\ &= 35.7 W \end{aligned}[/latex] As the motor is working at no load, power [latex]P_0[/latex] supplies no load losses. When the motor is on load, [latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a1} &= 3.5A\\ E_{a1}&=V_t-I_{a1}R_a \\ &= 25-3.5 \times 0.8\\ &= 22.2V\\ &\text{Power developed by the motor} \\ P_1=E_{a1}I_{a1} &=22.2 \times 3.5 \\ &= 77.7 W\\ &\text{Power available at shaft}\\ P_s&=P_1-\text{no load losses}\\ &=77.7-35.7=42W\\ \text{Efficiency}&=\frac{\text{Output power}}{input power} \times 100\\ &=\frac{P_0}{V_tT_{a_1}} \times 100\\ &=\frac{42}{25 \times 3.5} \times 100=48\% \end{aligned}[/latex]
2004.explanation_html:
At no load,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a0} &= 1.5A\\ \text{supply voltage} &= V_t=250V\\ &\text{Back emf at no load,}\\ E_{b0}&=V_t-I_{a0}R_a \\ &= 25-1.5 \times 0.8\\ &= 23.8V\\ &\text{Power developed by the motor} \\ P_0=E_{b0}I_{a0} &=23.8 \times 1.5 \\ &= 35.7 W \end{aligned}[/latex]
As the motor is working at no load, power [latex]P_0[/latex] supplies no load losses.
When the motor is on load,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_{a1} &= 3.5A\\ E_{a1}&=V_t-I_{a1}R_a \\ &= 25-3.5 \times 0.8\\ &= 22.2V\\ &\text{Power developed by the motor} \\ P_1=E_{a1}I_{a1} &=22.2 \times 3.5 \\ &= 77.7 W\\ &\text{Power available at shaft}\\ P_s&=P_1-\text{no load losses}\\ &=77.7-35.7=42W\\ \text{Efficiency}&=\frac{\text{Output power}}{input power} \times 100\\ &=\frac{P_0}{V_tT_{a_1}} \times 100\\ &=\frac{42}{25 \times 3.5} \times 100=48\% \end{aligned}[/latex]

Neglect losses and assume constant power input to the shaft. The accelerating torque in the generator in MNm at the time of fault will be

2004.explanation_text: Before fault, mechanical input [latex](P_m)=[/latex] Electrical output [latex](P_e)[/latex] [latex]= 500 \times 0.8=400MW[/latex] After fault, mechanical input remains same [latex]=P_m=400MW[/latex] While electrical output reduces by 40 %. So, electrical output at the time of fault [latex]=(P_e)_f= 0.6 \times 400 =240MW[/latex] Accelerating power [latex]=P_a=P_m-(P_e)_f[/latex] [latex]=400-240=160MW[/latex] Synchronous speed (in rpm) [latex]N_s=\frac{120 \times f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500\; rpm[/latex] Synchronous speed (in rad/sec) [latex]\omega _s=\frac{2 \pi N_s}{60}=\frac{2 \pi \times 1500}{60}=157 \text{ rad/sec}[/latex] [latex]P_a=T_a\omega[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;T_a\omega[/latex] (accelerating Torque) [latex]=\frac{P_a}{\omega _s}=\frac{160}{157}MN-m=1.018MN-m[/latex]

Before fault, mechanical input [latex](P_m)=[/latex] Electrical output [latex](P_e)[/latex]
[latex]= 500 \times 0.8=400MW[/latex]
After fault, mechanical input remains same [latex]=P_m=400MW[/latex]
While electrical output reduces by 40 %.
So, electrical output at the time of fault
[latex]=(P_e)_f= 0.6 \times 400 =240MW[/latex]
Accelerating power [latex]=P_a=P_m-(P_e)_f[/latex]
[latex]=400-240=160MW[/latex]
Synchronous speed (in rpm)
[latex]N_s=\frac{120 \times f}{P}=\frac{120 \times 50}{4}=1500\; rpm[/latex]
Synchronous speed (in rad/sec)
[latex]\omega _s=\frac{2 \pi N_s}{60}=\frac{2 \pi \times 1500}{60}=157 \text{ rad/sec}[/latex]
[latex]P_a=T_a\omega[/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;T_a\omega[/latex] (accelerating Torque)
[latex]=\frac{P_a}{\omega _s}=\frac{160}{157}MN-m=1.018MN-m[/latex]

2004.text:
The block diagram of a closed loop control system is given by figure. The values
of K and P such that the system has a damping ratio of 0.7 and an undamped
natural frequency [latex]\omega _n[/latex] of 5 rad/sec, are respectively equal to
2004.html: The block diagram of a closed loop control system is given by figure. The values of K and P such that the system has a damping ratio of 0.7 and an undamped natural frequency [latex]\omega _n[/latex] of 5 rad/sec, are respectively equal to
2004.subject: Control Systems - Time Response Analysis
2004.explanation_text: [latex]G(s)=\frac{k}{s(s+2)} [/latex] and [latex] H(s)=1+sP[/latex] Closed-loop transfer function, [latex]T(s)=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)} [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{\frac{k}{s(s+2)}}{1+\frac{k}{s(s+2)}\cdot (1+sP)} [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{k}{s(s+2)+k(1+sP)} [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \; T(s)=\frac{k}{s^2+(2+kP)s+k} [/latex] So, characteristic equation [latex]= s^2+(2+kP)s+k[/latex] Comparing with standard equation  [latex]=s^2+2\xi \omega _n s+\omega _n^2[/latex] [latex]\;\;\; k=\omega _n^2=5^2=25 [/latex] (where [latex]\omega _n = [/latex] undamped natueal frequency) [latex]\;\; 2\xi \omega _n=2+kP[/latex] [latex] \Rightarrow \; 2 \times 0.7 \times 5=2+25P [/latex] (where [latex]\xi =[/latex] damping ratio) [latex]P=0.2[/latex]
2004.explanation_html:
[latex]G(s)=\frac{k}{s(s+2)} [/latex] and [latex] H(s)=1+sP[/latex]
Closed-loop transfer function,
[latex]T(s)=\frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)H(s)} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{\frac{k}{s(s+2)}}{1+\frac{k}{s(s+2)}\cdot (1+sP)} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{k}{s(s+2)+k(1+sP)} [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \; T(s)=\frac{k}{s^2+(2+kP)s+k} [/latex]
So, characteristic equation [latex]= s^2+(2+kP)s+k[/latex]
Comparing with standard equation [latex]=s^2+2\xi \omega _n s+\omega _n^2[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; k=\omega _n^2=5^2=25 [/latex]
(where [latex]\omega _n = [/latex] undamped natueal frequency)
[latex]\;\; 2\xi \omega _n=2+kP[/latex]
[latex] \Rightarrow \; 2 \times 0.7 \times 5=2+25P [/latex]
(where [latex]\xi =[/latex] damping ratio)
[latex]P=0.2[/latex]

2004.explanation_text: T=Torque on the coil=NBAI where, [latex]\begin{aligned} N &= \text{Number of turns}=100 \\ B&= \text{Flux density}\\ &= 200mT =200 \times 10^{-3}T\\ A &= \text{Area of the coil} \\ &= \text{length} \times \text{depth}\\ &= (10 \times 10^{-3}) \times (20 \times 10^{-3})\\ &= 200 \times 10^{-6} m^2\\ I&= \text{Current through the coil}\\ &= 50mA=50 \times 10^{-3}\\ T&= NBAI \\ &=100 \times (200 \times10^{-3}) \times (200 \times 10^{-6}) \\ &= \times (50 \times 10^{-3})\\ &=2 \times 10^{-4} N-m=200\mu N-m \end{aligned}[/latex]

A single-phase load is connected between R and Y terminals of a 415 V,
symmetrical, 3-phase, 4-wire system with phase sequence RYB. A wattmeter is
connected in the system as shown in figure. The power factor of the load is 0.8
lagging. The wattmeter will read
2004.html: A single-phase load is connected between R and Y terminals of a 415 V, symmetrical, 3-phase, 4-wire system with phase sequence RYB. A wattmeter is connected in the system as shown in figure. The power factor of the load is 0.8 lagging. The wattmeter will read
2004.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Measurement of Energy and Power
2004.explanation_text: Line of line voltage [latex]=450V[/latex] Phase to neutral voltage [latex]=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}}V[/latex] Taking [latex]V_R[/latex] as the reference [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{RN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle 0^{\circ}V\\ V_{yN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -120^{\circ}V\\ \text{and } V_{BN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -240^{\circ}\\ V_{Ry} &=V_{RN}-V_{yN} \\ &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle 0^{\circ}- \frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -120^{\circ} \\ &=415 \angle 30^{\circ}V \\ & \text{Load current,}\\ I_L&= \frac{V_{Ry}}{Z}=\frac{415 \angle 30^{\circ}}{100 \angle 36.87^{\circ}}\\ &= 4.15 \angle -6.87^{\circ} A \end{aligned}[/latex] Current through current coil, [latex]I_{cc}=I_L=4.15\angle -6.87^{\circ}A [/latex] Voltage across pressure coil [latex]V_{BN}=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}}\angle -240^{\circ}V [/latex] Phase angle between [latex]V_{BN} \text{and} I_{cc}[/latex] [latex] \phi =-240^{\circ}-(-6.87^{\circ})=233.13^{\circ} [/latex] Wattmeter reading [latex]=|V_{BN}||I_L| \cos \phi[/latex] [latex]\;\;\; =\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \times 4.15 \times \cos 233.13[/latex] [latex]\;\;\; \approx -597W[/latex]
2004.explanation_html:
Line of line voltage [latex]=450V[/latex]
Phase to neutral voltage [latex]=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}}V[/latex]
Taking [latex]V_R[/latex] as the reference
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{RN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle 0^{\circ}V\\ V_{yN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -120^{\circ}V\\ \text{and } V_{BN} &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -240^{\circ}\\ V_{Ry} &=V_{RN}-V_{yN} \\ &=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle 0^{\circ}- \frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \angle -120^{\circ} \\ &=415 \angle 30^{\circ}V \\ & \text{Load current,}\\ I_L&= \frac{V_{Ry}}{Z}=\frac{415 \angle 30^{\circ}}{100 \angle 36.87^{\circ}}\\ &= 4.15 \angle -6.87^{\circ} A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Current through current coil,
[latex]I_{cc}=I_L=4.15\angle -6.87^{\circ}A [/latex]
Voltage across pressure coil
[latex]V_{BN}=\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}}\angle -240^{\circ}V [/latex]
Phase angle between [latex]V_{BN} \text{and} I_{cc}[/latex]
[latex] \phi =-240^{\circ}-(-6.87^{\circ})=233.13^{\circ} [/latex]
Wattmeter reading [latex]=|V_{BN}||I_L| \cos \phi[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; =\frac{415}{\sqrt{3}} \times 4.15 \times \cos 233.13[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; \approx -597W[/latex]

2004.explanation_text: Rated current during on state [latex]I=10[/latex] ON state resistance [latex]R_{ON}=0.15\Omega [/latex] MOSFET is ON [latex]\begin{aligned} 0\lt \omega t \lt \pi \\ 0 \lt t \lt \pi/ \omega \end{aligned}[/latex] MOSFET is OFF [latex]\begin{aligned} \pi \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi \\ \pi/ \omega \lt t \lt 2\pi/ \omega \end{aligned}[/latex] Average ON state Loss, [latex]\begin{aligned} P_{avg}&=\frac{1}{2 \pi/\omega }\int_{0}^{\pi/\omega }I^2R_{ON}dt\\ &=\frac{\omega }{2 \pi}\times I^2 R_{ON}\times \frac{\pi}{\omega }\\ &=\frac{I^2R_{ON}}{2}=\frac{10^2 \times 0.15}{2}=7.5W \end{aligned}[/latex]

Rated current during on state [latex]I=10[/latex]
ON state resistance [latex]R_{ON}=0.15\Omega [/latex]
MOSFET is ON
[latex]\begin{aligned} 0\lt \omega t \lt \pi \\ 0 \lt t \lt \pi/ \omega \end{aligned}[/latex]
MOSFET is OFF
[latex]\begin{aligned} \pi \lt \omega t \lt 2\pi \\ \pi/ \omega \lt t \lt 2\pi/ \omega \end{aligned}[/latex]

2004.text:
Figure shows a chopper operating from a 100 V dc input. The duty ratio of the
main switch S is 0.8. The load is sufficiently inductive so that the load current
is ripple free. The average current through the diode D under steady state is
2004.html: Figure shows a chopper operating from a 100 V dc input. The duty ratio of the main switch S is 0.8. The load is sufficiently inductive so that the load current is ripple free. The average current through the diode D under steady state is
2004.subject: Power Electronics - Choppers
2004.explanation_text: During the period [latex]T_{ON}[/latex] chopper on and load voltage is equal to source voltage ([latex]V_{s}=100V[/latex]). During the interval [latex]T_{OFF}[/latex], chopper is off, load current ([latex]I_{0}[/latex]) flows through the diode as result load voltage is zero during [latex]T_{OFF}[/latex]. Average load voltage, [latex]\begin{aligned} V_0 &=\frac{T_{ON}}{T_{ON}+T_{OFF}}V_s=\alpha V_s \\ &=\frac{0.8}{100}=80V \end{aligned}[/latex] Average load current, [latex]I_0=\frac{V_0}{R}=\frac{80}{10}=8A[/latex] As load current is ripple free, so average diode current, [latex]\begin{aligned} I_D&=\frac{1}{T}\int_{T_{ON}}^{T}I_0dt \\ &= \frac{(T-T_{ON})}{T}I_0\\ &=(1-\alpha )I_0\\ &=(1-0.8)\times 8=1.6A \end{aligned}[/latex]
2004.explanation_html:
During the period [latex]T_{ON}[/latex] chopper on and load voltage is equal to source voltage ([latex]V_{s}=100V[/latex]). During the interval [latex]T_{OFF}[/latex], chopper is off, load current ([latex]I_{0}[/latex]) flows through the diode as result load voltage is zero during [latex]T_{OFF}[/latex].
Average load voltage,
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_0 &=\frac{T_{ON}}{T_{ON}+T_{OFF}}V_s=\alpha V_s \\ &=\frac{0.8}{100}=80V \end{aligned}[/latex]
Average load current,
[latex]I_0=\frac{V_0}{R}=\frac{80}{10}=8A[/latex]
As load current is ripple free, so average diode current,
[latex]\begin{aligned} I_D&=\frac{1}{T}\int_{T_{ON}}^{T}I_0dt \\ &= \frac{(T-T_{ON})}{T}I_0\\ &=(1-\alpha )I_0\\ &=(1-0.8)\times 8=1.6A \end{aligned}[/latex]

2003.explanation_text: For [latex]0 \lt t \lt 2s[/latex] current varies linearly with time and given as [latex]i(t)=3t[/latex] and for [latex]2s \lt t \lt 4s[/latex] current is constant, [latex]i(t)=6A[/latex]. The energy absorbed by the inductor (Resistance neglected) in the first 2 sec, [latex]E_L=\int_{0}^{T}Li\frac{di}{dt}=E_{L_1}+E_{L_2} [/latex] [latex]E_{L_1}=\int_{0}^{2}Li \left (\frac{di}{dt} \right )dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2} 2 \times 3t \times 3\; dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=18\int_{0}^{2}t\; dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=18 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^2}{2} \end{matrix}\right|^2_0 [/latex] [latex]\;\;= 18 \times \left [ \frac{4}{2}-0 \right ]=36J [/latex] The energy absorbed by the inductor in ([latex]2\rightarrow 4[/latex]) second [latex]E_{L_2}=\int_{2}^{4}Li\left ( \frac{di}{dt}dt \right ) [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{2}{4}2 \times 6 \times 0 \;dt=0 J[/latex] A pure indictor does not dissipate enegy but only stores it. Due to resistance, some energy is dissipated in the resistor. Therefore, total energy stored in the inductor and the energy dissipated in the resistor. The energy dissipated by the resistance in 4 sec. [latex]E_R=\int_{0}^{T}i^2 R\;dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2}(3t)^2 \times 1 \;dt+\int_{2}^{4}6^2 \times 1 \; dt[/latex] [latex] \;\;=9\int_{0}^{2}t^2\;dt +36\int_{2}^{4}1 \; dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=9 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^3}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_0^2+36t|_2^4[/latex] [latex] \;\;=9 \times \left ( \frac{8}{3} \right )+36 \times 2 [/latex] [latex]\;\;=24+72=96J[/latex] The total energy absorbed by the inductor in 4 sec [latex] =96 J +36 J =132 J[/latex]
2003.explanation_html:
For [latex]0 \lt t \lt 2s[/latex] current varies linearly with time and given as [latex]i(t)=3t[/latex] and for [latex]2s \lt t \lt 4s[/latex] current is constant, [latex]i(t)=6A[/latex].
The energy absorbed by the inductor (Resistance neglected) in the first 2 sec,
[latex]E_L=\int_{0}^{T}Li\frac{di}{dt}=E_{L_1}+E_{L_2} [/latex]
[latex]E_{L_1}=\int_{0}^{2}Li \left (\frac{di}{dt} \right )dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2} 2 \times 3t \times 3\; dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=18\int_{0}^{2}t\; dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=18 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^2}{2} \end{matrix}\right|^2_0 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;= 18 \times \left [ \frac{4}{2}-0 \right ]=36J [/latex]
The energy absorbed by the inductor in ([latex]2\rightarrow 4[/latex]) second
[latex]E_{L_2}=\int_{2}^{4}Li\left ( \frac{di}{dt}dt \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{2}{4}2 \times 6 \times 0 \;dt=0 J[/latex]
A pure indictor does not dissipate enegy but only stores it. Due to resistance, some energy is dissipated in the resistor. Therefore, total energy stored in the inductor and the energy dissipated in the resistor.
The energy dissipated by the resistance in 4 sec.
[latex]E_R=\int_{0}^{T}i^2 R\;dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2}(3t)^2 \times 1 \;dt+\int_{2}^{4}6^2 \times 1 \; dt[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=9\int_{0}^{2}t^2\;dt +36\int_{2}^{4}1 \; dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=9 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^3}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_0^2+36t|_2^4[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=9 \times \left ( \frac{8}{3} \right )+36 \times 2 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=24+72=96J[/latex]
The total energy absorbed by the inductor in 4 sec
[latex] =96 J +36 J =132 J[/latex]

2003.explanation_text: By KCL, [latex]I_P+I_Q+I_C+I_L=0[/latex] [latex] 2+2+I_C+I_L=0 [/latex] But,  [latex]I_C=C \times \frac{dv}{dt} [/latex] [latex]\;\; =1 \times \frac{d}{dt}(4 \sin 2t) [/latex] [latex]\;\;=(8 \cos 2t) [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; I_L=-(2+1+8 \cos 2t) [/latex] [latex]\;\; \;\;=-3-8 \cos 2t [/latex] [latex]\therefore \;\; V_L=L\left ( \frac{di}{dt} \right )[/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=2 \times 2 \times 8 \sin 2t [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=32 \sin 2t[/latex] NOTE: KCL is based on the law of conservation of charges.

By KCL,
[latex]I_P+I_Q+I_C+I_L=0[/latex]
[latex] 2+2+I_C+I_L=0 [/latex]
But, [latex]I_C=C \times \frac{dv}{dt} [/latex]
[latex]\;\; =1 \times \frac{d}{dt}(4 \sin 2t) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=(8 \cos 2t) [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \;\; I_L=-(2+1+8 \cos 2t) [/latex]

[latex]\therefore \;\; V_L=L\left ( \frac{di}{dt} \right )[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=2 \times 2 \times 8 \sin 2t [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=32 \sin 2t[/latex]
NOTE: KCL is based on the law of conservation of charges.

2003.text:
A stand alone engine driven synchronous generator is feeding a partly inductive
load. A capacitor is now connected across the load to completely nullify the
inductive current. For this operating condition.
2003.html: A stand alone engine driven synchronous generator is feeding a partly inductive load. A capacitor is now connected across the load to completely nullify the inductive current. For this operating condition.
2003.subject: Electrical Machines - Synchronous Machines
2003.explanation_text: Assuming resistance of the armature to be zero. In first case, the generator is feeding a partly inductive load. It means that generator is supplying lagging power. The generator supplies a lagging power factor current when it is overexcited which is represented by [latex]E_{f_1}[/latex]. In second case, a capacitor is connected across the load to completely nullifythe inductive current. It means the generator supplies no reactive power and unity power factor current is drawn from the generator. The excitation ([latex]E_{f_2}[/latex]) corresponding to unity power factor is known as normal excitation. From the phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \gt E_{f_2}[/latex] and as the field current approximately directly proportional to excitation, the field current has to be reduced. From phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \sin \delta _1=E_{f_2} \sin \delta _2=\text{constant}[/latex] [latex]P_e(\text{ power delivered})=\frac{E_fV_t}{X_s}\sin \delta[/latex] Fuel input remains unaltered.

In second case, a capacitor is connected across the load to completely nullifythe inductive current. It means the generator supplies no reactive power and unity power factor current is drawn from the generator. The excitation ([latex]E_{f_2}[/latex]) corresponding to unity power factor is known as normal excitation.

2003.explanation_text: Power input at no-load [latex](P_0)[/latex] provided losses only as the shaft output is zero. These losses comprise [latex]P_i[/latex](Iron/core loss) and [latex]P_{wf}[/latex](windage and friction loss). As the voltage is reduced below the rated value, the core-loss decreases as the square of voltage. Since the slip does not increase significantly, the windage and friction loss remains almost constant. 2003.explanation_text: Field Control: Fieldcontrol provides constant power drive. Since the speed is inversely proportional to flux/pole [latex]\left ( \omega \propto \frac{1}{\phi } \right )[/latex] field can not be increased; It can only be weakended. So this control is suitable for speed control above base speed as torque is directly proportional to flux/pole [latex](T \propto \alpha )[/latex] for a given armature current. So, this control provides torque below base torque. Armature Control: It provides constant-torque drive. By keeping th field current at maximumvalue full load torque can be obtained at full load armature current at all speeds. This control provides speed below base speed.

2003.explanation_text: As the transformer is [latex]\Delta -Y[/latex] connected, it means line-to-line voltage on primary side induces line to neutral for phase voltage on secondary side due to transformer. [latex]\begin{aligned} \text{Turn ratio} &=\frac{N_1}{N_2}=a \\ &= \frac{11kV}{415\sqrt{3}}=\frac{11\sqrt{3}}{415} \times 10^3\\ V_{AB}&=aV_a \\ V_{BC}&=aV_b\\ V_{AC}&=aV_c \end{aligned} [/latex] When [latex]S_2[/latex] is closed, B and C are at same potential. So,  [latex]V_{BC}=V_B-V_C=0[/latex] Applying KVL in, [latex]\Delta[/latex] connection [latex] \begin{aligned} V_{AB}+V_{BC}+V_{AC} &=0 \\ \Rightarrow \;\; V_{AC} &=-V_{AB} \\ V_{AB}&= 11 \times 10^3 \angle 0^{\circ}\\ V_{AC}&= - 11 \times 10^3 \angle 0^{\circ}\\ &= 11 \times 10^3 \angle 180^{\circ} \end{aligned} [/latex] Voltage across terminals a and c, [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{ac} &=V_a-V_c \\ &=\frac{V_{AB}}{a}-\frac{V_{AC}}{a} \\ &= \frac{1}{a}[V_{AB}-V_{AC}]\\ &=\frac{415}{11\sqrt{3} \times 10^3} \\ &[11 \times 10^3 \angle 0^{\circ} - 11 \times 10^3 \angle 180^{\circ} ]\\ &=\frac{415}{11\sqrt{3} \times 10^3} [11 \times 10^3 \times 2]\\ &\approx 480 V \end{aligned}[/latex]

2003.explanation_text: In DC machine, field is provided at stator and armature is provided at rotor. Because of commutator and slip-rings, AC rotor winding current is converted inot dc. IN synchronous machine, it is difficult to provide armature in rotor because of many factor like insulation no of slip rings, rating of slip rings, high rating of armature. Therefore, armature is provided in stator and field in rotor Induction machines are singlyfed machine i.e. they draw excitation from the same supply. So no external field supply is required.

2003.subject: Electrical Machines - Synchronous Machines
2003.explanation_text: Inside a magnetic material, flux flows from S-pole to N-pole. Outside a magnetic material flux flow from N-pole to S-pole When stator winding is excited, it produces flux. If ABC is assumed to N-pole flux will link rotor. As we know, flux flows from N-pole to S-pole externally, abc from S-pole. Inside rotor, flux flows from surface abc to cda So, surface cda forms N-poles. To identify direction of torque The torque acts in a direction to reduce [latex]\delta[/latex] i.e. to align the two fields. So, torque on the rotor acrs in counter-clockwise direction to reduce [latex]\delta[/latex].

Back emf, [latex]E=v-I(R_a+R_{se}) [/latex]
[latex]\text{If},\;\;(R_a+R_{se})=R [/latex]
[latex]\text{them,}\;\; E=V-IR [/latex]
[latex]\text{where,}\;\; E=K_n \phi N [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;\;\;N=\frac{V-IR}{K_n \phi }[/latex]
In series motor, [latex]\phi \propto I [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] At constant power load
[latex]E \times I=T \times w=const [/latex]
[latex]\text{where,} \;\; T=K_a\phi I=K_a I^2[/latex]
If '[latex]w_n[/latex]' decrease by (1/4) of its rated value, then torque will increase 4 times to maintain power contant.
[latex] \therefore \;\; T\propto I^2 [/latex]
[latex]\therefore[/latex] current increase 2 times so that supply voltage approximately brought down to 0.5pu.

2003.html:
The following equation defines a separately excited dc motor in the form of a differential equation
[latex]\frac{d^{2}\omega }{dt}+\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}+\frac{K^{2}}{LJ}\omega =\frac{K}{LJ}V_{a}[/latex]
The above equation may be organized in the state-space form as follows
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \frac{d^2\omega}{dt^2}\\ \frac{d\omega}{dt} \end{bmatrix}=P\begin{bmatrix} \\frac{d\omega}{dt}\\ \omega \end{bmatrix}+QV_a[/latex]
where the P matrix is given by
2003.subject: Control Systems - State Variable Analysis
2003.explanation_text: Let, [latex]x_1=\frac{d\omega }{dt}[/latex] and [latex]x_2=\omega [/latex] [latex]\;\;\; \dot{x_2}=x_1 [/latex] [latex]\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}+\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}+\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega =\frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex] [latex]\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}=-\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}-\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega + \frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \dot{x_1}=-\frac{B}{J}x_1-\frac{k^2}{LJ}x_2+\frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex] [latex]\;\;\dot{x_2}=x_1 [/latex] [latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_1}\\ \dot{x_2} \end{bmatrix}=P\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}+QV_a [/latex] where, [latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -\frac{B}{J} & -\frac{k^2}{LJ}\\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] and [latex]Q=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{k}{LJ}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]
2003.explanation_html:
Let, [latex]x_1=\frac{d\omega }{dt}[/latex] and [latex]x_2=\omega [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\; \dot{x_2}=x_1 [/latex]
[latex]\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}+\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}+\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega =\frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex]
[latex]\frac{d^2\omega }{dt^2}=-\frac{B}{J}\frac{d\omega }{dt}-\frac{k^2}{LJ}\omega + \frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; \dot{x_1}=-\frac{B}{J}x_1-\frac{k^2}{LJ}x_2+\frac{k}{LJ}V_a [/latex]
[latex]\;\;\dot{x_2}=x_1 [/latex]
[latex]\begin{bmatrix} \dot{x_1}\\ \dot{x_2} \end{bmatrix}=P\begin{bmatrix} x_1\\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}+QV_a [/latex]
where,
[latex]P=\begin{bmatrix} -\frac{B}{J} & -\frac{k^2}{LJ}\\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} [/latex] and [latex]Q=\begin{bmatrix} \frac{k}{LJ}\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}[/latex]

[latex]=20\log k-20 \log (1.25)^{1/2} [/latex]
[latex]=20 \log k-0.97 dB [/latex]
From the plot
magnitude[latex]=20 \log k[/latex]
[latex] \therefore[/latex] error in dB gain = 0.97 dB
[latex] \angle G(j\omega )|_{\omega =0.5a}[/latex]
[latex]=-tan^{-1}\left ( \frac{0.5a}{a} \right )[/latex]
[latex]=26.56^{\circ}[/latex]
Since it is [latex]-45^{\circ}/dec [/latex] (-ve slope) at [latex]\omega =0.5a[/latex] phase [latex]=-22.5^{\circ}[/latex]

The block diagram of a control system is shown in figure. The transfer function
G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) of the system is
2003.html: The block diagram of a control system is shown in figure. The transfer function G(s) = Y(s)/U(s) of the system is
2003.subject: Control Systems - Mathematical Models of Physical Systems
2003.explanation_text: Integrator are represented as 1/s in s-domain As per the block diagram, the corresponding signal flow graph is drawn One forward path [latex]P_{1}\, =\, 2/s^{2}[/latex] The individual loops are, [latex]\; \; \; L_{1}\, =\, -\frac{3}{s},\: L_{2}\, =\, -\frac{12}{s} and L_{3}\, =\, -\frac{18}{s^{2}}[/latex] [latex]L_{1}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] are non-touching loops [latex]\; \; \; L_{1}L_{2}\, =\, \frac{36}{s^{2}}[/latex] The loops touches the forward path [latex]\Delta _{1}=1[/latex] The graph determinant is [latex]\; \; \; \Delta \, =\, 1-\left ( L_{1}+L_{2}+L_{3} \right )+L_{1}L_{2}[/latex] [latex]\; \; \; \; =1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}[/latex] Applying mason's gain formula, [latex]\; \; \; G\left ( s \right )=\frac{Y\left ( s \right )}{U\left ( s \right )}=\frac{P_{1}\Delta _{1}}{\Delta }[/latex] [latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{2/s^{2}}{1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}}[/latex] [latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{2}{s^{2}+15s+54}=\frac{2}{\left ( s+9 \right )\left ( s+6 \right )}[/latex] [latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{1}{27\left ( 1+\frac{s}{9} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{6} \right )}[/latex]
2003.explanation_html:
Integrator are represented as 1/s in s-domain



As per the block diagram, the corresponding signal flow graph is drawn



One forward path [latex]P_{1}\, =\, 2/s^{2}[/latex]
The individual loops are,
[latex]\; \; \; L_{1}\, =\, -\frac{3}{s},\: L_{2}\, =\, -\frac{12}{s} and L_{3}\, =\, -\frac{18}{s^{2}}[/latex]
[latex]L_{1}[/latex] and [latex]L_{2}[/latex] are non-touching loops
[latex]\; \; \; L_{1}L_{2}\, =\, \frac{36}{s^{2}}[/latex]
The loops touches the forward path [latex]\Delta _{1}=1[/latex]
The graph determinant is
[latex]\; \; \; \Delta \, =\, 1-\left ( L_{1}+L_{2}+L_{3} \right )+L_{1}L_{2}[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}[/latex]
Applying mason's gain formula,
[latex]\; \; \; G\left ( s \right )=\frac{Y\left ( s \right )}{U\left ( s \right )}=\frac{P_{1}\Delta _{1}}{\Delta }[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{2/s^{2}}{1+\frac{3}{s}+\frac{12}{s}+\frac{18}{s^{2}}+\frac{36}{s^{2}}}[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{2}{s^{2}+15s+54}=\frac{2}{\left ( s+9 \right )\left ( s+6 \right )}[/latex]
[latex]\; \; \; \; =\frac{1}{27\left ( 1+\frac{s}{9} \right )\left ( 1+\frac{s}{6} \right )}[/latex]

2003.text:
A wattmeter reads 400 W when its current coil is connected in the R-phase
and its pressure coil is connected between this phase and the neutral of a
symmetrical 3-phase system supplying a balanced star connected 0.8 p.f.
inductive load. This phase sequence is RYB. What will be the reading of this
wattmeter if its pressure coil alone is reconnected between the B and Y phases,
all other connections remaining as before ?
2003.html: A wattmeter reads 400 W when its current coil is connected in the R-phase and its pressure coil is connected between this phase and the neutral of a symmetrical 3-phase system supplying a balanced star connected 0.8 p.f. inductive load. This phase sequence is RYB. What will be the reading of this wattmeter if its pressure coil alone is reconnected between the B and Y phases, all other connections remaining as before ?
2003.subject: Electrical and Electronic Measurements - Measurement of Energy and Power
2003.explanation_text: Taking [latex]V_R[/latex] as the reference and assuming phase to neutral voltage [latex]=V[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} V_R &=V\angle 0^{\circ} \\ V_Y &= V\angle -120^{\circ}\\ and \;\; V_B &=V\angle -240^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex] [latex]\begin{aligned} V_RI_R \cos \phi &=400 W \\ VI_R \times 0.8&= 400W\\ VI_R&=400\;\;...(i) \\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex] [p.f. =0.8 lag, inductive load] [latex]\begin{aligned} V_{YB} &=V_{YB}-V_B \\ &= V\angle -120^{\circ}- V \angle -240^{\circ}\\ &=\sqrt{3}V\angle -90^{\circ} V\\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ}A \end{aligned}[/latex] Angle between [latex]V_{YB}[/latex] and [latex]I_{R}[/latex] [latex]\theta =-90^{\circ}-(-36.87^{\circ})=53.13^{\circ}[/latex] As pressure coil connected between Y and B phase. Reading of wattmeter[latex]=V_{YB}I_R\cos \theta[/latex] From equation (i) [latex]=\sqrt{3}V \times I_R \times \cos (-53.13) =\sqrt{3}\times 500 \times 0.6=519.6W[/latex]
2003.explanation_html:
Taking [latex]V_R[/latex] as the reference and assuming phase to neutral voltage [latex]=V[/latex]
[latex]\begin{aligned} V_R &=V\angle 0^{\circ} \\ V_Y &= V\angle -120^{\circ}\\ and \;\; V_B &=V\angle -240^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]

[latex]\begin{aligned} V_RI_R \cos \phi &=400 W \\ VI_R \times 0.8&= 400W\\ VI_R&=400\;\;...(i) \\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ} \end{aligned}[/latex]
[p.f. =0.8 lag, inductive load]

[latex]\begin{aligned} V_{YB} &=V_{YB}-V_B \\ &= V\angle -120^{\circ}- V \angle -240^{\circ}\\ &=\sqrt{3}V\angle -90^{\circ} V\\ I_R&=I_R\angle -36.87^{\circ}A \end{aligned}[/latex]
Angle between [latex]V_{YB}[/latex] and [latex]I_{R}[/latex]
[latex]\theta =-90^{\circ}-(-36.87^{\circ})=53.13^{\circ}[/latex]
As pressure coil connected between Y and B phase.
Reading of wattmeter[latex]=V_{YB}I_R\cos \theta[/latex]
From equation (i)
[latex]=\sqrt{3}V \times I_R \times \cos (-53.13) =\sqrt{3}\times 500 \times 0.6=519.6W[/latex]

2003.html: The inductance of a certain moving-iron ammeter is expressed as L = [latex]10+30 -\frac{\theta ^{2}}{4} \; \mu H[/latex], where [latex]\theta[/latex] is the deflection in radians from the zero position. 2003.explanation_text: Deflection torque in moving-iron ammeter, [latex]T_d=\frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta }[/latex] Inductance,   [latex]L=\left ( 10+3\theta -\frac{\theta ^2}{4} \right )\mu H [/latex] Rate of change of inductance with deflection [latex]\frac{dL}{d\theta }=\frac{d}{d\theta }\left ( 10+3\theta -\frac{\theta ^2}{4} \right ) [/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=\left ( 3- \frac{\theta }{2}\right )\mu H/rad [/latex] Current , [latex]I=5A [/latex] Deflecting torque, [latex]\begin{aligned} T_d &=\frac{1}{2}I^2\frac{dL}{d\theta } \\ T_d &= \frac{1}{2} \times 5^2 \times \left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right ) \times 10^{-6}\\ &= \frac{25}{2}\left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right )\times 10^{-6} Nm \end{aligned} [/latex] Controlling torque [latex]T_c=k\theta =25 \times 10^{-6}\theta [/latex] At equilibrium, [latex]\begin{aligned} T_c &= T_d\\ 25 \times 10^{-6}\theta &= \frac{25}{2}\left ( 3-\frac{\theta }{2} \right )\times 10^{-6} \\ \frac{5\theta }{2} &= 3\\ \theta &= 1.2 \text{rad} \end{aligned}[/latex]

2002.text:
A first order, low pass filter is given with R=50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and C=[latex]5\mu F[/latex]. What is the
frequency at which the gain of the voltage transfer function of the filter is 0.25?
2002.html: A first order, low pass filter is given with R=50 [latex]\Omega[/latex] and C=[latex]5\mu F[/latex]. What is the frequency at which the gain of the voltage transfer function of the filter is 0.25?
2002.subject: Electric Circuits - Magnetically Coupled Circuits, Network Topology and Filters
2002.explanation_text: [latex]T.F.=\frac{V_o}{V_i}=\frac{\frac{1}{j\omega C}}{R+\frac{1}{j\omega C}}[/latex] [latex]\;\;\;=\frac{1}{1+j\omega CR} [/latex] [latex]\therefore \; \; |Gain|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega CR)^2}} [/latex] [latex]\;\;0.25=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 50)^2}} [/latex] On solving, [latex]\omega =15.49 \times 10^3 r/s [/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow \;\; f=\frac{15.49}{2 \pi}=2.46 kHz[/latex]
2002.explanation_html:
[latex]T.F.=\frac{V_o}{V_i}=\frac{\frac{1}{j\omega C}}{R+\frac{1}{j\omega C}}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;\;=\frac{1}{1+j\omega CR} [/latex]
[latex]\therefore \; \; |Gain|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega CR)^2}} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;0.25=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega \times 5 \times 10^{-6} \times 50)^2}} [/latex]
On solving,
[latex]\omega =15.49 \times 10^3 r/s [/latex]
[latex]\Rightarrow \;\; f=\frac{15.49}{2 \pi}=2.46 kHz[/latex]

2002.explanation_text: [latex]\omega _0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}[/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{\sqrt{100 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{-6}}}=10^5 r/s [/latex] [latex]\Delta \omega =\frac{R}{L}=\frac{50}{100 \times 10^{-6}}[/latex] [latex]\;\;=50 \times 10^4 r/s [/latex] [latex]\omega _{lower}=\left [ \sqrt{\omega _0^2+\left ( \frac{\Delta \omega }{2} \right )^2}- \frac{\Delta \omega }{2}\right ] [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\left [ \sqrt{(10^5)^2+\left ( \frac{5 \times 10^5}{2} \right )^2}-\frac{5 \times 10^5}{2} \right ] [/latex] [latex]\;\;=10^5\left [ \sqrt{1+6.25}-2.5 \right ] [/latex] [latex]\;\;=0.193 \times 10^5 r/s [/latex] Hence, [latex] f_{lower}=\frac{\omega _{lower}}{2 \pi}[/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{0.193 \times 10^5}{2 \pi} [/latex] [latex]\;\;=3065 Hz\approx 3.055kHz[/latex]
2002.explanation_html:
[latex]\omega _0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{1}{\sqrt{100 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{-6}}}=10^5 r/s [/latex]
[latex]\Delta \omega =\frac{R}{L}=\frac{50}{100 \times 10^{-6}}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=50 \times 10^4 r/s [/latex]
[latex]\omega _{lower}=\left [ \sqrt{\omega _0^2+\left ( \frac{\Delta \omega }{2} \right )^2}- \frac{\Delta \omega }{2}\right ] [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\left [ \sqrt{(10^5)^2+\left ( \frac{5 \times 10^5}{2} \right )^2}-\frac{5 \times 10^5}{2} \right ] [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=10^5\left [ \sqrt{1+6.25}-2.5 \right ] [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=0.193 \times 10^5 r/s [/latex]
Hence, [latex] f_{lower}=\frac{\omega _{lower}}{2 \pi}[/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{0.193 \times 10^5}{2 \pi} [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=3065 Hz\approx 3.055kHz[/latex]
